options_html: Increase the degree of multiprogramming, since the CPU is idle.
Suspend one of the processes, freeing its frames for the others.
Increase the page size of every process.
Replace the page tables with inverted page tables.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The decision rule distinguishes two cases by disk utilisation. Low CPU with a low disk load means the system needs more work, so raise the degree of multiprogramming. Low CPU with a saturated paging disk means the system is thrashing, so reduce the number of resident processes.

Step by step.

  1. Disk at 97% says the bottleneck is paging, not a shortage of ready work.
  2. Adding a process would take frames from the ones already starved and raise the fault rate further.
  3. Suspending a process returns its frames, letting the survivors reach their working sets.
  4. Hence (B) is the correct action.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is exactly the feedback loop that causes thrashing.
  • (C) changes granularity without adding frames and can increase internal fragmentation.
  • (D) reduces table size, not the frame deficit.

Common misconception. Reading “CPU idle” as “add work”. That inference is valid only when the disk is also idle.

Takeaway. CPU low + disk low → add processes. CPU low + disk high → remove processes.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Which of the following statements about page-fault-frequency (PFF) control and working-set control are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about page-fault-frequency (PFF) control and working-set control are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Under PFF control, a process whose fault rate exceeds the upper bound is given additional frames.
Under PFF control, a process whose fault rate falls below the lower bound may have frames taken away.
If a process needs more frames and none are free, the system may suspend another process or swap one out.
Both schemes require the operating system to know each process's future reference string.
options_html: Under PFF control, a process whose fault rate exceeds the upper bound is given additional frames.
Under PFF control, a process whose fault rate falls below the lower bound may have frames taken away.
If a process needs more frames and none are free, the system may suspend another process or swap one out.
Both schemes require the operating system to know each process's future reference string.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Both schemes measure demand and allocate frames to match it. PFF watches the fault rate directly and keeps it inside a band; the working-set model computes WSSi from the last Δ references and allocates that many frames.

Step by step.

  1. PFF: rate above the upper bound means the process needs more frames, so (A) is true.
  2. PFF: rate below the lower bound means it holds more than it needs, so frames may be reclaimed — (B) is true.
  3. Frames are finite; when the demand cannot be met, the system reduces the degree of multiprogramming — (C) is true.
  4. Both use recent history, never the future, so (D) is false.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (D) describes OPT-style replacement, which needs the future and cannot be implemented online. PFF and working-set control are both online.

Common misconception. Assuming PFF only ever adds frames. It is a two-sided controller: the lower bound exists precisely so that frames can be reclaimed and shared.

Takeaway. PFF: a band on the fault rate. Working set: a window on the references. Both allocate frames from history.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question:
A process references the pages 2, 6, 1, 2, 4, 2, 6, 1, 2, 3. Using the working-set model with window Δ = 5, how many pages are in the working set at time t = 10, that is, after the tenth reference?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
A process references the pages 2, 6, 1, 2, 4, 2, 6, 1, 2, 3. Using the working-set model with window Δ = 5, how many pages are in the working set at time t = 10, that is, after the tenth reference?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The working set at time t is the set of distinct pages referenced in the window of the last Δ references, counting the current one. Repeated references add nothing to a set.

Step by step.

  1. Take the last five references, positions 6 to 10: 2, 6, 1, 2, 3.
  2. Form the set: {2, 6, 1, 3}.
  3. Page 2 appears twice but is counted once.
  4. |W(10)| = 4, so the process needs four frames to hold its working set.

Answer: 4.

Common misconception. Reporting 5 because the window is five references wide, or sliding the window one position too far and including 4. The window always ends at the current reference.

Takeaway. Working-set size = number of distinct pages in the window, which is at most Δ and usually less.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Let p be the page-fault rate, ma the memory access time and s the page-fault service time. Which expression gives the effective access time of a demand-paged system?
questions.question_html: Let p be the page-fault rate, ma the memory access time and s the page-fault service time. Which expression gives the effective access time of a demand-paged system?
options: (1 − p) × ma + p × s
ma + p × s
p × ma + (1 − p) × s
options_html: (1 − p) × ma + p × s
ma + p × s
p × ma + (1 − p) × s
questions.solution_html:
Concept. A reference falls into exactly two cases. With probability (1 − p) the page is resident and the reference costs one memory access ma; with probability p the page is absent and the reference costs the whole fault service time s, which already includes the access that is replayed after the page arrives. The effective access time is the probability-weighted average of the two.

Step by step.

  1. Case 1, page present: cost ma, probability (1 − p).
  2. Case 2, page fault: cost s, probability p.
  3. Average the two costs: EAT = (1 − p)·ma + p·s.
  4. Because s is three to six orders of magnitude larger than ma, the second term dominates as soon as p rises above about 10⁻⁵.

Answer: Option (A) — EAT = (1 − p)·ma + p·s.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) charges every reference the full access and the fault term, so the fault cost is paid even when no fault occurs.
  • (C) swaps the weights, making a fault the common case and a hit the rare one.
  • (D) has no basis in the two-case model and blows up as p approaches 1.

Common misconception. Writing ma + p·s by treating the fault as a surcharge added on top of a guaranteed access. The access and the fault are alternatives for the same reference, so they must be weighted, not added.

Takeaway. Two cases, two weights: EAT = (1 − p)·ma + p·s.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question:
In one run of a program, 250,000 memory references cause 750 page faults. Express the page-fault rate as faults per 10,000 references.
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
In one run of a program, 250,000 memory references cause 750 page faults. Express the page-fault rate as faults per 10,000 references.
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The page-fault rate is a ratio of faults to references, so it is converted between denominators by scaling: divide the fault count by the reference count to get faults per reference, then multiply by the new denominator.

Step by step.

  1. Faults per reference = 750 / 250,000 = 0.003.
  2. Multiply by 10,000: 0.003 × 10,000 = 30.
  3. Equivalently, 250,000 references is 25 blocks of 10,000, and 750 / 25 = 30 faults per block.

Answer: 30 faults per 10,000 references (a rate of 3 × 10⁻³ per reference).

Common misconception. Reporting 750 or 0.003 and forgetting the requested denominator. A rate is meaningless without its base, and a fault rate of 3 × 10⁻³ would already cost thousands of nanoseconds per reference in effective access time.

Takeaway. faults/references × new denominator; here 750/250,000 × 10,000 = 30.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Three frames currently hold pages 7, 2 and 9. The most recent reference to each was page 7 at time 3, page 9 at time 5 and page 2 at time 8. A fault now occurs and LRU replacement is used. Which page is evicted?
questions.question_html: Three frames currently hold pages 7, 2 and 9. The most recent reference to each was page 7 at time 3, page 9 at time 5 and page 2 at time 8. A fault now occurs and LRU replacement is used. Which page is evicted?
options: Page 7
Page 2
Page 9
It cannot be decided from this information
options_html: Page 7
Page 2
Page 9
It cannot be decided from this information
questions.solution_html:
Concept. LRU evicts the page whose most recent reference is earliest in time — the least recently used page, not the least frequently used and not the one loaded first.

Step by step.

  1. Order the three pages by their last reference: page 7 at time 3, page 9 at time 5, page 2 at time 8.
  2. The earliest of these is page 7.
  3. So page 7 is the least recently used and is the victim.

Answer: Option (A) — page 7 is evicted.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) page 2 was used at time 8, the most recent reference of the three, so it is the last page LRU would choose.
  • (C) page 9 was used at time 5, after page 7, so it survives this fault.
  • (D) the recency order is fully determined by the three timestamps, so the victim is decidable.

Common misconception. Confusing LRU with FIFO. FIFO would evict the page that has been resident longest, which is a different question from which page was used least recently.

Takeaway. LRU = smallest last-use timestamp wins the eviction.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: For a stack algorithm, the set of pages resident in memory with n frames is always ______ the set resident with n + 1 frames, for the same reference prefix.
questions.question_html: For a stack algorithm, the set of pages resident in memory with n frames is always ______ the set resident with n + 1 frames, for the same reference prefix.
options: a subset of
a superset of
disjoint from
exactly equal to
options_html: a subset of
a superset of
disjoint from
exactly equal to
questions.solution_html:
Concept. A stack algorithm orders pages by recency at every instant, independently of how many frames it has. With n + 1 frames it therefore holds the n + 1 most recent pages, and with n frames the n most recent pages — and the second list is a prefix of the first.

Step by step.

  1. LRU and OPT both keep the pages ranked by a criterion that does not depend on the frame count: recency for LRU, next-use distance for OPT.
  2. With n frames the algorithm holds the top n pages of that ranking; with n + 1 frames it holds the top n + 1.
  3. The top n pages are contained in the top n + 1 pages, so M(n) ⊆ M(n + 1).
  4. This inclusion property is exactly what rules out Belady's anomaly for these algorithms.

Answer: Option (A) — a subset, which is the inclusion property.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) the extra frame can only add a page, never remove one.
  • (C) the two sets overlap in at least the n pages of the smaller set.
  • (D) they differ whenever the extra frame holds a page the smaller set lacks, which is the normal case.

Common misconception. Reading the inclusion property as a statement about FIFO. FIFO's victim choice depends on load order, not on a frame-count-independent ranking, so its page sets need not nest — which is precisely why it can fault more with more frames.

Takeaway. Stack algorithm ⇒ M(n) ⊆ M(n + 1) ⇒ fault count monotone in frames.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: A process keeps the same reference string, but its working-set window Δ is increased from 5 to 10 references. What can be said about its working set at any fixed time t?
questions.question_html: A process keeps the same reference string, but its working-set window Δ is increased from 5 to 10 references. What can be said about its working set at any fixed time t?
options: It can only stay the same size or grow.
It can only stay the same size or shrink.
It is unchanged, because Δ is a window and not a frame count.
It exactly doubles.
options_html: It can only stay the same size or grow.
It can only stay the same size or shrink.
It is unchanged, because Δ is a window and not a frame count.
It exactly doubles.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The working set at time t with window Δ is the set of distinct pages referenced in the Δ most recent references. Enlarging Δ enlarges the interval being scanned, so it can only add pages, never remove them.

Step by step.

  1. The Δ = 5 window is the last five references; the Δ = 10 window is the last ten.
  2. The last five references are contained in the last ten, so the set of distinct pages of the shorter window is a subset of that of the longer one.
  3. Therefore |W(5, t)| ≤ |W(10, t)| for every t.
  4. The growth is not proportional: repeats inside the extra five references contribute no new pages, so the set often stays the same size.

Answer: Option (A) — it can only stay the same or grow.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the containment: the wider window cannot lose a page the narrower one already saw.
  • (C) ignores that Δ defines the interval, so changing it changes the set.
  • (D) the set counts distinct pages, and the extra references may all be repeats.

Common misconception. Assuming the working-set size is proportional to Δ. It is bounded by Δ but typically much smaller, because locality means a few pages are reused many times.

Takeaway. Larger Δ ⇒ weakly larger working set, never smaller.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question:
A process references the pages 2, 3, 2, 1, 5, 2, 4, 5, 3, 2, 5, 2 and is given 3 frames, all initially empty. Under FIFO replacement, how many page faults occur?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
A process references the pages 2, 3, 2, 1, 5, 2, 4, 5, 3, 2, 5, 2 and is given 3 frames, all initially empty. Under FIFO replacement, how many page faults occur?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Concept. FIFO evicts the page that has been in memory longest. A fault occurs exactly when the referenced page is not one of the resident pages; the first three distinct pages therefore always fault, since the frames start empty.

Step by step. Trace the frames, oldest first.

  1. 2 → fault, frames [2].
  2. 3 → fault, frames [2, 3].
  3. 2 → hit.
  4. 1 → fault, frames [2, 3, 1].
  5. 5 → fault, evict 2 (loaded first), frames [3, 1, 5].
  6. 2 → fault, evict 3, frames [1, 5, 2].
  7. 4 → fault, evict 1, frames [5, 2, 4].
  8. 5 → hit.
  9. 3 → fault, evict 5, frames [2, 4, 3].
  10. 2 → hit.
  11. 5 → fault, evict 2, frames [4, 3, 5].
  12. 2 → fault, evict 4, frames [3, 5, 2].

Counting. Faults at references 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 11, 12 — nine faults in twelve references; hits at 3, 8 and 10.

Answer: 9 page faults.

Common misconception. Evicting the page used longest ago instead of the page loaded longest ago. On this string LRU also gives 9, so the slip hides here; on longer strings the two policies diverge sharply.

Takeaway. Keep the FIFO queue in load order and pop the head on every fault once all frames are full.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Which of the following statements about demand paging are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about demand paging are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A page fault can be raised by an instruction fetch, not only by a data reference.
A page fault means that the page has never been in memory before.
Copy-on-write lets a parent and a child share pages read-only until one of them writes.
The number of frames given to a process affects its page-fault rate.
options_html: A page fault can be raised by an instruction fetch, not only by a data reference.
A page fault means that the page has never been in memory before.
Copy-on-write lets a parent and a child share pages read-only until one of them writes.
The number of frames given to a process affects its page-fault rate.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Demand paging resolves every reference through the valid–invalid bit of the page-table entry, so a fault is raised by whichever reference touches an invalid entry, and residency is a property of the moment, not of the page's history.

Step by step.

  1. (A) The instruction fetch is a memory reference like any other. A page containing the next instruction can be absent, and the fault is taken before the instruction executes.
  2. (B) False. A page that was evicted earlier has its valid bit cleared, so a later reference faults again even though the page was in memory once.
  3. (C) True. After fork the parent and child share frames marked read-only; the first write by either raises a protection fault that copies just that page.
  4. (D) True. Fewer frames means a smaller resident set for the same locality, hence more evictions and more faults; this is the quantity the working-set model tries to size.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. (B) is the classic error: students treat "not in memory" as "never loaded". Demand paging with replacement guarantees the opposite — the same page can fault many times in one run.

Takeaway. A fault is a statement about the valid bit now; the frame count and the replacement policy decide how often it fires.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the working-set model are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about the working-set model are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The working set at time t is the set of distinct pages referenced in the Δ most recent references.
For a fixed reference string, increasing Δ can enlarge the working set but can never shrink it.
If the working-set sizes of all resident processes add up to more than the frames available, the system is at risk of thrashing.
The working set is exactly the set of pages currently resident in the frames allocated to the process.
options_html: The working set at time t is the set of distinct pages referenced in the Δ most recent references.
For a fixed reference string, increasing Δ can enlarge the working set but can never shrink it.
If the working-set sizes of all resident processes add up to more than the frames available, the system is at risk of thrashing.
The working set is exactly the set of pages currently resident in the frames allocated to the process.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The working-set model estimates a process's demand from its recent past: W(t, Δ) is the distinct pages in the last Δ references, and D = Σ WSSᵢ is the total demand. Comparing D with the frames available m is the model's test for thrashing.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is the definition, with Δ called the working-set window.
  2. (B) follows from containment: the last Δ references are a subset of the last Δ + k references, so the distinct-page sets nest and the size is non-decreasing in Δ.
  3. (C) True. When D > m some process cannot keep its working set resident, faults rise, CPU utilisation falls, and the system thrashes.
  4. (D) False. The working set is a property of the reference string; the resident set is a property of the allocation. A process can hold pages it has not touched within Δ, and can lack pages it has.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Equating the working set with the resident set (D). The whole point of the model is that the two differ: the OS sizes the resident set to the working set, it does not define it that way.

Takeaway. W(t, Δ) is measured from the reference string; D > m is the thrashing test.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: A TLB miss occurs and the referenced page turns out to be present in memory. In a single-level paging system with no page fault, how many main-memory accesses does the reference take, and in what order?
questions.question_html: A TLB miss occurs and the referenced page turns out to be present in memory. In a single-level paging system with no page fault, how many main-memory accesses does the reference take, and in what order?
options: Two: one to read the page-table entry, then one to read the data itself.
One: the page-table entry is fetched from the TLB in parallel with the data access.
Three: the TLB, the page table and the data are each read once.
One: the frame number is recovered directly from the faulting address.
options_html: Two: one to read the page-table entry, then one to read the data itself.
One: the page-table entry is fetched from the TLB in parallel with the data access.
Three: the TLB, the page table and the data are each read once.
One: the frame number is recovered directly from the faulting address.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The TLB is a cache of page-table entries. A miss means the entry is not in that cache, so the hardware must walk the page table in main memory before it can form the physical address.

Step by step.

  1. The MMU probes the TLB; the probe fails.
  2. Access 1: read the page-table entry for the page number from main memory.
  3. The entry is valid, so its frame number is concatenated with the offset to form the physical address.
  4. Access 2: read the data word from that frame.
  5. Effective access time for this case is therefore 2 × ma (plus the TLB probe time), against ma on a hit.

Answer: Option (A) — two main-memory accesses, page table then data.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) a miss is precisely the case where the entry is not available in the TLB, so nothing can be fetched in parallel.
  • (C) the TLB probe is not a main-memory access; it is a small on-chip associative lookup.
  • (D) the frame number is not part of the virtual address; that is the whole reason translation exists.

Common misconception. Believing a TLB miss always implies a page fault. A miss means the mapping is not cached; the page may be perfectly resident, and then the penalty is one extra memory access rather than a disk transfer.

Takeaway. Hit: 1 access. Miss with page present: 2. Fault: the whole service time.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: For the reference string 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1, 4, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 with 3 frames, which one of the following gives the correct page-fault counts?
questions.question_html: For the reference string 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1, 4, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 with 3 frames, which one of the following gives the correct page-fault counts?
options: OPT 7, LRU 10, FIFO 9
OPT 7, LRU 9, FIFO 10
OPT 9, LRU 10, FIFO 9
OPT 9, LRU 9, FIFO 9
options_html: OPT 7, LRU 10, FIFO 9
OPT 7, LRU 9, FIFO 10
OPT 9, LRU 10, FIFO 9
OPT 9, LRU 9, FIFO 9
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The three policies differ only in the victim they choose, so on the same string they can differ in fault count. OPT is the offline lower bound; FIFO and LRU are online, and neither dominates the other.

Step by step.

  1. OPT (evict the page whose next use is farthest away): faults on 0, 1, 2, 3, 0(hit), 1(hit), 4, then 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — seven faults in all.
  2. LRU (evict the least recently used): after 4 replaces the least recent page, the later sweep 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 misses on every one of them, giving ten faults.
  3. FIFO (evict the page loaded longest ago): the same later sweep costs nine, because one of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 is still resident when it is referenced.
  4. So the counts are OPT 7 < FIFO 9 < LRU 10.

Answer: Option (A) — OPT 7, LRU 10, FIFO 9.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) and (C) give FIFO and LRU the wrong way round; on this string LRU is the worse of the two.
  • (D) no policy here needs nine faults for all three, and OPT is strictly better than nine.

Common misconception. Assuming LRU always beats FIFO. LRU approximates OPT in the long run, but on a short string that revisits an old block in order, FIFO can retain exactly the pages LRU has just discarded.

Takeaway. Only OPT is optimal; FIFO and LRU are incomparable on individual strings.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question:
A demand-paged system has a memory access time of 150 ns and a page-fault service time of 5 ms. The page-fault rate is 2 × 10-4 per reference. What is the effective access time, to the nearest nanosecond?
(Enter an integer, in ns.)
questions.question_html:
A demand-paged system has a memory access time of 150 ns and a page-fault service time of 5 ms. The page-fault rate is 2 × 10-4 per reference. What is the effective access time, to the nearest nanosecond?
(Enter an integer, in ns.)
questions.solution_html:
Concept. EAT = (1 − p)·ma + p·s. Convert every term to the same unit before multiplying, because s is given in milliseconds and ma in nanoseconds.

Step by step.

  1. s = 5 ms = 5 × 10⁶ ns.
  2. No-fault term: (1 − 2 × 10⁻⁴) × 150 = 0.9998 × 150 = 149.97 ns.
  3. Fault term: 2 × 10⁻⁴ × 5 × 10⁶ = 1000 ns.
  4. EAT = 149.97 + 1000 = 1149.97 ns.
  5. Rounded to the nearest nanosecond: 1150 ns.

Answer: 1150 ns (accepts 1149.97 rounded to 1150).

Common misconception. Multiplying 2 × 10⁻⁴ by 5 and forgetting the millisecond-to-nanosecond factor of 10⁶, which yields about 0.001 ns and an EAT that looks like a plain memory access. The fault term is always the dominant one.

Takeaway. Put p·s in nanoseconds first; here 1000 ns of the 1150 ns comes from faults alone.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: For the reference string 4, 1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5, 3 under FIFO, the page-fault counts with 3 frames and with 4 frames are
questions.question_html: For the reference string 4, 1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5, 3 under FIFO, the page-fault counts with 3 frames and with 4 frames are
options: 15 and 11, so the extra frame helps here and no anomaly occurs
11 and 15, so the extra frame hurts here
15 and 15, so the frame count makes no difference
11 and 11, so the string is fully resident either way
options_html: 15 and 11, so the extra frame helps here and no anomaly occurs
11 and 15, so the extra frame hurts here
15 and 15, so the frame count makes no difference
11 and 11, so the string is fully resident either way
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Belady's anomaly is not a property of FIFO in general but of particular reference strings. Most strings behave as expected — more frames, no more faults — and only some exhibit the inversion.

Step by step.

  1. Simulate FIFO with 3 frames over the sixteen references: 4, 1, 2 fault to fill; 4 hits; 5 evicts 4; 3 evicts 1; 4 evicts 2; 1 evicts 5; 2 evicts 3; 5 evicts 4; 3 evicts 1; 1 faults again; 4, 2 and 5 fault again. Total 15.
  2. Simulate with 4 frames: 4, 1, 2, 5 fill the frames; 3 evicts 4; 4 evicts 1; 1 evicts 2; 2 evicts 5; 5 evicts 3; 3 evicts 4; 1 evicts 1's slot only if absent — it is present, so 1, 4, 2, 5 hit. Total 11.
  3. Eleven is less than fifteen, so the fourth frame reduced the fault count.

Answer: Option (A) — 15 faults with 3 frames and 11 with 4.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the two counts; nothing here shows the anomaly.
  • (C) would mean the fourth frame never retains a useful page, which the trace contradicts.
  • (D) ignores the compulsory faults for the five distinct pages.

Common misconception. Concluding from one anomaly example that FIFO always misbehaves with more frames. The inversion depends on the reference string, which is why it must be tested per string and not assumed.

Takeaway. Anomaly or not is decided by simulation, string by string — 15 → 11 here means no anomaly.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Three processes have working-set sizes of 40, 35 and 30 pages, and the machine has 100 frames. Under the working-set model, what should the operating system do?
questions.question_html: Three processes have working-set sizes of 40, 35 and 30 pages, and the machine has 100 frames. Under the working-set model, what should the operating system do?
options: Suspend one process, or swap it out, so that the remaining working sets fit in 100 frames.
Give each process 33 frames, because fair sharing is what the model prescribes.
Nothing: the working-set model only measures, it does not act.
Increase Δ for every process so that the sets are recomputed.
options_html: Suspend one process, or swap it out, so that the remaining working sets fit in 100 frames.
Give each process 33 frames, because fair sharing is what the model prescribes.
Nothing: the working-set model only measures, it does not act.
Increase Δ for every process so that the sets are recomputed.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The model compares total demand D = Σ WSSᵢ with the frames available m. If D > m no allocation can keep every process's working set resident, so at least one process must be removed from the mix.

Step by step.

  1. D = 40 + 35 + 30 = 105 pages.
  2. m = 100 frames, so D > m by 5 frames.
  3. Every allocation therefore leaves some process short of its working set, and that process will fault repeatedly.
  4. The model's remedy is to suspend or swap out one process — here the 30-page one is the cheapest to remove — and resume it when frames free up.

Answer: Option (A) — suspend a process so the rest fit.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) equal shares ignore the fact that demand differs per process; 33 frames is below every working set here, so all three would thrash.
  • (C) the model is a control policy, not a measurement: it decides admission and suspension.
  • (D) a larger Δ reports even more demand and makes the shortfall worse.

Common misconception. Reading D > m as a hint to add memory or to shrink page size. Within one scheduling decision the only lever is the degree of multiprogramming.

Takeaway. Σ WSSᵢ ≤ m or remove a process; here 105 > 100, so one goes.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Which of the following statements about page-replacement algorithms and their implementation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about page-replacement algorithms and their implementation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Exact LRU needs a per-reference timestamp or a stack of page numbers, and both cost more hardware than GATE-style machines are assumed to provide.
The clock (second-chance) algorithm approximates LRU; it is not an exact implementation of it.
For a fixed reference string and frame count, OPT gives a lower bound on the number of faults any algorithm can have.
FIFO chooses its victim by how recently each resident page was last used.
options_html: Exact LRU needs a per-reference timestamp or a stack of page numbers, and both cost more hardware than GATE-style machines are assumed to provide.
The clock (second-chance) algorithm approximates LRU; it is not an exact implementation of it.
For a fixed reference string and frame count, OPT gives a lower bound on the number of faults any algorithm can have.
FIFO chooses its victim by how recently each resident page was last used.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Each policy is defined by its victim rule, and each rule has a hardware price. Exact LRU needs unbounded bookkeeping, so real machines approximate it; OPT needs the future, so it is only an offline yardstick.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Timestamp LRU needs a clock register, a field per entry and a comparison on every eviction; stack LRU needs a doubly linked list updated on every reference.
  2. (B) True. Clock keeps one reference bit per frame and gives a page a second chance, which is a one-bit approximation of recency, not recency itself.
  3. (C) True. OPT evicts the page whose next use is farthest away, which is the best any algorithm can do knowing the whole string, so its count is a lower bound.
  4. (D) False. FIFO's victim is the page loaded earliest; recency of use plays no part.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Believing clock is LRU because both are "recency based". Clock can evict a page used one reference ago if its bit happens to have been cleared on an earlier sweep, which LRU never does.

Takeaway. LRU costs hardware, clock approximates it, OPT bounds them all, FIFO ignores recency.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Which one of the following describes the second-chance (clock) algorithm?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following describes the second-chance (clock) algorithm?
options: It looks at the page FIFO would evict; if that page's reference bit is set, it clears the bit and moves on to the next page in the circular list.
It keeps a per-page counter of how many times each page was referenced and evicts the smallest counter.
It evicts the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future.
It evicts the page that was loaded most recently.
options_html: It looks at the page FIFO would evict; if that page's reference bit is set, it clears the bit and moves on to the next page in the circular list.
It keeps a per-page counter of how many times each page was referenced and evicts the smallest counter.
It evicts the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future.
It evicts the page that was loaded most recently.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Clock arranges the resident frames in a circle with a hand. On a fault the hand inspects the frame it points at: reference bit 0 means the page is old enough and is evicted; reference bit 1 means it was used recently, so the bit is cleared and the hand advances, giving the page one more chance.

Step by step.

  1. Every reference sets the reference bit of its page, which the hardware does automatically.
  2. On a fault, inspect the frame under the hand.
  3. Bit 0 → evict, load the new page, set its bit, advance the hand.
  4. Bit 1 → clear the bit, advance the hand, repeat. In the worst case the hand sweeps the whole circle once, clearing bits, and evicts on the second pass.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) describes an LFU-style counter scheme, not clock.
  • (C) is OPT, which needs the future reference string.
  • (D) is MRU, the opposite of the intent.

Common misconception. Thinking the reference bit is enough to order pages exactly. One bit distinguishes "used since the last sweep" from "not used", which is why clock is only an approximation of LRU.

Takeaway. Clock = FIFO plus one reference bit per frame and a hand that sweeps.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: A frame must be freed to service a page fault. Which one of the following victims can be discarded without writing it back to backing store?
questions.question_html: A frame must be freed to service a page fault. Which one of the following victims can be discarded without writing it back to backing store?
options: A clean page, whose dirty bit is 0, because memory and backing store already agree on its contents.
A dirty page, because its write-back can be deferred to the next fault.
Any page whose valid bit is 1.
A page that is still mapped in the TLB.
options_html: A clean page, whose dirty bit is 0, because memory and backing store already agree on its contents.
A dirty page, because its write-back can be deferred to the next fault.
Any page whose valid bit is 1.
A page that is still mapped in the TLB.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The dirty (modify) bit records whether a page has been written since it was loaded. A clean page is identical in memory and on backing store, so the frame can be reused at once; a dirty page must be written back first, doubling the fault cost.

Step by step.

  1. On a fault, the OS picks a victim by the replacement policy.
  2. If the victim's dirty bit is 0, the frame is simply reassigned and the page-table entry is invalidated.
  3. If the dirty bit is 1, the page is written to backing store, the entry is updated, and only then is the frame reused.
  4. So the cheap eviction is the clean one.

Answer: Option (A) — a clean page needs no write-back.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) a dirty page must be written back before its frame is reused; deferring the write would lose the modification.
  • (C) the valid bit says the page is resident, not that it is clean.
  • (D) a TLB mapping is irrelevant to the contents question and is flushed either way.

Common misconception. Forgetting the write-back in the fault-service time. A fault on a dirty victim costs a write plus a read, which is why page-fault service times in EAT problems are quoted for the worst case.

Takeaway. Clean victim: one transfer. Dirty victim: two.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: A program takes 40 page faults per 10,000 references with 64 frames. A designer predicts that with 128 frames it will take 20 per 10,000. Which statement is correct?
questions.question_html: A program takes 40 page faults per 10,000 references with 64 frames. A designer predicts that with 128 frames it will take 20 per 10,000. Which statement is correct?
options: The prediction need not hold: the fault rate depends on the reference pattern's locality and on the replacement policy, and with FIFO more frames can even raise the fault count.
The prediction holds exactly, because the fault rate is inversely proportional to the number of frames.
The prediction holds only under OPT, which is the optimal policy.
The fault rate is independent of the number of frames.
options_html: The prediction need not hold: the fault rate depends on the reference pattern's locality and on the replacement policy, and with FIFO more frames can even raise the fault count.
The prediction holds exactly, because the fault rate is inversely proportional to the number of frames.
The prediction holds only under OPT, which is the optimal policy.
The fault rate is independent of the number of frames.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Frame count is only one of three inputs to the fault rate: the reference string's locality, the replacement policy and the number of frames. Doubling the frames doubles the capacity, not the hit rate.

Step by step.

  1. If the working set already fits in 64 frames, the extra 64 change nothing and the rate stays at 40.
  2. If the working set is around 100 pages, 128 frames may cut faults sharply — better than half, because the whole set now fits.
  3. If the policy is FIFO, some strings fault more with more frames (Belady's anomaly).
  4. Only the shape of the reference string decides which of these happens, so no fixed ratio can be predicted.

Answer: Option (A) — the prediction is not guaranteed.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) there is no inverse-proportionality law; the fault count is a step-like function of frames, not a smooth 1/n curve.
  • (C) OPT is also non-linear in frames, so the ratio claim fails there too.
  • (D) the frame count plainly matters — that is what the working-set model sizes.

Common misconception. Treating memory as a linear dial for faults. Locality makes the curve plateau, and FIFO makes it non-monotone.

Takeaway. Faults depend on string, policy and frames — never on frames alone.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question:
For the reference string 4, 2, 3, 0, 4, 2, 1, 4, 2, 3, 0, 1 under FIFO with 4 frames, how many page faults occur?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
For the reference string 4, 2, 3, 0, 4, 2, 1, 4, 2, 3, 0, 1 under FIFO with 4 frames, how many page faults occur?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Concept. FIFO with four frames evicts the page that has been resident longest. Because FIFO's page set need not nest as the frame count grows, the count here must be obtained by tracing, not by assuming it is better than the three-frame count.

Step by step. Trace the frames, oldest first.

  1. 4 → fault, frames [4].
  2. 2 → fault, [4, 2].
  3. 3 → fault, [4, 2, 3].
  4. 0 → fault, [4, 2, 3, 0].
  5. 4 → hit.
  6. 2 → hit.
  7. 1 → fault, evict 4, [2, 3, 0, 1].
  8. 4 → fault, evict 2, [3, 0, 1, 4].
  9. 2 → fault, evict 3, [0, 1, 4, 2].
  10. 3 → fault, evict 0, [1, 4, 2, 3].
  11. 0 → fault, evict 1, [4, 2, 3, 0].
  12. 1 → fault, evict 4, [2, 3, 0, 1].

Counting. Faults at references 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 — ten faults, with hits only at 5 and 6.

Answer: 10 page faults.

Worth noting. With three frames this same string faults only nine times, so it is one of the strings that exhibits Belady's anomaly: the fourth frame costs an extra fault.

Common misconception. Expecting the four-frame count to be at most the three-frame count and answering 9 without tracing. That expectation is exactly what the anomaly disproves.

Takeaway. Trace FIFO frame by frame; never infer the count from the frame count.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question:
A process references the pages 5, 2, 5, 3, 5, 2, 7, 2, 5, 3, 7, 5. Using the working-set model with window Δ = 5, how many pages are in the working set after the twelfth reference?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
A process references the pages 5, 2, 5, 3, 5, 2, 7, 2, 5, 3, 7, 5. Using the working-set model with window Δ = 5, how many pages are in the working set after the twelfth reference?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The working set at time t with window Δ is the set of distinct pages among the Δ most recent references, that is the references at positions t − Δ + 1 to t.

Step by step.

  1. Number the references 1 to 12: 5, 2, 5, 3, 5, 2, 7, 2, 5, 3, 7, 5.
  2. At t = 12 with Δ = 5 the window is references 8 to 12: 2, 5, 3, 7, 5.
  3. Distinct pages in that window: {2, 5, 3, 7}.
  4. So the working set has 4 pages.

Answer: 4 pages.

Common misconception. Counting the five references in the window instead of the distinct pages, which gives 5. Page 5 appears twice inside the window and counts once.

Takeaway. Window = positions t − Δ + 1 … t; working set = the distinct pages in it.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: For the reference string 4, 1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5, 3 with 4 frames, how many page faults does LRU take?
questions.question_html: For the reference string 4, 1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5, 3 with 4 frames, how many page faults does LRU take?
questions.solution_html:
Concept. LRU evicts the page whose most recent reference is earliest. Because the string cycles through five distinct pages with only four frames, almost every reference evicts the page that will be wanted next — the worst case for a recency policy.

Step by step. Trace with four frames, evicting the least recently used page on each fault.

  1. ref 1, page 4: fault, load → {4}. 1
  2. ref 2, page 1: fault, load → {4, 1}. 2
  3. ref 3, page 2: fault, load → {4, 1, 2}. 3
  4. ref 4, page 4: hit.
  5. ref 5, page 5: fault, load → {4, 1, 2, 5}. 4
  6. ref 6, page 3: fault, evict 1 (used at ref 2) → {4, 2, 5, 3}. 5
  7. ref 7, page 4: hit.
  8. ref 8, page 1: fault, evict 2 (used at ref 3) → {4, 5, 3, 1}. 6
  9. ref 9, page 2: fault, evict 5 (used at ref 5) → {4, 3, 1, 2}. 7
  10. ref 10, page 5: fault, evict 3 (used at ref 6) → {4, 1, 2, 5}. 8
  11. ref 11, page 3: fault, evict 4 (used at ref 7) → {1, 2, 5, 3}. 9
  12. ref 12, page 1: hit.
  13. ref 13, page 4: fault, evict 2 (used at ref 9) → {1, 5, 3, 4}. 10
  14. ref 14, page 2: fault, evict 5 (used at ref 10) → {1, 3, 4, 2}. 11
  15. ref 15, page 5: fault, evict 3 (used at ref 11) → {1, 4, 2, 5}. 12
  16. ref 16, page 3: fault, evict 1 (used at ref 12) → {4, 2, 5, 3}. 13

Counting. Thirteen faults and three hits, at references 4, 7 and 12.

Answer: Option (B) — 13 page faults.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 11 is what FIFO takes on this string, not LRU; the extra frame is used better by a policy that ignores recency here.
  • (C) 14 is the three-frame LRU count, so it belongs to the smaller machine.
  • (D) 16 would mean every reference faults, but references 4, 7 and 12 hit.

Common misconception. Assuming LRU beats FIFO on any string. This string is the counterexample: LRU's precise recency information makes it discard pages FIFO would have kept, so LRU faults 13 times against FIFO's 11.

Takeaway. Trace, do not rank: with 4 frames this string gives FIFO 11, LRU 13 and OPT 7.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: For which one of the following reference strings does FIFO exhibit Belady's anomaly when the frame count rises from 3 to 4?
questions.question_html: For which one of the following reference strings does FIFO exhibit Belady's anomaly when the frame count rises from 3 to 4?
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The anomaly means faults(4 frames) > faults(3 frames) for the same string under FIFO. Since FIFO is not a stack algorithm, this can happen — but only for strings whose reuse pattern makes the larger resident set retain the wrong pages.

Step by step. Simulate each string under FIFO at 3 and at 4 frames.

  1. (A) 4, 2, 3, 0, 4, 2, 1, 4, 2, 3, 0, 1 — nine faults with 3 frames, ten with 4. Anomaly present.
  2. (B) 4, 3, 0, 0, 1, 4, 0, 2, 0, 2, 3, 4 — nine faults with 3 frames, six with 4.
  3. (C) 1, 2, 0, 2, 4, 1, 2, 4, 4, 4, 0, 1 — seven faults with 3 frames, four with 4.
  4. (D) 0, 2, 3, 3, 0, 0, 4, 4, 0, 3, 4, 2 — six faults with 3 frames, four with 4.

Why (A) misbehaves. With three frames, FIFO happens to hold 4, 2 and 3 when the second block 4, 2, 3 arrives, so those references hit. With four frames the extra frame holds 0 and FIFO's queue order changes, so 1 displaces 4 and the following 4, 2, 3 all fault.

Answer: Option (A) — 9 faults with 3 frames against 10 with 4.

Common misconception. Looking for a "large" or "looping" string. The anomaly needs a particular interleaving, not length: options (B), (C) and (D) are just as long and show none.

Takeaway. Only simulation settles it; compare faults(3) with faults(4) for each candidate.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Which of the following statements about stack algorithms and Belady's anomaly are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about stack algorithms and Belady's anomaly are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every stack algorithm is immune to Belady's anomaly.
The clock (second-chance) algorithm is a stack algorithm.
If FIFO shows the anomaly for a string when frames rise from 3 to 4, it must also show it for that string at every larger frame count.
For a fixed reference string, OPT's fault count with n + 1 frames is never greater than with n frames.
options_html: Every stack algorithm is immune to Belady's anomaly.
The clock (second-chance) algorithm is a stack algorithm.
If FIFO shows the anomaly for a string when frames rise from 3 to 4, it must also show it for that string at every larger frame count.
For a fixed reference string, OPT's fault count with n + 1 frames is never greater than with n frames.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. A stack algorithm ranks pages by a criterion independent of the frame count, so its page sets nest: M(n) ⊆ M(n + 1). Every page that is a hit with n frames is then also a hit with n + 1, which makes the fault count non-increasing in frames.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True, by the inclusion property just stated: nesting forces monotonicity, so no inversion is possible.
  2. (B) False. Clock's victim depends on the state of the reference bits, which in turn depends on how many frames are being swept, so its page sets need not nest.
  3. (C) False. The anomaly is a property of a particular pair of frame counts for a particular string; it can appear at 3 → 4 and disappear at 4 → 5.
  4. (D) True. OPT is a stack algorithm: with one more frame it holds one more of the pages ranked by next use, so it can only gain hits.

Answer: Options (A) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming "approximates LRU" means "behaves like LRU" (B). Approximation of the victim rule is not the same as the inclusion property; clock is not a stack algorithm.

Takeaway. Stack algorithm ⇔ nested page sets ⇔ no anomaly. LRU and OPT qualify; FIFO and clock do not.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: A machine has 200 frames. Every process has a working-set size of 45 pages. Under the working-set model, the largest degree of multiprogramming that avoids thrashing is
questions.question_html: A machine has 200 frames. Every process has a working-set size of 45 pages. Under the working-set model, the largest degree of multiprogramming that avoids thrashing is
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The model admits a process only if its working set can be kept resident, so the number of processes N must satisfy N × WSS ≤ m. The answer is the largest integer N meeting that inequality.

Step by step.

  1. Constraint: N × 45 ≤ 200.
  2. 200 / 45 = 4.44…
  3. The largest integer not exceeding 4.44 is 4.
  4. Check: 4 × 45 = 180 ≤ 200, while 5 × 45 = 225 > 200.
  5. The 20 frames left over cannot hold a fifth working set, so they stay free.

Answer: Option (B) — 4 processes.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 3 is safe but not the largest admissible value.
  • (C) 5 needs 225 frames, 25 more than exist, so at least one process would thrash.
  • (D) 45 confuses the number of processes with the pages per process.

Common misconception. Rounding 4.44 up because "the leftover frames are nearly enough". A working set is all-or-nothing under the model: a process short of its set faults continuously.

Takeaway. N = ⌊m / WSS⌋ = ⌊200/45⌋ = 4.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: A process makes 1.2 × 106 memory references per second and its page-fault rate is 2 × 10-2. Page-fault-frequency control uses an upper bound of 10,000 faults per second and a lower bound of 2,000, and no frames are free. What should the operating system do?
questions.question_html: A process makes 1.2 × 106 memory references per second and its page-fault rate is 2 × 10-2. Page-fault-frequency control uses an upper bound of 10,000 faults per second and a lower bound of 2,000, and no frames are free. What should the operating system do?
options: Give the process more frames, suspending another process to release them if necessary.
Take frames away from the process, since it is faulting too often.
Leave it alone: the fault frequency is inside the band.
Increase Δ, because a larger window lowers the fault rate.
options_html: Give the process more frames, suspending another process to release them if necessary.
Take frames away from the process, since it is faulting too often.
Leave it alone: the fault frequency is inside the band.
Increase Δ, because a larger window lowers the fault rate.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Page-fault-frequency control measures faults per unit time. A process above the upper bound needs more memory; one below the lower bound has memory to spare. The frequency, not the raw rate, is compared with the bounds.

Step by step.

  1. PFF = references per second × fault rate = 1.2 × 10⁶ × 2 × 10⁻².
  2. = 1.2 × 10⁶ × 0.02 = 24,000 faults per second.
  3. Compare with the band: 2,000 ≤ 24,000 ≤ 10,000 is false, because 24,000 > 10,000.
  4. The process is above the upper bound, so it needs a larger resident set.
  5. With no free frames, the OS suspends or swaps out another process to obtain frames — the same remedy the working-set model prescribes when D > m.

Answer: Option (A) — allocate more frames, suspending another process if needed.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) fewer frames means more faults, worsening the condition.
  • (C) is an arithmetic slip — 24,000 is more than double the upper bound of 10,000.
  • (D) Δ is a measurement window; enlarging it reports a larger working set and does not itself reduce faults.

Common misconception. Comparing the fault rate 0.02 with the bounds 10,000 and 2,000 and concluding it is far below them. The bounds are frequencies; the rate must be multiplied by the reference rate first.

Takeaway. PFF = references/s × fault rate; here 24,000 > 10,000, so add frames.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the effective access time of a demand-paged system are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about the effective access time of a demand-paged system are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The fault term dominates as soon as p is even moderately large, because the service time is three to six orders of magnitude larger than a memory access.
Doubling the memory access time while leaving p and the service time unchanged roughly doubles the effective access time only when the fault term is negligible.
Reducing the page size always reduces the page-fault rate.
The page-fault service time includes writing back the victim page when that page is dirty.
options_html: The fault term dominates as soon as p is even moderately large, because the service time is three to six orders of magnitude larger than a memory access.
Doubling the memory access time while leaving p and the service time unchanged roughly doubles the effective access time only when the fault term is negligible.
Reducing the page size always reduces the page-fault rate.
The page-fault service time includes writing back the victim page when that page is dirty.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. EAT = (1 − p)·ma + p·s is a weighted average of two very different costs, so the sensitivity of EAT to ma and to s depends on which term is larger.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. With ma in nanoseconds and s in milliseconds, s/ma is between 10³ and 10⁶; even p = 10⁻⁵ adds tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, dwarfing a 100 ns access.
  2. (B) True. Doubling ma doubles the first term only. EAT doubles exactly when p·s ≈ 0; otherwise EAT grows by less than the factor applied to ma.
  3. (C) False. A smaller page halves the internal waste but doubles the number of pages and hence the number of faults, and the transfer overhead per fault rises. The fault rate typically worsens.
  4. (D) True. Servicing a fault on a dirty victim is a write plus a read; on a clean victim it is a read alone.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing a smaller page always helps (C). Page size is a trade-off: less internal fragmentation against more page-table entries, more faults and more I/O per fault.

Takeaway. EAT is dominated by p·s; page size trades waste against fault count.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: In linked allocation a file is a linked list of disk blocks, and the blocks may be scattered anywhere on the disk. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: In linked allocation a file is a linked list of disk blocks, and the blocks may be scattered anywhere on the disk. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: Any block of the file is reached in one disk read, because its address is computed from the first block.
It suffers no external fragmentation, but every block gives up space for a pointer, and reaching the k-th block costs k disk reads.
It requires the blocks of a file to be contiguous, so it suffers from external fragmentation.
If one pointer is damaged, only the block it points to is lost and the rest of the file is still reachable.
options_html: Any block of the file is reached in one disk read, because its address is computed from the first block.
It suffers no external fragmentation, but every block gives up space for a pointer, and reaching the k-th block costs k disk reads.
It requires the blocks of a file to be contiguous, so it suffers from external fragmentation.
If one pointer is damaged, only the block it points to is lost and the rest of the file is still reachable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Linked allocation stores each block with a pointer to the next block of the same file, so the file is a chain that can be built from any free blocks. Two consequences follow at once: no free space is left unusable between files, and no block can be located without walking the chain.

Step by step.

  1. Because blocks are taken from anywhere, there is no external fragmentation — any free block will do.
  2. Each block must carry the pointer, so a block of size B with a pointer of p bytes holds only B − p bytes of data. That is a cost paid on every block.
  3. To read logical block k, the system must start at the first block and follow k pointers, so direct access is lost.
  4. If a pointer is corrupted, the rest of the chain is unreachable — the file loses everything from that point on, not merely one block.

Answer: Option (B) — no external fragmentation, but a pointer per block and no direct access.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) describes contiguous allocation, where the address is start + k.
  • (C) reverses the point of linking: blocks are deliberately scattered.
  • (D) understates the damage. Losing a pointer orphans the whole remainder of the chain.

Common misconception. Reading “linked list” as “cheap”. The chain is cheap in space management and expensive in access: sequential access is fine, random access is not.

Takeaway. Linked allocation trades direct access for the elimination of external fragmentation and for trivial file growth.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: A disk has 2²⁴ blocks, and free space is tracked by a bitmap with one bit per block. What is the size of the bitmap?
questions.question_html: A disk has 2²⁴ blocks, and free space is tracked by a bitmap with one bit per block. What is the size of the bitmap?
options: 256 KB
1 MB
2 MB
16 MB
options_html: 256 KB
1 MB
2 MB
16 MB
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A bitmap stores one bit per block, so its size in bits equals the number of blocks; converting to bytes divides by 8.

Step by step.

  1. Bits needed = 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 bits.
  2. Bytes = 16,777,216 ÷ 8 = 2,097,152 bytes.
  3. Megabytes = 2,097,152 ÷ 2²⁰ = 2 MB.
  4. Shortcut: 2²⁴ bits = 2²⁴ ÷ 2³ bytes = 2²¹ bytes = 2 × 2²⁰ bytes = 2 MB.

Answer: Option (C) — 2 MB.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 256 KB is what you get by dividing by 8 twice, i.e. treating the answer as 2²⁴ ÷ 64.
  • (B) 1 MB forgets that one byte holds 8 bits.
  • (D) 16 MB is 2²⁴ bytes, i.e. one byte per block.

Common misconception. Losing the factor of 8 in one direction or the other. Write the unit chain explicitly: bits → bytes (÷8) → KB (÷2¹⁰) → MB (÷2²⁰).

Takeaway. Bitmap size in bytes = number of blocks ÷ 8; here 2²⁴ ÷ 8 = 2 MB.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.subtopic_label: Disk scheduling: FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK
questions.question: Which disk-scheduling policy services requests strictly in the order of their arrival, so that the head may sweep back and forth across the disk?
questions.question_html: Which disk-scheduling policy services requests strictly in the order of their arrival, so that the head may sweep back and forth across the disk?
options: SSTF
FCFS
SCAN
C-SCAN
options_html: SSTF
FCFS
SCAN
C-SCAN
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A disk-scheduling policy decides the order in which pending requests are served. Only one of the standard policies ignores the current head position altogether: FCFS, which serves the queue as it stands.

Step by step.

  1. FCFS takes the requests in arrival order, so the head can jump from cylinder 98 to 183 and back to 37 — sweeping in both directions as the queue dictates.
  2. SSTF always takes the nearest request, so the head moves monotonically toward a locality and does not sweep the whole disk.
  3. SCAN and C-SCAN impose a direction on the sweep by construction.
  4. Hence the only policy whose order is fixed by arrival time alone is FCFS.

Answer: Option (B) — FCFS.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) SSTF reorders the queue by distance from the head on every step.
  • (C) SCAN sweeps to the end of the disk in one direction before reversing.
  • (D) C-SCAN sweeps in one direction only and returns to the start without servicing.

Common misconception. Assuming FCFS is “fair but useless”. It is the baseline: it can be very expensive in head movement, but its behaviour is easy to predict and it never reorders requests.

Takeaway. FCFS = arrival order; SSTF = nearest first; SCAN/C-SCAN = sweep with a direction.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: A Unix-like file has permission mode 640, read as rw- r-- ---. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: A Unix-like file has permission mode 640, read as rw- r-- ---. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: The owner may read and write, members of the group may read, and all other users have no access.
The owner may read and write, members of the group may read and write, and all other users may read.
The owner may read only, the group may read and write, and all other users have no access.
The owner may read, write and execute, the group may read, and all other users may read.
options_html: The owner may read and write, members of the group may read, and all other users have no access.
The owner may read and write, members of the group may read and write, and all other users may read.
The owner may read only, the group may read and write, and all other users have no access.
The owner may read, write and execute, the group may read, and all other users may read.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A three-digit octal mode gives the rights of the owner, the group and everyone else, one digit each. Within a digit, read = 4, write = 2 and execute = 1, added together.

Step by step.

  1. Owner digit 6 = 4 + 2 = read + write, no execute.
  2. Group digit 4 = read only.
  3. Other digit 0 = no rights at all.
  4. So the file is writable by its owner, readable by the group, and closed to everyone else.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) would be mode 664.
  • (C) would be mode 460, which also gives the group write.
  • (D) would be mode 744.

Common misconception. Reading the digits as counts of users rather than as bit sums. The digit is an octal number, not a quantity.

Takeaway. 6 = rw, 5 = r-x, 4 = r--, 0 = ---. Three digits, three classes of user.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Which one of the following is the advantage that contiguous allocation has over linked allocation?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following is the advantage that contiguous allocation has over linked allocation?
options: A file never suffers external fragmentation.
The address of the k-th block is start + k, so that block is reached with a single disk access.
A file can grow without moving any of its blocks.
A file never wastes space in its last block.
options_html: A file never suffers external fragmentation.
The address of the k-th block is start + k, so that block is reached with a single disk access.
A file can grow without moving any of its blocks.
A file never wastes space in its last block.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Contiguous allocation gives a file one run of consecutive blocks. That single decision buys the best possible access behaviour and costs flexibility in growth.

Step by step.

  1. Because the blocks are consecutive, block k of the file lives at block start + k: one arithmetic step, one disk access.
  2. The same contiguity makes sequential access fast, because consecutive logical blocks are physically adjacent and the head hardly moves.
  3. Growth is the price. To extend a file the blocks immediately after it must be free, otherwise the file must be copied elsewhere.
  4. Free space becomes a set of holes between surviving files, which is external fragmentation.

Answer: Option (B) — computed block addresses give direct access.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Contiguous allocation is the scheme that suffers external fragmentation most visibly.
  • (C) Growth is precisely its weakness.
  • (D) The last block of a file is partly empty in every block-based scheme; only the amount differs.

Common misconception. Crediting contiguous allocation with the absence of fragmentation. It has no internal fragmentation in the paging sense, but external fragmentation is its signature defect.

Takeaway. Contiguous: fastest access, worst growth. Linked: any growth, no direct access.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question:
A disk has 1,000,000 blocks and its free-space bitmap uses one bit per block. How many bytes does the bitmap occupy?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
A disk has 1,000,000 blocks and its free-space bitmap uses one bit per block. How many bytes does the bitmap occupy?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. One bit per block, so the number of bits equals the number of blocks; dividing by 8 gives bytes.

Step by step.

  1. Bits required = 1,000,000.
  2. Bytes = 1,000,000 ÷ 8.
  3. 1,000,000 ÷ 8 = 125,000 exactly, because 1,000,000 is divisible by 8.

Answer: 125,000 bytes (about 122 KB).

Common misconception. Reporting 1,000,000 bytes by keeping one byte per block, or rounding to 125,001 to “allow a spare bit”. No spare bit is needed: 1,000,000 is an exact multiple of 8.

Takeaway. Bitmap bytes = blocks ÷ 8; only round up when the block count is not a multiple of 8.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.subtopic_label: Disk scheduling: FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK
questions.question:
A disk has 200 cylinders numbered 0 to 199. The head is at cylinder 53, and the pending queue in arrival order is 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. Under FCFS, what is the total head movement, in cylinders?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
A disk has 200 cylinders numbered 0 to 199. The head is at cylinder 53, and the pending queue in arrival order is 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. Under FCFS, what is the total head movement, in cylinders?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Head movement is the sum of the absolute differences between consecutive cylinders visited, starting from the current head position. Under FCFS the visit order is the arrival order.

Step by step.

  1. 53 → 98 = 45
  2. 98 → 183 = 85
  3. 183 → 37 = 146
  4. 37 → 122 = 85
  5. 122 → 14 = 108
  6. 14 → 124 = 110
  7. 124 → 65 = 59
  8. 65 → 67 = 2
  9. Total = 45 + 85 + 146 + 85 + 108 + 110 + 59 + 2 = 640.

Answer: 640 cylinders.

Common misconception. Summing the request positions (710) instead of the gaps between consecutive positions. Movement is about travel, not about where the requests are.

Takeaway. Under FCFS the head zig-zags across the queue; the 146-cylinder jump from 183 back to 37 is most of the waste.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes an access-control list from a capability list?
questions.question_html: Which statement correctly distinguishes an access-control list from a capability list?
options: An access-control list is stored with the object and names the subjects allowed to use it; a capability is held by a subject and names an object together with the rights the subject may exercise on it.
An access-control list is held by the subject and a capability list is stored with the object.
An access-control list can express only read and write rights, while a capability can express any right.
The two are the same mechanism under different names, differing only in whether the list is sorted.
options_html: An access-control list is stored with the object and names the subjects allowed to use it; a capability is held by a subject and names an object together with the rights the subject may exercise on it.
An access-control list is held by the subject and a capability list is stored with the object.
An access-control list can express only read and write rights, while a capability can express any right.
The two are the same mechanism under different names, differing only in whether the list is sorted.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Protection information can be attached to the object or to the subject. Attached to the object it is an access-control list; attached to the subject it is a capability.

Step by step.

  1. An ACL on a file lists pairs (user or group, rights). The check at open time is “does this subject appear in the file's list?”
  2. A capability is a token held by the subject, for example a descriptor that names a file and carries read/write rights. The check is “does the subject hold a token for this object?”
  3. ACLs are easy to inspect and revoke for one object, but hard to answer “what can this user reach?”. Capabilities are the reverse.
  4. The two therefore differ in where the list lives, not in the kind of rights it can express.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) swaps the two placements.
  • (C) both mechanisms can express any right.
  • (D) they are duals, not the same thing: one is per-object, the other per-subject.

Common misconception. Treating a capability as “an ACL entry copied to the user”. A capability is a protected token the user can present; losing control of it means losing the rights it carries.

Takeaway. ACL = column of the access matrix stored with the object. Capability list = row of the access matrix held by the subject.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question:
A file system uses indexed allocation in which each file has exactly one index block, and the index block holds 256 block pointers. The block size is 1 KB. What is the largest file, in KB, that this scheme can represent?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
A file system uses indexed allocation in which each file has exactly one index block, and the index block holds 256 block pointers. The block size is 1 KB. What is the largest file, in KB, that this scheme can represent?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With one index block, the file can point at exactly as many data blocks as the index block has entries. Maximum file size = entries × block size.

Step by step.

  1. The index block holds 256 pointers.
  2. Each pointer addresses one 1 KB data block.
  3. Maximum size = 256 × 1 KB = 256 KB.

Answer: 256 KB.

Common misconception. Adding the index block itself (257 KB) or subtracting it. The index block holds metadata, not file data, so it does not count towards the file's size.

Takeaway. Single-level indexing caps a file at (pointers per block) × (block size); to go beyond it, a second level is needed.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: In the counting method of free-space management, each free block stores a count together with a pointer to the next free block. What does the count record?
questions.question_html: In the counting method of free-space management, each free block stores a count together with a pointer to the next free block. What does the count record?
options: The number of files that currently share the block.
The number of consecutive free blocks that follow this one, so a run of k free blocks is described by a single entry.
The number of bits in the bitmap that are still unused.
The number of times the block has been written since it was formatted.
options_html: The number of files that currently share the block.
The number of consecutive free blocks that follow this one, so a run of k free blocks is described by a single entry.
The number of bits in the bitmap that are still unused.
The number of times the block has been written since it was formatted.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The counting method compresses the free list: instead of one entry per free block, one entry describes a whole run of contiguous free blocks.

Step by step.

  1. A free block stores (count, next), where next is the address of the next entry and count is how many contiguous free blocks start at this address.
  2. A disk with large free runs is then represented by a short list, so the list fits in memory more easily.
  3. Allocation takes the first entry with a large enough count and reduces that count.
  4. The count is therefore a length of a run, not a usage statistic.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) sharing is not tracked in the free-space structure at all.
  • (C) the counting method does not use a bitmap.
  • (D) a write counter has no role in allocation.

Common misconception. Confusing counting with grouping. Grouping stores many free-block addresses in one free block; counting stores one address and a run length.

Takeaway. Counting = run-length encoding of the free list.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.subtopic_label: Disk scheduling: FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK
questions.question: The head is at cylinder 53 on a 200-cylinder disk (0 to 199), and the pending queue is 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. Which one of the following is the order in which SSTF services these requests?
questions.question_html: The head is at cylinder 53 on a 200-cylinder disk (0 to 199), and the pending queue is 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. Which one of the following is the order in which SSTF services these requests?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. SSTF always serves the pending request nearest to the current head position, recomputing the nearest after every service. It is a greedy policy, not a sweep.

Step by step. From 53 the distances are 45 (98), 130 (183), 16 (37), 69 (122), 39 (14), 71 (124), 12 (65), 14 (67).

  1. 53 → 65 (12 cylinders). Nearest remaining to 65 is 67.
  2. 65 → 67 (2). From 67 the nearest is 37 (30), then 14 (23).
  3. 67 → 37 → 14. From 14 the nearest is 98 (84).
  4. 14 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183, each step taking the closest of what remains.
  5. Total movement = 12 + 2 + 30 + 23 + 84 + 24 + 2 + 59 = 236.

Answer: Option (A) — 53, 65, 67, 37, 14, 98, 122, 124, 183, total 236 cylinders.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is LOOK moving toward cylinder 0, which goes to 14 before turning; total 208.
  • (C) is the FCFS arrival order; total 640.
  • (D) is an outward sweep from 53 that ignores 37 and 14 until the end, which SSTF would never do.

Common misconception. Sweeping outward from the head and calling it SSTF. SSTF reverses direction whenever the other side becomes nearer — here it turns at 67 and heads down to 14.

Takeaway. SSTF: at each step, take the nearest; the path may zig-zag.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Which of the following statements about file protection are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about file protection are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Revoking a capability is expensive, because capabilities are held by subjects and must be found one by one.
An access-control list answers “what may this user do with this file?” easily, but answers “what may this user do with anything?” only by scanning every object.
The three permission classes rwx for owner, group and others carry the same information as a full access-control list over all users of the system.
In Unix, the execute bit on a directory grants the right to traverse that directory in order to reach a named file inside it.
options_html: Revoking a capability is expensive, because capabilities are held by subjects and must be found one by one.
An access-control list answers “what may this user do with this file?” easily, but answers “what may this user do with anything?” only by scanning every object.
The three permission classes rwx for owner, group and others carry the same information as a full access-control list over all users of the system.
In Unix, the execute bit on a directory grants the right to traverse that directory in order to reach a named file inside it.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Protection can be organised per object (ACLs) or per subject (capabilities), and the cost of the two operations that matter — checking a right and revoking one — falls differently on each.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. A capability is a token in the subject's own table, so revoking it means locating every holder; there is no single place to delete an entry.
  2. (B) True. An ACL is the natural per-object view; the per-subject question needs a scan of all objects.
  3. (C) False. Three classes cannot express per-user entries: two users in the same group are indistinguishable under the mode bits, and there is no way to name an individual outside the group.
  4. (D) True. On a directory, x means “may pass through”, r means “may list the names”, and w means “may create or delete entries”. Traversal needs x, not r.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are true; (C) is false.

Common misconception. Reading the directory r bit as “permission to open files inside”. Listing and traversal are separate rights; a directory with mode 711 can be traversed by everyone while its contents remain unlistable.

Takeaway. ACLs answer per-object questions cheaply, capabilities answer per-subject questions cheaply; directory x is the traversal right.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: An inode holds 12 direct pointers, one single-indirect pointer and one double-indirect pointer. The block size is 4 KB and a block pointer is 4 bytes. Counting logical blocks from 0, which pointer chain is used to reach logical block 5000?
questions.question_html: An inode holds 12 direct pointers, one single-indirect pointer and one double-indirect pointer. The block size is 4 KB and a block pointer is 4 bytes. Counting logical blocks from 0, which pointer chain is used to reach logical block 5000?
options: A direct pointer
The single-indirect pointer
The double-indirect pointer
No chain — a file of this size cannot be represented
options_html: A direct pointer
The single-indirect pointer
The double-indirect pointer
No chain — a file of this size cannot be represented
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Multi-level indexing partitions the logical block numbers into ranges: the direct pointers cover the first few blocks, the single-indirect pointer the next (block size ÷ pointer size) blocks, and the double-indirect pointer everything after that.

Step by step.

  1. Pointers per block = 4096 ÷ 4 = 1024.
  2. Direct pointers cover blocks 0 to 11 — that is 12 blocks.
  3. Single indirect covers 1024 blocks: 12 to 1035.
  4. Double indirect covers 1024² = 1,048,576 blocks: 1036 to 1,049,611.
  5. 5000 lies between 1036 and 1,049,611, so the double-indirect pointer is used: the first-level index gives the second-level index block, and that block gives the data block.

Answer: Option (C) — the double-indirect pointer, with two index blocks traversed.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) a direct pointer reaches only blocks 0 to 11.
  • (B) the single-indirect pointer stops at block 1035.
  • (D) the structure addresses over a million blocks, so 5000 is well within reach.

Common misconception. Forgetting that the 12 direct blocks shift every later range by 12, or computing 1024² = 1,048,576 as if the pointer size were the block size. Keep the three ranges explicit.

Takeaway. Ranges: direct 0–11, single 12–1035, double 1036–1,049,611 for 4 KB blocks and 4-byte pointers.

questions.subject: operating-systems
questions.question: Which free-space method makes it cheapest to decide whether the disk holds a run of 8 consecutive free blocks?
questions.question_html: Which free-space method makes it cheapest to decide whether the disk holds a run of 8 consecutive free blocks?
options: A linked free list
The counting method
