questions.question: Which one of the following is a genuine advantage of user-level threads over kernel-level threads?
options: A blocking system call in one thread does not block the others.
Several threads of the process can run on several cores at once.
Switching between two threads needs no trap into the kernel.
The kernel can schedule each thread independently.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. User-level threads are managed entirely by a library in user space. Because the kernel knows only the process, a thread switch is a library call that saves and restores registers — no trap, no mode change, no kernel scheduler.

Step by step.

  1. A kernel-level thread switch requires a system call into the kernel and a scheduling decision.
  2. A user-level switch is a function call inside the process; it is typically an order of magnitude cheaper.
  3. The price is that the kernel cannot see the threads, so it cannot run them in parallel or unblock one of them independently.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the opposite: a blocking call blocks the whole process under the many-to-one model.
  • (B) A user-level library cannot put two threads on two cores; only the kernel can.
  • (D) Independent per-thread scheduling is exactly what the kernel needs to know about the threads to do, which user-level threads deny it.

Common misconception. Assuming cheaper means better. The cheap switch is paid for with the loss of parallelism and of independent blocking.

Takeaway. User-level threads: cheap switch, no parallelism. Kernel threads: real parallelism, expensive switch.

questions.question: A process uses the many-to-many model with 4 kernel threads and 10 user-level threads. All 10 user threads are CPU-bound and make no system calls. On an 8-core machine, how many of the user threads can be executing at the same instant?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In the many-to-many model the kernel schedules the kernel threads and the library multiplexes user threads onto them. Only a user thread that currently has a kernel thread can be on a CPU, so the instantaneous parallelism is bounded by the smaller of the kernel-thread count and the core count.

Step by step.

  1. Kernel threads available: 4.
  2. Cores available: 8.
  3. User threads can occupy at most one kernel thread each, so at most min(4, 8) = 4 run at once.
  4. The other 6 user threads are runnable inside the library but have no kernel thread to run on.

Answer: Option (B), 4.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) One would be the many-to-one answer; here there are 4 kernel threads.
  • (C) 8 is the core count, but there are only 4 kernel threads to occupy them.
  • (D) 10 is the user-thread count, which no model can run in parallel beyond its kernel threads.

Common misconception. Reading the many-to-many model as unlimited. The multiplexing ratio bounds concurrency from above; the kernel thread count is the real ceiling.

Takeaway. Parallelism = min(kernel threads, cores); the user-thread count only decides how much work is queued behind them.

questions.question: Which one of the following is TRUE of non-preemptive scheduling?
options: A process keeps the CPU until it blocks or terminates.
A process is removed from the CPU as soon as a higher-priority process becomes ready.
It needs a periodic timer interrupt in order to function.
It always produces a lower average waiting time than preemptive scheduling.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Non-preemptive means the scheduler runs only when the running process gives up the CPU voluntarily — by blocking on I/O, by calling exit(), or by yielding.

Step by step.

  1. The dispatcher hands the CPU to a process.
  2. The process keeps it; no arrival of another process can displace it.
  3. Only a voluntary relinquish returns control to the scheduler.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Displacing a running process on a higher-priority arrival is precisely preemption.
  • (C) A timer is what enables preemption; a non-preemptive scheduler does not need one.
  • (D) No such general claim holds; preemptive SRTF has the minimum average waiting time.

Common misconception. Believing non-preemptive means no interrupts. Device interrupts still occur; they just do not cause a scheduling decision for the running process.

Takeaway. Preemption is about who may take the CPU away — only the running process itself, or the kernel as well.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about response time are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Response time is measured from submission of the process to the first instant it gets the CPU.
For a long queue of CPU-bound jobs, preemptive round robin bounds the worst-case response time, while first come first served does not.
Response time and waiting time are the same quantity.
Under a non-preemptive scheduler the response time of a newly arrived process can be as large as the longest remaining burst in the system.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Response time is the delay before the first CPU service; waiting time is the total time spent in the ready queue. For a process that is dispatched once and never preempted they coincide, which is why they are so often confused.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: that is the definition.
  2. (B) True: with quantum q and n ready processes, a new arrival waits at most (n − 1)·q before its first slice; under FCFS it waits for every burst queued ahead of it.
  3. (C) False: a process preempted many times has a large waiting time but its response time was small.
  4. (D) True: a new arrival cannot start until the running process gives up the CPU, which may take as long as its remaining burst.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (C) They differ exactly when preemption occurs, which is the interesting case.

Common misconception. Treating response time as an average. It is usually quoted as a worst case, because an interactive user cares about the longest stall, not the mean.

Takeaway. Response time = first service; waiting time = all ready-queue time. Preemption improves the first and can worsen the second.

questions.question:
Four processes arrive as shown and are scheduled by preemptive shortest remaining time first (SRTF). All times are in milliseconds. How many times is a running process preempted? Do not count the initial dispatch of the first process.
ProcessArrivalBurst
P109
P225
P342
P461
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. SRTF compares remaining times at every arrival instant. A preemption occurs only when a newly arrived process has strictly less remaining time than the running one; the running process is never displaced by one that is merely equal or longer.

Step by step.

  1. t = 0: only P1 exists, so P1 runs. Remaining: P1 = 9.
  2. t = 2: P2 arrives with burst 5. P1 has 7 left, and 5 < 7, so P2 preempts P1. Preemption 1.
  3. t = 4: P2 has 3 left; P3 arrives with burst 2, and 2 < 3, so P3 preempts P2. Preemption 2.
  4. t = 6: P3 completes. P4 arrives at t = 6 with burst 1. Waiting are P2 with 3 left and P1 with 7 left; 1 is the smallest, so P4 runs — but P3 had already finished, so this is a dispatch, not a preemption.
  5. t = 7: P4 completes. P2 (3 left) runs to t = 10.
  6. t = 10: P1 runs its remaining 7 ms and completes at t = 17.

Answer: 2 preemptions.

Common misconception. Counting every change of the running process. A dispatch after the previous process completed is not a preemption; the count is only of processes displaced while still runnable.

Takeaway. Draw the Gantt chart and mark only those boundaries at which the outgoing process still had work left.

questions.question: Why does a preemptive scheduler need a hardware timer?
options: To measure the burst time of each process.
To regain control of the CPU from a process that neither blocks nor terminates.
To choose the next process when several are ready.
To save the context of the preempted process.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The kernel runs only when it is entered — by a system call, an exception or an interrupt. A CPU-bound process that makes no system calls never enters the kernel on its own, so without a periodic timer interrupt the kernel could never take the CPU back.

Step by step.

  1. The timer is programmed to interrupt after the quantum.
  2. The interrupt transfers control to the kernel's handler.
  3. The handler charges the running process, marks the quantum expired and invokes the scheduler.
  4. The scheduler may then switch to another process.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Burst times are not measured by the timer; they are observed or predicted.
  • (C) Selection is the scheduler's job, not the timer's.
  • (D) The context switch routine saves the context; the timer only triggers it.

Common misconception. Thinking the timer chooses the next process. It only guarantees the kernel gets a chance to choose.

Takeaway. The timer is the mechanism that makes preemption possible; the scheduler is the policy that uses it.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements comparing preemptive shortest remaining time first (SRTF) with non-preemptive shortest job first (SJF) is TRUE?
options: For the same set of processes, SRTF never has a larger average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.
For the same set of processes, non-preemptive SJF never has a larger average waiting time than SRTF.
The two always give the same average waiting time, because both always pick the shortest job.
SRTF can only be implemented as one level of a multilevel feedback queue.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. SRTF is the optimal algorithm for average waiting time among all schedulers that must decide without knowing future arrivals. It re-decides at every arrival, so its set of feasible schedules contains every schedule non-preemptive SJF can produce, and it always takes the best of them.

Step by step.

  1. Non-preemptive SJF fixes an order when the CPU is free; a long job that starts cannot be interrupted by a short arrival.
  2. SRTF interrupts it, which can only move short jobs earlier.
  3. Shortening the jobs that run early cannot increase the total waiting time, so SRTF's average is at most SJF's — and strictly smaller whenever a short job arrives during a long one.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the containment: SJF cannot beat the optimum.
  • (C) They differ whenever an arrival has a shorter remaining time than the running process.
  • (D) SRTF is an ordinary priority scheduler with remaining time as the key; a multilevel feedback queue only approximates it when bursts are unknown.

Common misconception. Assuming optimality carries over to turnaround time. SRTF minimises average waiting time; it can increase turnaround for long jobs.

Takeaway. SRTF ≤ SJF on average waiting time, always, and SRTF can starve the long job that SJF would at least have started.

questions.question: Two processes update a shared counter with an ordinary read-modify-write sequence and no synchronisation. Which one of the following failures becomes possible only because the scheduler is preemptive?
options: A page fault on the page holding the counter.
A deadlock in which each process waits for a resource the other holds.
A process being stopped because its time quantum has expired.
A lost update: both processes read the same old value and one of the increments is overwritten.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A read-modify-write is not atomic. If the scheduler can stop a process between the read and the write, another process can read the same old value, and one of the two increments disappears. Under non-preemptive scheduling a process runs that sequence to completion, so the interleaving cannot occur.

Step by step.

  1. Both processes read the counter, say 5.
  2. P1 is preempted before it writes.
  3. P2 computes 6 and writes 6.
  4. P1 resumes, computes 6 from its stale 5 and writes 6. One increment is lost.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Page faults arise from memory access patterns, not from the scheduling policy.
  • (B) Deadlock needs each process to hold one resource and wait for another; it can happen with or without preemption.
  • (C) Quantum expiry is the normal operation of preemption, not a failure caused by it.

Common misconception. Believing that a single machine instruction is automatically atomic with respect to other processes. Only genuinely atomic instructions, or critical sections, give that guarantee.

Takeaway. Preemption turns any non-atomic shared update into a race; that is why critical sections exist.

questions.question: Round robin is run with a time quantum that is at least as large as the longest burst in the ready queue. Which algorithm does it then behave like?
options: First come first served
Shortest job first
Shortest remaining time first
Priority scheduling
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Round robin preempts only when the quantum expires. If the quantum is longer than any burst, no process is ever preempted, so each runs to completion in arrival order — which is exactly FCFS.

Step by step.

  1. A process is dispatched from the head of the ready queue.
  2. It finishes before the quantum expires, so it is never preempted.
  3. The next process is taken from the head, which is the earliest arrival.
  4. The order is therefore arrival order: FCFS.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) and (C) require comparing burst or remaining lengths, which round robin never does.
  • (D) requires a priority field, which round robin ignores.

Common misconception. Thinking a huge quantum is harmless. It removes the responsiveness that round robin exists to provide.

Takeaway. Quantum → ∞ is FCFS; quantum → 0 is processor sharing with unbounded switch overhead.

questions.question:
Three processes arrive as shown and are scheduled by round robin with a time quantum of 2 ms. A process that arrives at the same instant a quantum expires is placed in the queue ahead of the process that has just been preempted. All times are in milliseconds. What is the average waiting time?
ProcessArrivalBurst
P106
P224
P342
(Enter a number; decimals are allowed.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Under round robin the preempted process goes to the tail of the ready queue, so every runnable process gets one slice before it gets a second. Waiting time = completion − arrival − burst.

Step by step.

  1. t = 0–2: P1 runs (6 → 4 left).
  2. t = 2–4: P2 runs (4 → 2 left). P1 rejoined the queue behind P2.
  3. t = 4–6: P3 arrived at t = 4, and it is queued ahead of the just-preempted P2; P3 runs (2 → 0, completes at 6).
  4. t = 6–8: P1 runs (4 → 2 left).
  5. t = 8–10: P2 runs (2 → 0, completes at 10).
  6. t = 10–12: P1 runs (2 → 0, completes at 12).
  7. Completion times: P1 = 12, P2 = 10, P3 = 8.
  8. Waiting times: P1 = 12 − 0 − 6 = 6; P2 = 10 − 2 − 4 = 4; P3 = 8 − 4 − 2 = 2.
  9. Average = (6 + 4 + 2) / 3 = 12 / 3 = 4 ms.

Answer: 4 ms.

Common misconception. Appending the preempted process ahead of the newcomer. Round robin puts the preempted process at the tail; the newcomer joins ahead of it, which is what gives the newcomer its first slice at t = 4.

Takeaway. Draw the queue explicitly at each instant; the tie-break rule at an arrival boundary decides the whole schedule.

questions.question: Which one of the following correctly relates turnaround time, waiting time and burst time?
options: Waiting = completion − arrival; turnaround = waiting − burst.
Response time = turnaround − waiting time.
Turnaround = completion − arrival; waiting = turnaround − burst.
Waiting time counts only the interval before the first dispatch.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Turnaround time is the total time from arrival to completion. Waiting time is that total minus the time actually spent executing, which is the burst.

Step by step.

  1. Turnaround = completion time − arrival time.
  2. Turnaround = waiting time + burst time, because a process either waits or runs.
  3. Therefore waiting time = turnaround − burst.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) swaps the two definitions.
  • (B) is not an identity: response time is the first-service delay, unrelated to turnaround minus waiting in general.
  • (D) describes response time, not waiting time.

Common misconception. Using completion − arrival as the waiting time and forgetting to subtract the burst. For a preempted process the two differ substantially.

Takeaway. One identity does most of the work: turnaround = waiting + burst, with turnaround = completion − arrival.

questions.question:
A scheduler predicts the next burst of a process by exponential averaging, τn+1 = α tn + (1 − α) τn. The initial prediction is τ0 = 10 ms, the next two actual bursts are 14 ms and 6 ms, and α = 0.5. What is the prediction after these two observations, in ms?
(Enter a number; decimals are allowed.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Exponential averaging folds the newest observation into the old estimate with weight α, so recent behaviour dominates when α is large and history dominates when α is small. It is how SJF is approximated without knowing the next burst.

Step by step.

  1. τ1 = 0.5 × 14 + 0.5 × 10 = 7 + 5 = 12 ms.
  2. τ2 = 0.5 × 6 + 0.5 × 12 = 3 + 6 = 9 ms.

Answer: 9 ms.

Common misconception. Applying the formula to the initial estimate instead of the previous prediction — that is, computing 0.5 × 6 + 0.5 × 10 = 8. Each step uses the prediction produced by the previous step, not τ0.

Takeaway. Update once per observation, carrying the new τ forward; the estimate lags the true burst by a factor that shrinks as α grows.

questions.question: A low-priority process holds a lock that a high-priority process needs, and a medium-priority process that needs no lock is runnable. The holder is repeatedly preempted by the medium-priority process, so the high-priority process waits far longer than its priority warrants. What is this situation called, and what is the standard remedy?
options: Starvation; aging steadily raises the priority of every waiting process.
Deadlock; the scheduler breaks the lock and restarts the holder.
The convoy effect; the scheduler falls back to first come first served.
Priority inversion; priority inheritance temporarily raises the lock holder's priority to that of the highest waiter.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Priority inversion is a high-priority task being delayed by a lower-priority one that holds a resource it needs, made worse by an unrelated middle-priority task. Priority inheritance makes the holder run at the waiter's priority until it releases the lock, so the middle-priority task can no longer preempt it.

Step by step.

  1. L holds the lock and is preempted by M, which is runnable and has higher priority than L.
  2. H becomes ready, but cannot proceed because the lock is held.
  3. L cannot run because M keeps taking the CPU, so H waits for M — a task of lower priority than itself.
  4. With inheritance, L runs at H's priority while it holds the lock, so M cannot preempt it and L releases the lock quickly.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Aging addresses a process that never gets the CPU; here the problem is a lock held by a process that is being preempted.
  • (B) There is no circular wait, so this is not deadlock.
  • (C) The convoy effect is short jobs queuing behind a long one, not a lock dependency.

Common misconception. Calling it deadlock. Nothing is permanently stuck: the high-priority task would finish if the medium-priority one were not interfering.

Takeaway. Priority inversion needs a lock, three priority levels and preemption; priority inheritance removes the third factor's effect.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about priority scheduling are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: With static priorities, a low-priority process can be starved indefinitely by a steady stream of higher-priority arrivals.
Aging raises the priority of a process the longer it waits, which bounds the wait.
In UNIX-like systems a smaller numeric priority value conventionally means a higher scheduling priority.
Priority scheduling can never be preemptive, because the priority is fixed when the process is created.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Priority scheduling picks the highest-priority ready process. Its two classic problems are starvation and the preemptive/non-preemptive choice; its standard cure for starvation is aging.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: if arrivals of higher priority never stop, the low-priority process is never selected.
  2. (B) True: aging increments the priority of a waiting process, so eventually it outranks every arrival and its wait is bounded.
  3. (C) True: UNIX and Linux nice values run from −20 (most favourable) to +19 (least favourable), so smaller means higher priority.
  4. (D) False: priority scheduling is commonly preemptive — a higher-priority arrival displaces the running process.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (D) confuses the value of the priority with the policy; whether priorities are static has nothing to do with whether the scheduler preempts.

Common misconception. Reading "smaller number, higher priority" as a universal rule. It is a UNIX convention; many textbooks use the opposite, so always check the question's stated convention.

Takeaway. Priority scheduling is preemptive or not by configuration; aging is the standard defence against starvation.

questions.question: A multilevel queue scheduler keeps separate queues with absolute priority between them, and a process never moves from one queue to another. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A process in a lower-priority queue can be starved by a continuous stream of arrivals in a higher-priority queue.
It differs from a multilevel feedback queue in that a process does not migrate between queues.
Any scheduling algorithm may be used inside each queue.
It guarantees a bounded response time for every process.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A multilevel queue partitions the ready set permanently — typically foreground, background, system — and services the queues in a fixed priority order. Each queue may use its own internal algorithm. The multilevel feedback queue is the variant that lets processes move between queues.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: absolute priority means a lower queue is served only when every higher queue is empty, so a continuous higher-priority stream starves it.
  2. (B) True: that is precisely the difference — feedback queues demote and promote.
  3. (C) True: round robin in the interactive queue and FCFS in the batch queue is the standard arrangement.
  4. (D) False: a lower-priority process has no bound at all under absolute priority.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (D) contradicts (A); only a time-sliced share between queues would give a bound.

Common misconception. Treating multilevel queue and multilevel feedback queue as synonyms. The word feedback is the migration.

Takeaway. Fixed partition → starvation possible; feedback → migration, starvation reduced but not eliminated.

questions.question: A correct software solution to the critical-section problem must satisfy three requirements. Which one of the following is NOT one of them?
options: Mutual exclusion. At most one process may execute in its critical section at any instant.
Progress. A process that is not in its critical section cannot prevent another process from entering, and the choice of who enters next cannot be postponed indefinitely.
Bounded waiting. After a process has requested entry, there is a bound on how many times other processes may enter before its request is granted.
Equal CPU share. Every process must receive exactly the same amount of processor time while it waits to enter.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The three requirements are mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting. They constrain who may be inside the critical section, who may decide the next entrant, and how long a waiting process may be delayed. Nothing in them mentions how much CPU time a process receives.

Step by step.

  1. Mutual exclusion forbids two processes inside the critical section at once.
  2. Progress forbids a process outside its critical section from blocking the entry of others, and forbids an indefinite postponement of the decision itself.
  3. Bounded waiting forbids starvation: after a request, only finitely many other entries may precede it.
  4. CPU share is a scheduling question. A solution can be perfectly correct while giving a waiting process no CPU at all for a long time, as a pure busy-wait does.

Answer: Option (D) — equal CPU share is a scheduling goal, not a critical-section requirement.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A), (B) and (C) are the three textbook requirements, in order.
  • (D) is not required by any of them; a busy-wait solution deliberately burns CPU while waiting and is still correct.

Common misconception. Adding “fairness” or “no deadlock” to the list. Fairness in the CPU sense is not required; what is required is that a process waiting to enter is not starved, which is bounded waiting.

Takeaway. Three words to recall under time pressure: exclusion, progress, bound.

questions.question: Peterson's two-process solution sets flag[i] = true and then turn = j before testing while (flag[j] && turn == j);. Suppose the assignment turn = j is deleted, so that each process only sets its own flag and then spins while the other flag is true. Which property of the original algorithm is lost?
options: Mutual exclusion is lost: both processes can be inside the critical section at the same time.
Bounded waiting is lost, but mutual exclusion and progress still hold.
Progress is lost: the two processes can set both flags and then wait for each other forever, while mutual exclusion still holds.
Nothing is lost; turn is redundant because the flags already carry the information.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In Peterson's algorithm the flag array alone is not enough. Two processes can both raise their flags before either tests, and then each sees the other's flag true and waits: a deadlock in the entry section. That is a failure of progress, because the decision of who enters next is postponed forever. Mutual exclusion is untouched, because nobody is inside.

Step by step.

  1. P0 sets flag[0] = true; P1 sets flag[1] = true.
  2. P0 tests flag[1], sees true, spins. P1 tests flag[0], sees true, spins.
  3. Neither flag is ever cleared, because clearing happens only in the exit section, which neither process can reach. Both wait forever.
  4. No process is inside the critical section at any moment, so mutual exclusion is not violated; the failure is that the system as a whole makes no progress.
  5. turn breaks exactly this tie: whoever wrote turn last lets the other one in, so at most one process is ever blocked by the other's flag.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the trap. A deadlock in the entry section means nobody enters, so the shared data is never touched concurrently. Mutual exclusion survives.
  • (B) misidentifies the casualty: the wait here is unbounded and simultaneous, which is progress, and bounded waiting cannot even be assessed once the system is stuck.
  • (D) turn is not redundant; it is the only tie-breaker between two raised flags.

Common misconception. Reading any failure as a mutual-exclusion failure. Ask instead can two processes be inside? Here they cannot; they cannot even get in.

Takeaway. Flags give exclusion; turn gives progress and the bound. Delete either and a different requirement dies.

questions.question: In Peterson's two-process algorithm, what does the shared variable turn accomplish that the flag array cannot?
options: It counts how many processes are waiting to enter the critical section.
It replaces the flag array, so a single variable is enough for mutual exclusion.
It makes the reads and writes of the flags atomic.
It breaks the tie when both processes want to enter, deciding which one waits, and that is what bounds the wait.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each flag says “I want to enter”. If both are raised, someone must be chosen to go second; turn records whose turn it is to yield. The process that wrote turn last is the one that defers.

Step by step.

  1. Both processes may raise their flags simultaneously; the flags alone cannot resolve that.
  2. turn is written by each process just before it tests, so the later writer is the one that lets the other in.
  3. Consequently a process that is waiting is guaranteed to enter after the other process leaves at most once: the wait is bounded.
  4. Mutual exclusion itself comes from the flags; turn adds progress and the bound.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) turn is a process index, not a counter.
  • (B) with turn alone, strict alternation, a process that does not want to enter blocks the other: progress fails.
  • (C) atomicity of the individual loads and stores is an assumption of the algorithm, not something turn provides.

Common misconception. Believing turn provides mutual exclusion. In fact the flags do, and turn is the courtesy variable that stops the two flags from deadlocking.

Takeaway. flag = “I want in”, turn = “you go first”.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Peterson's two-process algorithm are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: It assumes that a load or a store of flag[i] or turn is atomic and is not reordered with the other accesses in the entry section.
It works unchanged for any number of processes, provided each process has its own flag.
For two processes it satisfies mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.
It remains correct on a weakly ordered multiprocessor even if no memory barrier or fence is used.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Peterson's algorithm is a two-process solution whose proof rests on the sequential consistency of its four shared accesses. It meets all three requirements for n = 2 and needs explicit fences on machines that reorder stores.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. If the store flag[i] = true were delayed past the read of flag[j], both processes could read false and both enter.
  2. (B) False. With three or more processes a single turn cannot arbitrate; the algorithm needs the level/victim generalisation (filter lock) or the bakery algorithm.
  3. (C) True. Mutual exclusion from the flags, progress from turn, and bounded waiting because a process that waits is entered ahead of the other at most once.
  4. (D) False. On x86-TSO or ARM the stores may become visible out of order, so a fence (or an atomic exchange) is required between raising the flag and reading the other's.

Answer: Options (A) and (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is the commonest over-claim about Peterson's algorithm; its correctness proof is for two processes.
  • (D) ignores memory reordering, which breaks the algorithm without any change to the source code.

Common misconception. Treating a source-level algorithm as if the hardware executed it in program order. Every software solution to the critical-section problem silently assumes that.

Takeaway. Two processes, sequential consistency, three properties.

questions.question:
The filter-lock generalisation of Peterson's algorithm for n threads keeps one entry per thread in the array level[n] and one entry per level in the array victim[n − 1], with levels numbered 0 to n − 2. For n = 7 threads, what is the total number of array cells used by the two arrays together?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The filter lock adds one “waiting room” per thread beyond the first, so n threads need n − 1 levels. Each thread stores its current level, giving n cells in level[], and each level has one victim, giving n − 1 cells in victim[].

Step by step.

  1. Levels run from 0 to n − 2, so there are n − 1 = 7 − 1 = 6 levels.
  2. level[] has one cell per thread: 7.
  3. victim[] has one cell per level: 6.
  4. Total: 7 + 6 = 13 cells.

Answer: 13 array cells (7 in level, 6 in victim).

Common misconception. Counting n cells for both arrays, or n levels instead of n − 1. The top level is the critical section itself and needs no victim, because only one thread can be there.

Takeaway. n threads, n − 1 levels, n + (n − 1) = 2n − 1 cells; here 13.

questions.question: Lamport's bakery algorithm has each process set choosing[i] = true, read all ticket numbers to compute its own, publish it, and then clear choosing[i]. A process entering the critical section waits for every other process j while j is choosing, or while j holds a smaller ticket (ties broken by process id). Why is the choosing array necessary?
options: Without it a process could read another's ticket number while that number was still being written, and two processes could end up with the same ticket and enter together.
Without it the ticket numbers would eventually overflow and wrap around.
Without it a process could never leave the critical section, because the exit section needs the flag.
Without it the algorithm would be unfair to processes with large ids, which would wait for ever.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The ticket is computed as 1 + max(number[1..n]), which is a read of n cells followed by a write of one. A reader that observes a stale or half-written value can compute a ticket that is not greater than the one it should have avoided, and two processes can then hold the same ticket with no ordering between them. choosing is the flag that makes a process's number “not yet valid” while it is being computed.

Step by step.

  1. P1 sets choosing[1] = true and starts scanning the other numbers.
  2. P2 does the same at the same time; each reads the other's old number, say 0.
  3. Both compute 1 and publish it. Equal tickets are broken by id, so ordering survives, but a process that read the other's number before it was published can also miss it entirely.
  4. With choosing, a waiting process must wait until the other has finished choosing, so the number it eventually compares against is final.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) overflow is a practical concern for a bounded integer, not the reason for the flag.
  • (C) the exit section only writes number[i] = 0.
  • (D) id order is exactly what makes large-id processes wait a little longer, not for ever.

Common misconception. Assuming the maximum is computed atomically. It is not; the flag is what turns a racy scan into a safe one.

Takeaway. Every software solution to the critical-section problem assumes atomic reads and writes of single cells; the bakery algorithm assumes nothing more, which is why it is famous.

questions.question: An atomic instruction test_and_set(&lock) returns the previous value of lock and sets lock to true, indivisibly. Which statement about it is TRUE?
options: It sets the variable to true and returns the new value, so every caller observes true.
It returns the old value and sets the variable to true in one indivisible step, so exactly one of several concurrent callers can observe false.
It blocks the calling process until the lock becomes false, then sets it to true.
It is really two instructions, a load and a store, and must itself be protected by another lock.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The value of test_and_set is not that it reads or writes, but that it does both without any window in between. Returning the old value is what lets a caller learn whether it was the one that flipped the lock from false to true.

Step by step.

  1. Caller reads the returned value: false means the lock was free and is now mine.
  2. True means someone else held it; the caller spins and tries again.
  3. Because the read and the write are one atomic step, two callers cannot both see false.
  4. That single guarantee is enough for mutual exclusion; ordering (who goes next) is a separate matter.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) returning the new value would tell every caller true and no caller could tell whether it had won.
  • (C) blocking is not part of the instruction; blocking is built on top of it with a queue.
  • (D) the whole point of the instruction is that it is not a load followed by a store.

Common misconception. Thinking the atomicity is about speed. It is about the absence of an interleaving point between the read and the write.

Takeaway. Returns old, writes true, one step.

questions.question: Why does disabling interrupts in the entry section fail to give mutual exclusion on a multiprocessor?
options: Interrupts cannot be disabled for longer than a single instruction, so the protection lapses immediately.
Disabling interrupts also stalls the memory bus, which prevents the shared variable from being read.
The interrupt-disable instruction affects only the CPU that executes it, so a thread running on another CPU can still be inside, or enter, the critical section.
It does not fail: disabling interrupts is a correct general solution on any machine.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Disabling interrupts prevents a context switch on that CPU, so on a uniprocessor it does give mutual exclusion. On a multiprocessor the other CPUs keep running, and their threads reach the same shared data.

Step by step.

  1. Thread T1 on CPU0 executes disable_interrupts() and enters the critical section.
  2. Thread T2 on CPU1 is unaffected; no interrupt mask is shared between processors.
  3. T2 enters the critical section at the same time: mutual exclusion is violated.
  4. Hence multiprocessors need an atomic instruction on a shared memory location, such as test-and-set or compare-and-swap.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) the disable lasts until it is re-enabled; duration is not the issue.
  • (B) disabling interrupts does not stall the memory bus.
  • (D) is true only for a uniprocessor kernel.

Common misconception. Believing an interrupt mask is a global machine state. It is per-CPU state.

Takeaway. Interrupt masking protects one CPU; atomic instructions protect a memory location across CPUs.

questions.question: A spinlock busy-waits on an atomic instruction until the lock is free. Under which condition is a spinlock preferable to a lock that blocks the waiting thread?
options: The critical section is long and the machine has a single processor.
The expected wait is shorter than the time needed for two context switches, as with very short critical sections on a multiprocessor.
The waiting thread must sleep to save power, as on a battery-powered device.
The lock is held by a process running on a different machine in a distributed system.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Blocking costs two context switches, one out and one back. Spinning costs CPU time but no switches. Spinning wins exactly when the expected wait is shorter than that switch cost, and when there is another processor on which the holder can make progress.

Step by step.

  1. Let the expected wait be w and the cost of a block-and-wake be 2c.
  2. If w < 2c, spinning wastes less than blocking.
  3. On a uniprocessor the holder cannot run while the spinner spins, so the spin can only waste a full quantum: blocking is then the right choice.
  4. On a multiprocessor with short critical sections, spinning usually finds the lock free within a few attempts.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) long critical sections and a single processor make spinning the worst option.
  • (C) power saving argues for blocking.
  • (D) a lock on another machine cannot be spun on by a local atomic instruction; that needs a distributed protocol.

Common misconception. “Spinning is always wasteful.” For a wait of a few hundred nanoseconds it is cheaper than two context switches of several microseconds.

Takeaway. Spin if wait < 2 context switches and another CPU exists.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about a lock built from test_and_set are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: It guarantees mutual exclusion but gives no bounded-waiting guarantee.
Its release may be an ordinary store of false, because only the acquisition has to be atomic.
Under heavy contention the spinning threads keep re-executing the atomic instruction on the same cache line, and that traffic can slow the holder down.
It hands the lock to the waiting threads in the order in which they started spinning.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. test_and_set gives exclusion, not fairness, and the release does not need to be atomic because only one thread can be inside. Contention turns the lock word into a hot cache line.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Whichever spinner happens to execute next after the release wins; a thread can lose arbitrarily many times, so no bound exists.
  2. (B) True. A plain store of false is safe because the exiting thread is the only writer at that moment.
  3. (C) True. Every spin iteration is an atomic read-modify-write on the shared line, which invalidates the copies held by other cores.
  4. (D) False. There is no queue; ordering is decided by timing and by the interconnect.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (D) describes a ticket lock or a queued lock, not a bare test-and-set spinlock.

Common misconception. Assuming a fair lock because the code “looks” first-come first-served. A spinlock is a race restarted at every release.

Takeaway. Atomic acquire, ordinary release, no fairness, hot cache line.

questions.question:
A ticket lock uses two integers, next_ticket and now_serving, both initially 0. A thread acquires a ticket with one atomic fetch_and_add(next_ticket, 1) and then spins until now_serving equals its ticket. Eight threads arrive and take tickets 0 to 7 in that order. The thread holding ticket 3 acquires the lock and is then preempted and never runs again. How many threads are blocked on the lock for ever?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A ticket lock is first-come first-served: now_serving advances by one only when the current holder releases. A holder that never releases stops every thread behind it, for ever.

Step by step.

  1. Tickets 0, 1 and 2 are served and released; now_serving reaches 3.
  2. The thread with ticket 3 acquires the lock and then never runs again, so now_serving stays at 3.
  3. Threads with tickets 4, 5, 6 and 7 spin for ever waiting for it to become 4, 5, 6 and 7.
  4. That is 4 blocked threads. The stalled thread itself is not blocked on the lock; it owns it.

Answer: 4 threads.

Common misconception. Answering 5 by counting the stalled holder. It is not waiting; it is the reason the others wait. Also note this is a liveness failure of the scheduler, not of the lock protocol, which is perfectly fair.

Takeaway. Tickets give FIFO order, and FIFO order means one preempted holder can stop everybody behind it.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about atomic instructions and memory ordering are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: test_and_set can be implemented as an ordinary load followed by an ordinary store with a memory barrier in between, and it stays atomic.
On a multiprocessor, mutual exclusion cannot be achieved by disabling interrupts alone.
On a weakly ordered machine the release of a spinlock needs a release fence so that the writes made inside the critical section become visible before the unlock does.
compare_and_swap can emulate test_and_set, but test_and_set cannot emulate compare_and_swap.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Atomicity and ordering are different guarantees. A barrier orders accesses; it does not make a load-store pair indivisible. compare_and_swap is strictly more expressive than test_and_set, because it compares before it writes.

Step by step.

  1. (A) False. Another processor can slip between the load and the store even with a barrier; only a single indivisible instruction (or a load-linked/store-conditional pair) gives atomicity.
  2. (B) True. An interrupt mask is per-CPU, so a thread on another CPU still enters.
  3. (C) True. Without the fence, another core can observe the unlocked flag while the data written inside the critical section is still in flight, and then read stale values.
  4. (D) True. test_and_set is the special case of compare_and_swap with expected value false; the converse emulation does not exist because test_and_set cannot test a value other than false.

Answer: Options (B), (C) and (D).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (A) confuses ordering with atomicity. A fence says “do not reorder”; it does not say “nobody else may look”.

Common misconception. Thinking a volatile variable or a fence is a substitute for an atomic read-modify-write. Locks need both: an atomic acquire and correctly ordered release.

Takeaway. Acquire = atomic; release = ordered. CAS > TAS in power.

questions.question: A counting semaphore S currently has the value −3. What does that tell you?
options: Three processes are blocked waiting on S.
Three more wait operations can complete without blocking.
The semaphore has been initialised wrongly, because a semaphore value can never be negative.
Three processes are inside the critical section protected by S.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In the classic definition the value of a counting semaphore is the number of available units when it is non-negative, and minus the number of blocked processes when it is negative. A wait decrements and blocks if the result is negative; a signal increments and wakes one waiter if it was negative.

Step by step.

  1. Start from some value and apply each wait as a decrement.
  2. The first three decrements below zero each block the caller rather than letting it proceed.
  3. So −3 means exactly three blocked processes.
  4. Those processes are queued on the semaphore, not inside the critical section.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) describes a positive value.
  • (C) is only true of the alternative definition in which the value is clamped at zero and the queue is counted separately; the classic formulation allows negatives.
  • (D) a semaphore with a negative value admits nobody.

Common misconception. Reading a negative value as an error. It is the standard way of recording the length of the waiting queue.

Takeaway. Non-negative = free units; negative = blocked processes.

questions.question: Which statement about a binary semaphore and a mutex is TRUE?
options: They are identical in every respect, including ownership.
A mutex may take any integer value, whereas a binary semaphore is limited to 0 and 1.
A binary semaphore may be signalled by a process other than the one that waited on it; a mutex can be released only by the thread that locked it.
A binary semaphore guarantees that waiting processes are woken in FIFO order.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A mutex has an owner: the thread that locked it must unlock it, which lets a kernel detect misuse and supports priority inheritance. A binary semaphore has no owner, so it works as a signalling device between two threads, for example an interrupt handler that signals a waiting thread.

Step by step.

  1. Binary semaphore: value 0 or 1, no owner, signal allowed from anywhere.
  2. Mutex: value locked or unlocked, an owner is recorded, unlock by a non-owner is an error.
  3. Because ownership is what differs, a producer-consumer handshake can use semaphores, while a critical section is better guarded by a mutex.
  4. Neither primitive promises FIFO wake-up unless the implementation says so.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) ignores ownership, the defining difference.
  • (B) reverses the definitions.
  • (D) wake-up order is an implementation property of the queue, not of the primitive.

Common misconception. Using a binary semaphore as a mutex and then signalling it from a different thread. It “works” until someone unlocks a critical section they never locked.

Takeaway. Semaphore = signalling, mutex = ownership.

questions.question: A counting semaphore of capacity 5 must be implemented using only binary semaphores and ordinary integer variables. What is the minimum number of binary semaphores needed?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The value of a counting semaphore needs two things: a protected counter and a way to put a process to sleep when the counter would go negative. One binary semaphore protects the counter; a second is used as the block/wake channel.

Step by step.

  1. wait: acquire mutex, decrement the counter; if it became negative, release mutex and block on delay; otherwise release mutex.
  2. signal: acquire mutex, increment the counter; if it is still not positive, release a waiter by signalling delay; then release mutex.
  3. mutex keeps the counter consistent; delay carries the “you may proceed” token.
  4. Two binary semaphores suffice for any capacity, so 2 is the minimum.

Answer: Option (B) — 2.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) one semaphore cannot both protect the counter and block a process, because a blocked process would hold it.
  • (C) and (D) confuse the capacity of the counting semaphore with the number of binary semaphores needed to implement it.

Common misconception. Thinking one binary semaphore per unit of capacity is needed. The counter is a plain integer; only its updates need protecting.

Takeaway. Counter + mutex + block channel = 2 binary semaphores, whatever the capacity.

questions.question:
A counting semaphore S is initialised to 12. Processes then perform 20 wait(S) and 11 signal(S) operations, in an order chosen so that no process ever blocks. What is the final value of S?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each wait decrements the semaphore by one and each signal increments it by one, whatever the interleaving. If nobody ever blocks, the final value is just the initial value plus the signals minus the waits.

Step by step.

  1. Signals first: 12 + 11 = 23 available.
  2. Then the 20 waits: 23 − 20 = 3.
  3. No decrement ever takes the value below zero, so indeed no process blocks and the ordering is consistent with the question.
  4. Final value: 3.

Answer: 3.

Common misconception. Adding the operations as 12 + 20 − 11 = 21. A wait takes a unit away; a signal gives one back.

Takeaway. Final value = initial − waits + signals, provided nothing ever blocks.

questions.question:
Five identical printers are guarded by a counting semaphore S initialised to 5. Twelve processes each execute exactly one wait(S) and, before any of them can reach its signal(S), all twelve have executed the wait. How many processes are blocked at that moment?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A counting semaphore admits as many processes as it has units. Every further wait decrements below zero and blocks, and the negative value counts the blocked processes.

Step by step.

  1. Five waits take the value 5 → 0; those five processes proceed.
  2. The remaining 12 − 5 = 7 waits each decrement below zero: −1, −2, …, −7.
  3. Each of those seven blocks, and the semaphore now has the value −7.
  4. So 7 processes are blocked and 5 are using the printers.

Answer: 7 processes.

Common misconception. Answering 12 or 5. Only the processes beyond the capacity wait, and the value −7 states that number directly.

Takeaway. Blocked count = max(0, waits − units).

questions.question:
A counting semaphore S is initialised to 1 and an integer x is initialised to 0. Process P executes
wait(S); x = x + 1; wait(S); x = x + 1; signal(S);
and process Q executes
wait(S); print(x); signal(S);
P starts first and runs until it blocks. What happens?
options: Q prints 1.
Q prints 2.
P blocks for ever on its second wait(S), so Q never enters and nothing is printed.
Q prints 0.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A semaphore is not re-entrant. A process that acquires the same semaphore twice without releasing it in between holds the only unit and then waits for itself: a self-deadlock.

Step by step.

  1. P executes the first wait(S): S goes from 1 to 0, P enters.
  2. P sets x = 1.
  3. P executes the second wait(S): S goes from 0 to −1 and P blocks. P is the only process that could signal, and it is blocked.
  4. Q is also blocked on its own wait(S), so the print never happens. The programme deadlocks with x = 1 and no output.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (B) assume the second wait succeeds, which it cannot while S is 0.
  • (D) would require Q to run before P's first increment, which the stated schedule excludes.

Common misconception. Treating wait as if a process could hold several units of the same semaphore. It can only hold what has been released, and here only one unit exists.

Takeaway. Never nest two waits on the same semaphore; that is a self-deadlock, not mutual exclusion.

questions.question: In the bounded-buffer producer–consumer solution with n buffer slots, protected by a mutex and two counting semaphores, what are the correct initial values?
options: mutex = 1, empty = n, full = 0.
mutex = 1, empty = 0, full = n.
empty = 1, full = n, and no mutex is needed.
mutex = n, empty = 0, full = 0.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. empty counts free slots and full counts filled ones, so they start at n and 0. The mutex protects the buffer itself and starts unlocked, at 1.

Step by step.

  1. Producer: wait(empty), wait(mutex), insert, signal(mutex), signal(full).
  2. Consumer: wait(full), wait(mutex), remove, signal(mutex), signal(empty).
  3. With n free slots at the start, the producer may fill the whole buffer before blocking.
  4. The mutex is needed because the buffer update itself must be atomic, even though the semaphores already order producer against consumer.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) starts with no empty slot and n full ones, i.e. a full buffer with nothing in it.
  • (C) a single slot semaphore cannot express both counts, and without a mutex two producers can corrupt the buffer index.
  • (D) a mutex does not take the value n.

Common misconception. Thinking the counting semaphores make the mutex redundant. They order the two roles; they do not protect the shared buffer from two producers at once.

Takeaway. mutex 1, empty n, full 0 — and always wait on the counting semaphore before the mutex.

questions.question: In the dining-philosophers problem with five philosophers and five forks, each philosopher picks up the left fork and then the right one. Allowing at most four philosophers to sit at the table at any time prevents deadlock by removing which of the four necessary conditions?
options: Mutual exclusion of the forks.
Hold and wait.
No preemption of a fork already picked up.
Circular wait.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The classic deadlock arises because every philosopher holds one fork and waits for the next: a cycle of five waiters around the table. With at most four seated, one fork is always free, so the cycle of five cannot close.

Step by step.

  1. Deadlock requires a cycle of processes each waiting for a resource held by the next.
  2. Each philosopher holds exactly one fork and needs exactly one more, so the wait-for graph is a cycle of the seated philosophers.
  3. With only four seated, at most four forks are held, so at least one fork is free and some seated philosopher can proceed; no cycle can include all four.
  4. Hence the condition removed is circular wait.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) forks are still held exclusively; mutual exclusion remains.
  • (B) each philosopher still holds one fork while waiting for another.
  • (C) a fork is still not taken away from a holder.

Common misconception. Believing the seating limit adds preemption. It only removes the possibility of a full cycle.

Takeaway. Ordering the forks globally or limiting the seated count both break circular wait.

questions.question: In the readers–writers solution, the first reader locks wrt and increments readcount, later readers only increment readcount, and the last reader unlocks wrt. Suppose the first reader forgets to lock wrt. What is the consequence?
options: The readers deadlock among themselves on readcount.
A writer can acquire wrt and modify the data while readers are still reading.
readcount becomes negative.
The last reader will be unable to unlock wrt, so it stays locked for ever.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. wrt is the semaphore shared between the reader group and the writers. Readers as a group must hold it while any reader is inside; the first reader takes it on behalf of the group and the last one returns it.

Step by step.

  1. If the first reader does not take wrt, the semaphore remains free at value 1.
  2. A writer arriving then succeeds in wait(wrt) and enters.
  3. Readers are inside concurrently, because they never gate themselves on wrt after the first.
  4. So a read and a write overlap: mutual exclusion between readers and writers is violated.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) readers only serialise on mutex around readcount, which is untouched.
  • (C) the counter is still incremented and decremented once per reader.
  • (D) the last reader's signal(wrt) would simply be an extra signal, which is harmless for a semaphore but indicates a protocol error.

Common misconception. Thinking each reader must hold wrt. Only the group does, which is exactly why the first and last readers are special.

Takeaway. wrt is a group lock: first in takes it, last out releases it.

questions.question: In the bounded-buffer producer–consumer solution, suppose the producer executes wait(mutex) before wait(empty). Which failure can result?
options: Deadlock: a producer that finds the buffer full blocks while holding the mutex, so no consumer can enter to free a slot.
A lost update on the buffer index, but the system still makes progress.
Only a performance loss, because the producer spins instead of blocking.
Nothing changes, because the two semaphores commute.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A process must never block while holding a lock that the process able to unblock it also needs. The buffer-full condition is resolved by the consumer, and the consumer needs the mutex to work, so holding the mutex while waiting for a free slot deadlocks the pair.

Step by step.

  1. Buffer full: empty = 0, full = n.
  2. Producer executes wait(mutex), taking the mutex.
  3. Producer executes wait(empty) and blocks, because there is no free slot.
  4. The consumer tries wait(full), succeeds, then blocks on wait(mutex), which the blocked producer holds. Neither can proceed: deadlock.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) there is no interleaving of the index updates; the failure is liveness, not consistency.
  • (C) a semaphore blocks; it does not spin.
  • (D) the two operations do not commute: the order decides whether a lock is held while blocking.

Common misconception. Believing the mutex only needs to cover the buffer statement. It does, but it must not be held across a blocking wait.

Takeaway. Always take the counting semaphore first, the mutex last, and release the mutex first.

questions.question:
In the standard dining-philosophers setup there are five philosophers around a circular table and exactly five forks, one between each pair of neighbours; a philosopher needs both adjacent forks to eat. What is the maximum number of philosophers who can be eating at the same time, whatever protocol they follow?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each eating philosopher consumes two distinct forks, and a fork cannot be shared. With five forks the count is bounded by the number of disjoint pairs of adjacent forks, which is floor(5/2) = 2.

Step by step.

  1. Each of the five forks can serve at most one eating philosopher.
  2. Each eating philosopher needs exactly two forks.
  3. So at most floor(5 / 2) = 2 philosophers can be eating.
  4. Two is achievable: philosophers 1 and 3 use forks (1,2) and (3,4), leaving fork 5 idle.

Answer: 2 philosophers.

Common misconception. Answering 5 by counting one fork per philosopher, or answering 1 by assuming any eating philosopher blocks all neighbours. Only the two immediate neighbours are blocked, so two non-adjacent philosophers can eat together.

Takeaway. Concurrency here is a matching problem: floor(forks / 2).

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the readers–writers problem are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The readers-preference solution can starve a writer that is waiting.
A writer-preference solution can starve readers.
Under readers-preference, a reader that arrives while a writer is already waiting is still allowed to enter.
Guarding the whole database with a single mutex gives readers-preference behaviour.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The two classical variants trade one form of starvation for the other. Readers-preference lets any reader in whenever no writer is inside, so a stream of readers can hold the lock for ever. Writer-preference blocks new readers as soon as a writer is waiting, so a stream of writers can starve readers.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. The writer waits on wrt, which the readers as a group hold continuously while any reader is inside.
  2. (B) True. With writer-preference a waiting writer blocks new readers, and successive writers can keep the lock busy.
  3. (C) True. In the readers-preference code a new reader only tests wrt, which the waiting writer has not yet acquired.
  4. (D) False. A single mutex serialises everyone, so readers do not proceed concurrently at all; that is not readers-preference.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (D) removes concurrency between readers, which is the whole point of distinguishing readers from writers.

Common misconception. Assuming one of the two variants is “correct”. Both are correct solutions to different requirements; starvation-freedom needs a fair policy such as FIFO ordering of arrivals.

Takeaway. Preference decides who starves. Fairness needs an arrival order, not a preference.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the classical synchronisation problems are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Allowing at most four philosophers to sit at the table removes the possibility of a circular wait.
With one binary semaphore per fork and no other mechanism, deadlock is possible in the dining-philosophers problem.
In the producer–consumer problem with n slots, replacing the two counting semaphores by a single mutex still preserves correctness.
In the readers–writers solution, a semaphore wrt initialised to 1 ensures that at most one writer is inside at a time.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each classical problem isolates one failure mode: circular wait for the philosophers, a full or empty buffer for the producer and consumer, and writer exclusion for the readers and writers.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. With four seated, at most four forks are held, so at least one is free and no cycle of all five can form.
  2. (B) True. If all five pick up their left fork at once, each waits for the right one held by a neighbour: a cycle.
  3. (C) False. A single mutex gives exclusion but no way to block a producer on a full buffer or a consumer on an empty one; busy-waiting inside the mutex deadlocks, and blocking outside it loses the count.
  4. (D) True. Writers hold wrt for the whole write, so two writers cannot overlap.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (C) confuses mutual exclusion with condition synchronisation. The counting semaphores carry state about the buffer that a mutex does not represent.

Common misconception. Believing one mutex is a universal fix. A mutex answers “may I touch this?”; a counting semaphore answers “is there room, or an item?”.

Takeaway. Exclusion and condition synchronisation are different jobs and need different primitives.

questions.question: A system has one resource type R₁ with 2 instances and another resource type R₂ with 1 instance. Which one of the following CANNOT appear in a valid resource allocation graph of this system?
options: Two assignment edges, R₁ → P₁ and R₁ → P₂
Two assignment edges, R₂ → P₁ and R₂ → P₂
A request edge P₁ → R₁ while P₁ already holds an instance of R₁
Two request edges, P₁ → R₁ and P₃ → R₁
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An assignment edge R → P records that one instance of R is held by P. A resource type drawn with k dots can therefore carry at most k assignment edges. Request edges carry no such limit: any number of processes may queue for the same type, because a request is only a claim on a future free instance.

Step by step.

  1. R₁ has 2 instances, so 2 assignment edges are possible — (A) is valid.
  2. R₂ has 1 instance, so at most one process can hold it. Two assignment edges out of R₂ would hand out two units of a one-unit resource — (B) is impossible.
  3. (C) is valid and common: a process holds one unit and asks for another unit of the same type. That is how multi-unit contention arises.
  4. (D) is valid: request edges are unlimited, and two processes competing for R₁ is exactly the state the graph is meant to show.

Answer: Option (B) — R₂ has one instance, so it cannot be assigned to two processes.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) uses both instances of R₁, which is allowed.
  • (C) is the hold-and-request pattern, not an error.
  • (D) request edges are not bounded by the instance count.

Common misconception. Students bound all edges touching a resource type by its instance count. Only assignment edges consume instances; request edges consume nothing yet.

Takeaway. Count dots against outgoing assignment edges. If the assignment edges exceed the dots, the graph is not a picture of any reachable state.

questions.question: R₁ has 2 instances and R₂ has 2 instances. P₁ holds one instance of R₁ and requests one instance of R₂; P₂ holds one instance of R₂ and requests one instance of R₁. The graph therefore contains the cycle P₁ → R₂ → P₂ → R₁ → P₁. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: The system is deadlocked, because a cycle in a resource allocation graph always means a deadlock.
The system is not deadlocked: one instance of each type is still free, so a request can be granted and the cycle breaks.
The system is deadlocked only if P₁ and P₂ issue their requests at the same instant.
The system is not deadlocked only because R₁ and R₂ are different resource types.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With several instances per resource type a cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock. The cycle only records who holds and who asks; whether anyone is actually stuck depends on the free instances.

Step by step.

  1. Free instances of R₁ = 2 − 1 = 1.
  2. Free instances of R₂ = 2 − 1 = 1.
  3. P₁'s request for one R₂ can be met immediately, so P₁ is not blocked.
  4. P₁ finishes and releases both its units, so R₁ now has 2 free instances and P₂'s request succeeds.

Answer: Option (B) — a free instance on each side of the cycle means no process on it is blocked.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) treats a necessary condition as a sufficient one — true only when every type has a single instance.
  • (C) deadlock is a property of a state, not of a timing accident. Since both requests are grantable, no interleaving of the two requests produces a deadlock.
  • (D) the identity of the types is irrelevant; only the free instances matter.

Common misconception. Spotting the cycle and stopping. Before calling it a deadlock, check whether every instance on the cycle is held by a process on the cycle.

Takeaway. Cycle = a warning. Deadlock = a cycle with no free instance able to break it.

questions.question: In a wait-for graph a knot is a set S of vertices such that every vertex reachable from a vertex of S also lies in S, and no edge leaves S. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: A knot is exactly the same thing as a cycle.
The system is deadlocked if and only if its wait-for graph contains a knot.
A knot is a single vertex whose out-degree is zero.
A knot can exist only when exactly one process is deadlocked.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A knot is a set of processes closed under reachability with no edge leaving it. Every process in a knot waits only on processes inside the knot, so nothing outside can ever release it. For single-instance resources the standard result is: a deadlock exists if and only if the wait-for graph contains a knot.

Step by step.

  1. A simple cycle is not automatically a knot. Take P₁ → P₂ → P₁ together with an edge P₂ → P₃ where P₃ is not blocked: the set {P₁, P₂} is a cycle but an edge leaves it, so it is not a knot.
  2. Here P₃ will run and release what P₂ needs, so the cycle dissolves. Nothing is deadlocked.
  3. Now close the set: if every edge from the set stays inside it, no process in it can ever be released, which is exactly a deadlock.
  4. So the existence of a knot characterises deadlock, while a bare cycle does not.

Answer: Option (B) — a knot is necessary and sufficient for deadlock in a wait-for graph.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) a cycle with an outgoing edge is not a knot.
  • (C) out-degree zero means the process is waiting for nothing — it is runnable, the opposite of a knot.
  • (D) a knot may contain any number of processes.

Common misconception. Using "cycle" and "knot" interchangeably. The distinction is the whole point: a knot is a cycle that nothing can escape.

Takeaway. Reachability closure is the test. If a blocked set can reach a runnable process, it is not a knot and not a deadlock.

questions.question: Every resource type in a system has several instances. The graph contains the cycle P₁ → R₁ → P₂ → R₂ → P₁, and every instance of R₁ and of R₂ is held by P₁ or by P₂. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: Nothing can be concluded, because a cycle never implies a deadlock once resource types have several instances.
The system is deadlocked, because each process on the cycle waits for a type whose every instance is held by a process on the cycle.
The system is deadlocked only if P₁ and P₂ are the only two processes in the system.
The system cannot be deadlocked, because a deadlock needs at least three processes.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With multiple instances the useful sufficient condition is: a cycle in which every resource type on the cycle has all of its instances held by processes on the cycle. Then no process on the cycle can ever be satisfied from outside, because there is nothing outside to release.

Step by step.

  1. P₁ requests R₁. Every instance of R₁ is held by P₁ or P₂, and P₁ is the requester, so it holds none — all instances are with P₂.
  2. P₂ requests R₂, and by the same argument every instance is with P₁.
  3. Neither can proceed until the other releases, and neither will release before it is satisfied.
  4. No process outside the cycle holds an instance of either type, so no outside event can break the cycle.

Answer: Option (B) — a cycle whose every instance is held inside the cycle is a deadlock.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) over-corrects: a cycle is not sufficient in general, but this extra condition makes it sufficient.
  • (C) processes outside the cycle hold nothing on it, so their existence changes nothing.
  • (D) two processes deadlocking on two resources is the smallest possible deadlock.

Common misconception. Having learned "a cycle does not always mean a deadlock", students reject every cycle. The right test is where the instances on the cycle are held.

Takeaway. Two questions, in order: is there a cycle? Are all instances on it held inside it? Yes to both — deadlock.

questions.question: Which one of the following implements deadlock prevention by denying the no preemption condition?
options: Requiring a process to request, in a single operation, every resource it will ever need before it starts.
Allowing the system to take resources away from a process that holds them and to give them to a requester, saving the victim's state so it can be restored later.
Requiring every process to request resource types in one fixed global order.
Admitting a new process only when enough resources are free for it to run to completion.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The four necessary conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Prevention denies one of them structurally. No preemption says a resource is released only voluntarily; denying it means the system may reclaim a held resource.

Step by step.

  1. Option (A) forces a process to hold everything or nothing — that denies hold and wait.
  2. Option (B) lets the system take a held resource away. The victim must be rolled back to a state from which it can re-acquire the resource later, so its state is saved — that denies no preemption.
  3. Option (C) makes a cycle impossible — that denies circular wait.
  4. Option (D) is deadlock avoidance (a Banker's-style admission test), not prevention.

Answer: Option (B) — preemption of held resources denies the no-preemption condition.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) denies hold and wait.
  • (C) denies circular wait.
  • (D) avoids rather than prevents: it checks the future state instead of removing a condition.

Common misconception. Reading "request everything at once" as preemption. It is the opposite — nothing is ever taken back; the process simply never holds partially.

Takeaway. Keep a four-row table in memory: all-at-once → hold and wait; preemption → no preemption; ordering → circular wait; spooling or read-only sharing → mutual exclusion.

questions.question: In the resource-allocation-graph scheme for deadlock avoidance, a claim edge Pᵢ → Rⱼ drawn dashed records that Pᵢ may request Rⱼ in the future. A request may be granted only if:
options: Rⱼ still has a free instance.
converting the claim edge Pᵢ → Rⱼ into a request edge leaves the graph acyclic.
the total number of claim edges in the graph does not increase.
Pᵢ is holding no other resource at the moment of the request.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Avoidance needs knowledge of the future, which the claim edge supplies. A request is simulated: the claim edge becomes a request edge, and the grant is allowed only if the graph still has no cycle. If a cycle would appear, the process must wait.

Step by step.

  1. Every resource type is single-instance in this scheme, so a cycle is exactly a deadlock.
  2. Before granting, convert Pᵢ → Rⱼ from claim to request.
  3. If that conversion creates a cycle, the grant is refused and Pᵢ waits; the edge reverts to a claim edge.
  4. When Pᵢ releases Rⱼ, the request edge becomes a claim edge again.

Answer: Option (B) — the grant must not create a cycle.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) a free instance is necessary but not sufficient; granting on availability alone is precisely how deadlock arises under naive allocation.
  • (C) the number of claim edges is bookkeeping, not a safety test.
  • (D) holding other resources is normal and is exactly what makes the cycle test necessary.

Common misconception. Treating availability as permission. Availability answers "can I physically hand it over?"; the cycle test answers "should I?".

Takeaway. Prevention asks which condition to remove; avoidance asks whether granting this request keeps the graph acyclic.

questions.question: Four processes share three resource types A, B and C, with 9, 8 and 6 instances in total. P₁ holds (2,0,2), P₂ holds (3,2,1), P₃ holds (0,2,1) and P₄ holds (2,1,1), so the available vector is (2,3,1). Their remaining needs are P₁ (2,3,0), P₂ (3,2,1), P₃ (2,2,1) and P₄ (1,2,2). Which one of the following requests can be granted without leaving the system in an unsafe state?
options: P₁ requests (1,0,0)
P₂ requests (1,0,0)
P₄ requests (1,0,0)
P₂ requests (0,2,0)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A request passes three tests: it must not exceed the process's remaining need, it must not exceed the available vector, and the state left after a pretend allocation must still be safe. All four requests here pass the first two tests, so the safety scan alone decides.

Step by step. The current state is safe: P₁ (2,3,0) fits in (2,3,1), and once it finishes everything else follows.

  1. (A) P₁ takes one A: available becomes (1,3,1) and its need (1,3,0), which still fits. P₁ finishes and returns its (3,0,2) of allocation, giving (4,3,3); P₂, P₃ and P₄ then fit in turn. Safe, so the request is granted.
  2. (B) the same unit given to P₂ leaves available (1,3,1) with P₂ needing (2,2,1). P₁ needs 2 of A and so do P₂ and P₃; P₄ needs 2 of C but only 1 is free. Nothing fits — unsafe.
  3. (C) the same unit given to P₄ leaves (1,3,1) with P₄ needing (0,2,2). Again no need fits: the three others want 2 of A and P₄ still wants 2 of C. Unsafe.
  4. (D) P₂ taking two B leaves (2,1,1) with its need (3,0,1). P₁ and P₃ want 3 and 2 of B, and only 1 is free. Unsafe.

Answer: Option (A) — one unit of A is safe for P₁ and unsafe for P₂ and P₄.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) and (C) are the identical request aimed at a process whose need is larger, so the freed resources do not cover the remaining needs.
  • (D) takes away B, which three processes still want.

Common misconception. Judging a request by its size. Options (A), (B) and (C) are the same one-unit request; whether it is safe depends entirely on what the receiving process still needs.

Takeaway. Always run the pretend allocation and then a full safety scan. Never judge a request by availability, and never by its magnitude.

questions.question: In the deadlock-detection algorithm for a system in which a resource type may have several instances, a process Pᵢ is marked as able to finish in the current pass exactly when:
options: Requestᵢ ≤ Available component by component.
Allocationᵢ ≤ Available component by component.
both Requestᵢ and Allocationᵢ are zero.
Pᵢ has not been marked finished in an earlier pass.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Detection is the safety algorithm with a different question. A process can finish when everything it is still asking for is available right now; when it finishes, its whole allocation returns to the available vector.

Step by step.

  1. Initialise Work = Available and Finishᵢ = false for every process.
  2. Find an i with Finishᵢ = false and Requestᵢ ≤ Work.
