  3. Set Work = Work + Allocationᵢ and Finishᵢ = true, then repeat.
  4. When no such i remains, every process still false is deadlocked.

Answer: Option (A) — the test is Requestᵢ ≤ Available.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) compares what the process already holds, which is irrelevant: holding more never stops it finishing.
  • (C) is too strong; a process with a pending request can still finish if the request can be met.
  • (D) is a condition on the bookkeeping, not a test of whether the process can proceed.

Common misconception. Testing Allocation instead of Request. The allocation is what the process will give back, not what it needs.

Takeaway. Need is the avoidance word, Request is the detection word. Both compare against the work vector, never against the allocation.

questions.question: The detection algorithm for n processes and m resource types repeatedly scans the whole process list, marking a process finished whenever its request can be met from the current work vector. What is the cost of one invocation of the algorithm?
options: O(mn²)
O(mn log n)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The algorithm is a scan inside a loop that repeats while any progress is made. Each scan compares up to n request vectors of length m, and there can be at most n successful scans, because each one finishes at least one process.

Step by step.

  1. One comparison of a request vector with the work vector costs O(m).
  2. One scan tests all n processes: O(mn).
  3. At most n scans can make progress, since each scan marks at least one new process finished.
  4. Total: O(mn) × O(n) = O(mn²).

Answer: Option (C) — O(mn²) per invocation.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (B) ignore the repeated scans.
  • (D) suggests sorting or a divide-and-conquer structure, but the algorithm has neither.

Common misconception. Answering O(mn) by counting one scan. The outer repetition is the expensive part.

Takeaway. This is why the invocation frequency is a policy decision: each call costs O(mn²), so calling it after every request is expensive.

questions.question: Five processes share three resource types with 4, 3 and 3 instances. The allocation is P₁ (2,0,1), P₂ (0,1,0), P₃ (2,0,1), P₄ (0,0,1) and P₅ (0,1,0), leaving the available vector (0,1,0). The outstanding requests are P₁ (2,0,0), P₂ (0,0,0), P₃ (2,0,0), P₄ (0,0,0) and P₅ (0,1,0). How many processes are deadlocked?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With multiple instances, deadlock is decided by the reduction, not by looking for cycles: repeatedly finish every process whose request can be met, adding its allocation back to the work vector. Whatever is left unfinished at the end is deadlocked.

Step by step.

  1. P₁ wants 2 of A, but A is 0 — blocked. P₂ requests nothing — it finishes, returning (0,1,0): work becomes (0,2,0).
  2. P₄ requests nothing — it finishes, returning (0,0,1): work becomes (0,2,1).
  3. P₅ requests (0,1,0) ≤ (0,2,1) — it finishes, returning (0,1,0): work becomes (0,3,1).
  4. P₁ still wants 2 of A and P₃ still wants 2 of A, but no process outside them holds an instance of A: the three that finished released only B and C.
  5. So A stays at 0 while two processes each need 2 units of it — both are permanently blocked.

Answer: Option (C) — 2 processes are deadlocked.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) ignores that A can never become free for P₁ and P₃.
  • (B) counts only one of the two symmetric waiters.
  • (D) wrongly counts the processes that finish; P₂, P₄ and P₅ all complete.

Common misconception. Expecting a cycle. This deadlock has no cycle at all — two processes simply wait for the same type that neither holds enough of. Cycles only characterise single-instance deadlocks.

Takeaway. Run the reduction to the end. The count of unfinished processes is the answer, whether or not a cycle appears.

questions.question: In the readers-preference solution to the readers-writers problem, a writer may wait forever while readers keep arriving. Which one of the following describes that situation?
options: A deadlock, because the writer holds a resource that the readers need.
Starvation, because the writer is blocked indefinitely without any cycle in the wait-for relation.
A circular wait, because the writer and the readers wait for each other.
Hold and wait, because the writer holds a resource while it waits.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Starvation is indefinite blocking with no cycle: the process is not deadlocked, because the resource it waits for is repeatedly released and immediately re-acquired by others. Deadlock needs a cycle in which each holder waits for another.

Step by step.

  1. The writer waits on the mutual-exclusion semaphore for the data.
  2. Under reader preference, a new reader is never blocked by a waiting writer, so it increments the reader count and enters.
  3. The writer's condition — no reader inside — never becomes true while readers arrive faster than they leave.
  4. Nothing is circular and nothing is permanently held by a blocked process: the resource is being used and released all the time. That is starvation.

Answer: Option (B) — starvation without deadlock.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) the writer holds nothing; it is waiting, not holding.
  • (C) no cycle exists: the writer waits for a resource, and no process waits for the writer.
  • (D) hold and wait requires the process to be holding one resource while requesting another.

Common misconception. Calling every indefinite wait a deadlock. Deadlock is a cycle; starvation is an unfair queue.

Takeaway. Ask two questions: is there a cycle? Is anything permanently held? No and no means starvation.

questions.question: A system prevents deadlock by numbering its resource types and requiring every process to request them in strictly increasing order. Which one of the following can still happen?
options: A circular wait, because two processes may each hold a lower-numbered resource.
A process can wait indefinitely if requests for the higher-numbered resources keep being granted to other processes first.
Two processes can deadlock by each holding an instance of the same resource type.
A process that already holds a resource can be forced to give it up before it finishes.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A total order on resource types removes circular wait, and with it deadlock. It says nothing about fairness: the scheme only forbids certain orderings of requests, not certain outcomes of contention.

Step by step.

  1. A cycle needs a process holding a higher-numbered resource and requesting a lower-numbered one. The rule forbids exactly that edge, so no cycle can form — (A) and (C) are impossible.
  2. Fairness is a different matter. If several processes keep requesting R₅ and each is granted it before a particular waiter, that waiter can be postponed without bound.
  3. Nothing in the scheme preempts a held resource, so (D) is also impossible.

Answer: Option (B) — deadlock-free does not mean starvation-free.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (C) both describe a cycle, which the ordering rules out.
  • (D) ordering is a request discipline; it does not add preemption.

Common misconception. Reading "prevents deadlock" as "guarantees every process finishes". The two guarantees are independent.

Takeaway. Prevention removes cycles; bounded waiting needs a queue or aging on top of it.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: Every starved process is deadlocked.
Every deadlocked process is starved.
Starvation always appears as a cycle in the wait-for graph.
A deadlocked process is not blocked.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Deadlock implies indefinite blocking, and indefinite blocking is starvation. The converse fails: starvation can occur with no cycle at all, for example under strict priority scheduling or reader preference.

Step by step.

  1. If a process is deadlocked it will never receive what it waits for, so it waits forever — it is starved. Hence (B) is true.
  2. A low-priority process can be starved forever while every other process keeps finishing. Nothing is permanently held by a blocked process, so there is no deadlock — (A) is false.
  3. Starvation needs no cycle, so (C) is false.
  4. A deadlocked process is by definition blocked, so (D) is false.

Answer: Option (B) — deadlock is a special case of starvation.

Common misconception. Treating the two as synonyms in either direction. The containment is one-way: deadlock ⊂ starvation.

Takeaway. If a question says "starved but not deadlocked", the answer must involve unfair scheduling with no permanent holder.

questions.question: A deadlock is broken by repeatedly pre-empting resources, and the same process can be chosen as victim again and again. Which one of the following is the standard remedy?
options: Always choose as victim the process that holds the largest number of resources.
Include the number of times a process has already been rolled back in the cost of choosing it as victim.
Terminate every deadlocked process at the first detection.
Stop running the detection algorithm once a deadlock has been broken.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Recovery by preemption must itself be starvation-free. The standard cost measure for a victim combines the resources it holds, the work it has already done, and the number of times it has been rolled back. Making the last term grow with each rollback guarantees that no process is chosen forever.

Step by step.

  1. Without the rollback term, a process that is cheap to pre-empt stays cheap for ever.
  2. Adding its rollback count raises its cost each time it is chosen.
  3. Eventually another process becomes the cheapest victim, so the choice rotates.
  4. This is aging applied to victim selection.

Answer: Option (B) — charge each rollback to the victim's cost.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) the largest holder is not necessarily the cheapest to pre-empt; that is what the cost function decides.
  • (C) terminating everyone is the blunt option and loses the most work.
  • (D) new deadlocks would then go undetected.

Common misconception. Thinking recovery ends the problem. Recovery creates a second scheduling problem — which victim — that can itself starve a process.

Takeaway. Every time a system is allowed to choose a victim, add aging or the choice becomes a starvation source.

questions.question: A resource allocation graph in which some resource types have several instances contains no cycle. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: The system may still be deadlocked.
The system cannot be deadlocked.
Exactly one process must be blocked.
Nothing can be concluded, because a cycle is irrelevant when instances are multiple.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A cycle is a necessary condition for deadlock in every resource allocation graph, whatever the instance counts. A graph with no cycle therefore describes a state that is not deadlocked.

Step by step.

  1. In a deadlock every process on the deadlock is blocked, waiting for a resource held by another member.
  2. Following those wait relations must return to the starting process, which traces a cycle.
  3. So a deadlock always leaves a cycle behind; no cycle means no deadlock.
  4. The converse fails only in the other direction: with multiple instances a cycle may exist without a deadlock.

Answer: Option (B) — no cycle means no deadlock.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) contradicts the necessity of a cycle.
  • (C) nothing follows about how many processes are blocked; several may be waiting with no deadlock.
  • (D) the necessity direction is unaffected by instance counts.

Common misconception. Having learned "a cycle is not sufficient with multiple instances", students drop the necessity too. Necessity survives; only sufficiency is lost.

Takeaway. No cycle → definitely safe. Cycle → need the free-instance or reduction check before concluding anything.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about resource allocation graphs are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: When every resource type has exactly one instance, a cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock.
When a resource type has several instances, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock.
A graph with no cycle may still describe a deadlocked system.
If the graph can be reduced completely, by repeatedly removing a process whose requests can all be met, then no process is deadlocked.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Three facts govern the graph. A cycle is always necessary for deadlock. With single instances it is also sufficient. With several instances it is not, and there the reduction test is decisive.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: with one instance per type, a cycle means each process on it waits for something held by the next, so none can proceed.
  2. (B) True: a free instance somewhere on the cycle may let a member finish and break the cycle.
  3. (C) False: since a cycle is necessary, no cycle means no deadlock.
  4. (D) True: complete reducibility means every process can, in some order, be satisfied and finish, which is exactly the absence of deadlock.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (C) reverses the necessity of a cycle — the classic misreading of the multi-instance case.

Common misconception. Learning that "cycles do not always mean deadlock" and concluding that cycles are unrelated to deadlock. Only sufficiency is lost.

Takeaway. Necessity always; sufficiency only for single instances; reduction for everything else.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the banker's algorithm are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every process must declare in advance its maximum claim on each resource type.
If every request is granted only when the resulting state is safe, a deadlock cannot occur.
An unsafe state proves that the system will deadlock.
The algorithm works when a resource type has several instances.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The banker's algorithm is avoidance: it needs future knowledge, checks each request against a simulated state, and refuses any grant that would leave an unsafe state.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: the maximum-claim matrix is the algorithm's input; without it there is no way to look ahead.
  2. (B) True: safety means some completion order exists, and granting only safe requests preserves that invariant, so no deadlock can arise.
  3. (C) False: unsafe means "deadlock is possible", not "deadlock will happen". The processes may still behave well and finish.
  4. (D) True: unlike the claim-edge graph scheme, the banker's algorithm handles multiple instances through the allocation, max and available matrices.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (C) confuses an unsafe state with a deadlocked one. Unsafe is a warning; deadlock is a fact.

Common misconception. Treating unsafe as deadlocked. A system can run for a long time in an unsafe state and never deadlock — it has simply lost its guarantee.

Takeaway. Safe → no deadlock possible. Unsafe → no guarantee, but not a deadlock.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about deadlock detection and recovery are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Running the detection algorithm after every allocation request removes the need for prevention and avoidance, but costs O(mn²) per request.
Detection through the wait-for graph is valid only when every resource type has a single instance.
A process left unfinished when the detection algorithm terminates is deadlocked.
Recovery by terminating one process at a time always needs at most one termination.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Detection is an alternative to prevention and avoidance: let deadlock happen, find it, then recover. Its cost is paid per invocation, and the frequency of invocation is a policy choice.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: detecting immediately after every grant means a deadlock is caught the instant it forms, so no structural prevention is needed — at O(mn²) per request.
  2. (B) True: the wait-for graph collapses a resource to a single edge, which only makes sense when the resource has one instance. With several instances a reduction over the allocation and request matrices is required.
  3. (C) True: that is precisely how the algorithm reports a deadlock — the unfinished set.
  4. (D) False: terminating one process may not break every cycle, and the algorithm has to be re-run; several terminations may be needed.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (D) overstates what one termination achieves; recovery is iterative, and each round costs another detection pass.

Common misconception. Assuming detection is free because it is "just a graph search". At O(mn²) per call, invoking it after every request can dominate the system's cost.

Takeaway. Detection frequency trades CPU for the size of the deadlock you may have to undo. Wait-for graphs are single-instance only.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about starvation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Aging raises the priority of a long-waiting process until it is eventually selected.
First-come first-served scheduling cannot starve a process.
Strict priority scheduling can starve a low-priority process indefinitely.
A deadlocked process will eventually proceed if it waits long enough.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Starvation is indefinite postponement. It is a fairness property of a policy, not a correctness property, and it is cured by bounding the wait, not by removing a cycle.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: aging increases the priority of a waiting process, so its wait is bounded.
  2. (B) True: under FCFS every process is served in arrival order, so the number of processes ahead of any one is fixed and finite.
  3. (C) True: a steady stream of higher-priority work can postpone a low-priority process for ever — the classic case.
  4. (D) False: deadlock is not a waiting-time problem. No amount of waiting releases a resource that is held in a cycle.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (D) confuses starvation with deadlock; the first is cured by fairness, the second only by breaking a cycle.

Common misconception. Believing that a long enough wait fixes everything. For a starved process it may; for a deadlocked one it never will.

Takeaway. Aging and bounded waiting cure starvation. Only preemption, rollback or termination cure deadlock.

questions.question: Four processes share three resource types with 5, 4 and 3 instances. P₁ holds (1,0,1) and needs (1,1,0); P₂ holds (1,1,0) and needs (2,1,0); P₃ holds (1,1,1) and needs (1,2,0); P₄ holds (1,1,1) and needs (2,2,0). The available vector is (1,1,0). Which of the following are safe sequences? (Select all that apply.)
options: ⟨P₁, P₂, P₃, P₄⟩
⟨P₁, P₂, P₄, P₃⟩
⟨P₁, P₃, P₂, P₄⟩
⟨P₂, P₁, P₃, P₄⟩
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A sequence is safe if, taking the processes in that order, each one's remaining need fits in the available vector at its turn, after which its whole allocation is added back.

Step by step. Start from available (1,1,0).

  1. P₁ needs (1,1,0) and fits exactly — available becomes (1,1,0) + (1,0,1) = (2,1,1).
  2. P₂ needs (2,1,0), which fits in (2,1,1) — available becomes (2,1,1) + (1,1,0) = (3,2,1).
  3. From (3,2,1) both P₃ (1,2,0) and P₄ (2,2,0) fit, so the last two can be taken in either order. Options (A) and (B) are safe.
  4. Option (C) takes P₃ second: it needs 2 of B but only 1 is available at that point. Unsafe.
  5. Option (D) takes P₂ first: it needs 2 of A but only 1 is available. Unsafe.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) fails at the second position — P₃ wants more B than is free.
  • (D) fails at the first position — P₂ wants more A than is free.

Common misconception. Checking only whether each process can eventually finish, ignoring the order. Safety is about an order that works step by step.

Takeaway. Simulate the sequence position by position; a process that would be fine later may be impossible now.

questions.question:
R₁ has 4 instances, R₂ has 3 and R₃ has 2. P₁ holds 2 instances of R₁ and 1 of R₂; P₂ holds 1 instance of R₁ and 1 of R₃. No other instance is allocated. How many instances in the system are currently unallocated?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Instances are conserved: the unallocated count is the total number of instances minus the number of assignment edges in the graph. Each assignment edge consumes exactly one instance.

Step by step.

  1. Total instances = 4 + 3 + 2 = 9.
  2. Allocated = 2 + 1 (from P₁) + 1 + 1 (from P₂) = 5.
  3. Unallocated = 9 − 5 = 4.

Answer: 4 instances (any integer value 4 is accepted).

Common misconception. Counting resource types instead of instances. Three types hold nine instances; the answer is not 3 − 2.

Takeaway. The available vector is simply total minus the column sums of the allocation matrix. Compute it that way, never by eye.

questions.question:
Three processes share two resource types A and B with 6 and 5 instances. P₁ holds (1,2) and needs (1,1); P₂ holds (2,1) and needs (2,3); P₃ holds (1,0) and needs (2,2). The available vector is (2,2). P₂ now asks for k instances of B in a single request. What is the largest k for which the resulting state is still safe?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Three tests again: the request must not exceed the remaining need, must not exceed availability, and the state after a pretend allocation must be safe. The claim limit alone is never the answer.

Step by step.

  1. k is bounded by P₂'s need of 3 units of B, and by the 2 free units of B.
  2. k = 1: available becomes (2,1) and P₂'s need (2,2). P₁ (1,1) fits, releasing (1,2) to give (3,3); then P₂ fits, then P₃. Safe.
  3. k = 2: available becomes (2,0) and the need (2,1). Nothing fits — P₁ wants 1 of B, P₂ wants 1 of B, P₃ wants 2 of B, and B is 0. Unsafe.
  4. k = 3 would exceed the available 2 units of B and could not be granted at all.

Answer: 1.

Common misconception. Answering 3 because the remaining need is 3. The claim limit is an upper bound on what may be asked, not on what may be granted.

Takeaway. Take the minimum of three bounds: the remaining need, the available units, and the largest value that keeps the state safe.

questions.question:
Every resource type in a system has exactly one instance. The wait-for graph has the edges P₁ → P₂, P₂ → P₃, P₃ → P₁, P₄ → P₃, P₅ → P₆ and P₆ → P₅. How many processes lie on a cycle in this graph?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With single-instance resources the wait-for graph is exact: a cycle is a deadlock. Identify every cycle, then count the distinct processes that lie on one.

Step by step.

  1. P₁ → P₂ → P₃ → P₁ is a 3-cycle: P₁, P₂, P₃.
  2. P₅ → P₆ → P₅ is a 2-cycle: P₅, P₆.
  3. P₄ → P₃ is an edge into the first cycle, not part of any cycle, so P₄ is not counted.
  4. Distinct processes on a cycle: 3 + 2 = 5.

Answer: 5.

Common misconception. Counting P₄ because it is blocked forever too. The question asks for cycle membership; a process that merely waits on a cycle is blocked, but it is not on the cycle.

Takeaway. Read the question's exact wording: "on a cycle" and "blocked" are different counts, and both appear in GATE papers.

questions.question:
A system has three processes and three resource types, with 2 instances of A, 2 of B and 2 of C. P₁ holds (0,1,1) and needs (2,0,0); P₂ has been allocated nothing yet and needs (2,1,0); P₃ holds (2,0,1) and needs (0,2,0). The available vector is (0,1,0). What is the smallest number of additional instances of resource A that must be added so that a safe sequence exists?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A safe sequence exists when some process's remaining need can be met, releasing its allocation and repeating. Adding instances enlarges the available vector, and the question asks for the smallest enlargement that makes the first step possible.

Step by step.

  1. With 0 extra: available (0,1,0). P₁ and P₂ each want 2 of A with none free, and P₃ wants 2 of B with only 1 free. Unsafe.
  2. With 1 extra: available (1,1,0). Still nothing fits — both A-needers want 2, and P₃ still wants 2 of B.
  3. With 2 extra: available (2,1,0). P₁ (2,0,0) fits, releasing (0,1,1) to give (2,2,1).
  4. P₂ (2,1,0) fits, releasing nothing, so the work vector stays (2,2,1).
  5. P₃ (0,2,0) fits. Safe.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Answering 1 because a process becomes satisfiable — it does not: with one extra A the available vector is (1,1,0) and both A-needers still want 2 units.

Takeaway. Find the smallest remaining need on the scarce resource, add exactly enough to meet it, then confirm that the rest of the sequence follows.

questions.question:
A readers-writers solution gives readers preference: a writer waits until no reader is inside the critical section, and a waiting writer never delays a new reader. From t = 0 a writer waits, and readers arrive so that at least one reader is inside the critical section for the whole of the next 500 seconds. How many times does the writer enter its critical section during those 500 seconds?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Reader preference gives readers priority over any waiting writer. The writer's entry condition — no reader inside — is therefore never satisfied while readers keep arriving.

Step by step.

  1. The writer can enter only when the reader count is zero and no new reader is admitted ahead of it.
  2. Reader preference explicitly allows a new reader to enter even while a writer waits.
  3. Since at least one reader is inside for the entire interval, the count never reaches zero.
  4. So the writer's condition never becomes true and it enters 0 times — indefinite postponement, that is, starvation.

Answer: 0.

Common misconception. Assuming the writer must eventually get a turn. Under reader preference there is no bound on the number of readers that may pass a waiting writer, so no turn is guaranteed.

Takeaway. Preference rules decide who starves. Readers-preference starves writers; writers-preference starves readers; a fair solution bounds the wait for both.

questions.question: A process is loaded into a contiguous region whose base register holds 8000 and whose limit register holds 600. The memory unit adds the base to every offset it is given, but only after the limit check. Which one of the following offsets is rejected with a trap?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A base–limit pair defines the legal window of a process. The limit register holds the size of the region, not its last address, so the legal offsets are 0 ≤ offset < limit. The hardware compares the offset with the limit before it forms base + offset.

Step by step.

  1. The window is [8000, 8000 + 600) = [8000, 8600) in physical memory.
  2. Offset 0 gives physical address 8000 — legal.
  3. Offset 350 gives 8350 — legal.
  4. Offset 599 gives 8599, the last byte of the region — legal.
  5. Offset 600 gives 8600, one byte past the region. The comparison 600 < 600 is false, so the reference traps.

Answer: Option (D) — offset 600 is the first offset that fails the limit check.

Common misconception. Treating the limit as the highest legal address. It is a length, so the highest legal offset is limit − 1. Reading the limit as an inclusive bound makes 600 look legal and also lets a one-byte overrun through.

questions.question: Which one of the following schemes can suffer internal fragmentation but can never suffer external fragmentation?
options: Contiguous allocation with first fit
Fixed-size partitions
Pure segmentation
Dynamic contiguous allocation with compaction
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Internal fragmentation is space wasted inside an allocated block, because the block is larger than the request. External fragmentation is free space wasted outside the allocated blocks, in holes too small to serve a request. A scheme in which every block is the same fixed size always wastes the tail of the block and never produces holes of varying size, so it has the first and not the second.

Step by step.

  1. Fixed partitions are of one size. A request smaller than the partition wastes the remainder inside the partition — internal fragmentation.
  2. Every free partition is exactly one partition in size, so any request that fits the partition size fits some free partition. No free space is stranded in odd-sized holes — no external fragmentation.
  3. First fit, worst fit and the rest allocate variable-size blocks from variable-size holes, so they can strand space externally.
  4. Pure segmentation allocates variable-size segments, which also strands space externally.

Answer: Option (B) — fixed-size partitions.

Common misconception. Believing that paging-style schemes have neither kind. Paging and fixed partitions have internal fragmentation only; pure segmentation and dynamic contiguous allocation have external fragmentation only; paged segmentation has internal fragmentation and no external fragmentation.

questions.question: Four free holes of 100 KB, 500 KB, 300 KB and 600 KB lie in that address order. A request for 250 KB arrives. Which one of the following states correctly which hole first fit and best fit choose?
options: First fit takes the 500 KB hole; best fit also takes the 500 KB hole.
First fit takes the 500 KB hole; best fit takes the 300 KB hole.
First fit takes the 300 KB hole; best fit also takes the 300 KB hole.
First fit takes the 600 KB hole; best fit takes the 300 KB hole.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. First fit scans the free list in address order and stops at the first hole that is large enough. Best fit scans the whole list and takes the smallest hole that is large enough. Worst fit takes the largest hole.

Step by step.

  1. First fit meets 100 KB (too small) and then 500 KB, which is the first hole that fits 250 KB. It takes 500 KB and leaves a 250 KB remnant.
  2. Best fit compares every hole that fits: 500 KB, 300 KB and 600 KB. The smallest is 300 KB.
  3. Best fit therefore takes the 300 KB hole and leaves a 50 KB remnant.

Answer: Option (B) — first fit takes 500 KB, best fit takes 300 KB.

Common misconception. Thinking first fit and best fit coincide whenever the first hole that fits is also a good fit. Here the first fitting hole is 500 KB while the smallest fitting hole is 300 KB, so the two policies split different holes and leave different remnants (250 KB against 50 KB).

questions.question:
Free holes of 300 KB, 150 KB, 500 KB and 250 KB lie in that address order. Three requests arrive in the order 200 KB, 120 KB and 400 KB. The allocator uses first fit with no compaction. What is the total size of all free memory remaining, in KB, after the three requests have been placed?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. First fit walks the holes in address order and splits the first hole that is large enough, leaving the remainder in place. The remainders of earlier requests are therefore still candidates for later requests, and the order of the requests changes the outcome.

Step by step.

  1. Request 200 KB: 300 KB is the first hole that fits. It becomes 100 KB. Holes: 100, 150, 500, 250.
  2. Request 120 KB: 100 is too small, 150 fits. It becomes 30 KB. Holes: 100, 30, 500, 250.
  3. Request 400 KB: 100 and 30 are too small, 500 fits. It becomes 100 KB. Holes: 100, 30, 100, 250.
  4. Total free memory = 100 + 30 + 100 + 250 = 480 KB.

Answer: 480 KB.

Common misconception. Subtracting the request sizes from the total and reporting 1200 − 720 = 480 as if it were a check on the allocation. The arithmetic agrees here only because every request was placed; it would not detect a request that failed for want of a large enough hole. Track the holes, not just the totals.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about dynamic contiguous allocation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Under the 50-percent rule, if N blocks have been allocated, about N/2 further blocks are expected to be lost to fragmentation.
Next fit restarts its scan at the beginning of the free list on every request.
Worst fit tends to leave behind holes that are too small to be useful.
Compaction removes external fragmentation but costs processor time and requires that every process be able to move at run time.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The four facts that decide these options are the 50-percent rule, the difference between next fit and first fit, the remnant each policy leaves, and the price of compaction.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. The statistical result is that for every N allocated blocks roughly N/2 more blocks are lost to fragmentation, so about a third of memory is unusable. The reason is that the average remnant is half the average request.
  2. (B) False. That describes first fit. Next fit continues the scan from the point where the previous allocation finished, wrapping to the start of the list, so that the search does not always begin at low addresses.
  3. (C) False. Worst fit takes the largest hole, so the remnant it leaves is the largest of the three policies. It is best fit that leaves tiny, unusable remnants.
  4. (D) True. Compaction slides the allocated blocks together, which is a copy of memory and therefore processor time, and it is only possible if addresses can be relocated at run time — which is why base–limit or paging hardware is a precondition.

Answer: Options (A) and (D).

Common misconception. The names invite the error in (C): "worst" suggests the worst outcome. Worst fit is the policy that leaves the best remnants; it is merely wasteful because it never preserves a large hole for a large request.

questions.question: Free holes of 120 KB, 150 KB and 400 KB lie in that address order. Three requests arrive in the order 260 KB, 140 KB and 150 KB, and no compaction is available. Which allocation policy can satisfy all three requests?
options: First fit only
Best fit only
Both first fit and best fit
Neither first fit nor best fit
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. No policy dominates. First fit is faster and usually at least as good, but it can consume a large hole that a later request needs while best fit happens to leave that hole untouched. The only way to answer is to simulate both.

Step by step.

  1. First fit. 260 KB: the first hole that fits is 400 KB, which becomes 140 KB. Holes: 120, 150, 140. Next, 140 KB: the first hole that fits is 150 KB, which becomes 10 KB. Holes: 120, 10, 140. Next, 150 KB: no hole is large enough — the request fails.
  2. Best fit. 260 KB: the only hole that fits is 400 KB, which becomes 140 KB. Holes: 120, 150, 140. Next, 140 KB: the smallest fitting hole is the 140 KB remnant, which becomes 0. Holes: 120, 150, 0. Next, 150 KB: the 150 KB hole fits exactly and becomes 0. All three requests are placed.
  3. So the sequence is feasible under best fit and infeasible under first fit.

Answer: Option (B) — best fit only.

Common misconception. Remembering "first fit is generally better than best fit" as a theorem. It is an empirical average over workloads, not a guarantee: the counterexample above shows a request sequence on which first fit fails and best fit succeeds.

questions.question: A system uses single-level paging with the page table held in main memory and has no TLB. How many main-memory accesses does one ordinary load or store take?
options: Two: one to read the page-table entry and one to reach the data
One: the page table is consulted by dedicated hardware that does not touch memory
Three: the page table, a segment table and then the data
One extra access for every level of the page table, and none for the data
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With the page table in memory, the page number must be translated into a frame number before the data can be addressed, and that translation is itself a memory read.

Step by step.

  1. The CPU forms a virtual address; its page number indexes the page table.
  2. Access 1: read the page-table entry at PTBR + page × entry size. This yields the frame number and the valid and protection bits.
  3. Access 2: form frame × page size + offset and read or write the data.
  4. So a reference costs two memory accesses, which is why the effective access time roughly doubles and why a TLB is worth its cost.

Answer: Option (A) — two accesses.

Common misconception. Assuming the page table lives in fast registers or in a cache the hardware consults for free. Only the page-table base register is a register; the table itself is in memory, and with two levels of paging a reference without a TLB costs three accesses.

questions.question: A TLB has 128 entries and the page size is 8 KB. Assuming perfect replacement, what is the TLB reach — the amount of memory that can be mapped without a page-table walk?
options: 128 KB
512 KB
1 MB
8 MB
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The TLB reach is the number of TLB entries multiplied by the page size: it is the working set that the TLB can cover at once.

Step by step.

  1. Entries = 128 = 2⁷.
  2. Page size = 8 KB = 2¹³ bytes.
  3. Reach = 2⁷ × 2¹³ = 2²⁰ = 1 MB.
  4. The practical consequence: with 8 KB pages, 128 entries cover 1 MB, so a program whose hot working set exceeds 1 MB will thrash the TLB unless the page size or the number of entries is increased.

Answer: Option (C) — 1 MB.

Common misconception. Multiplying by the frame number width or by the entry size. The reach counts bytes of address space covered, so it is entries × page size; entry size affects the cost of the TLB, not its coverage.

questions.question: A single-level page table has 2¹⁹ entries and each entry is 8 bytes wide. How much main memory does the table itself occupy?
options: 2 MB
4 MB
8 MB
512 KB
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A page table is an array: its size is the number of entries times the width of one entry. The entries are needed for the whole virtual page range of the process, whether or not the pages are in use.

Step by step.

  1. Entries = 2¹⁹ = 524288.
  2. Size = 2¹⁹ × 8 = 2¹⁹ × 2³ = 2²² = 4194304 bytes.
  3. 2²² bytes = 4 MB.
  4. This is exactly the pressure that motivates two-level and inverted tables: a 4 MB array per process, most of it empty, is wasteful when the process touches a few megabytes.

Answer: Option (B) — 4 MB.

Common misconception. Confusing the number of entries with the number of bytes, or using 2¹⁹ entries as if it were 2²⁰. Keep the two powers of two separate: the entry count and the entry width multiply.

questions.question:
A TLB search costs 20 ns and a main-memory access costs 100 ns. The system uses a single-level page table in memory. The effective access time is 20 + 100 + (1 − h) × 100 ns, where h is the TLB hit ratio. What is the smallest hit ratio, in per cent, that keeps the effective access time at or below 130 ns?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Every reference pays the TLB search and the data access. A hit adds nothing more; a miss adds one extra memory access for the page-table entry.

Step by step.

  1. Hit path: 20 + 100 = 120 ns.
  2. Miss path: 20 + 100 + 100 = 220 ns.
  3. Expected time: h × 120 + (1 − h) × 220 = 220 − 100h, which is the same as 120 + 100(1 − h).
  4. Require 120 + 100(1 − h) ≤ 130, so 100(1 − h) ≤ 10 and 1 − h ≤ 0.1.
  5. Hence h ≥ 0.9, that is 90 per cent. At exactly 90 per cent the effective time is 130 ns, which meets the bound.

Answer: 90 (per cent).

Common misconception. Charging the TLB search only on a hit. The TLB is looked up on every reference, so its 20 ns is paid unconditionally; only the extra 100 ns is probabilistic.

questions.question: On a machine with 64-bit virtual addresses and 4 KB pages, a single-level page table would need 2⁵² entries. The main reason two-level paging helps is that it:
options: halves the width of each page-table entry
reduces the number of page faults
lets the system allocate page tables only for the parts of the address space a process actually uses
removes the need for a TLB
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A single-level table must be contiguous and must cover the whole virtual range, so its size is set by the address width, not by what the process touches. Splitting the page number into an outer and an inner index lets the outer table point at inner tables that are created only when the corresponding region is used.

Step by step.

  1. Single level: one array of 2⁵² entries — petabytes of table for a process that may touch a few megabytes.
  2. Two levels: an outer table of 2²⁹ entries (for an 18/18/12 split) whose entries point at inner tables of 2¹⁸ entries each. An inner table exists only if some page in that region is mapped.
  3. Total table memory therefore grows with the used address space, which is the saving.
  4. The costs are an extra memory access per miss and a worse locality pattern; the entry width and the page-fault rate are unchanged.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Believing a multi-level table is smaller per entry or cheaper per reference. It is neither — it is exactly the opposite per reference. The gain is purely that unused regions cost nothing.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the choice of page size are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Increasing the page size reduces the number of page-table entries and increases the TLB reach.
Increasing the page size increases internal fragmentation, because the last page of an object is partly unused.
Increasing the page size increases the number of page faults for a program that scans memory sequentially.
Decreasing the page size reduces the number of bytes transferred per page fault but increases the size of the page tables.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Page size trades three quantities against one another: table size, TLB coverage and internal fragmentation, with fault granularity riding on the same choice.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Doubling the page size removes one bit from the page number, so the number of entries halves; the TLB reach, entries × page size, grows.
  2. (B) True. Allocation is in whole pages, so on average half a page is wasted per object. A larger page wastes more per object.
  3. (C) False. Sequential scanning touches every byte, so the number of pages covered — and hence the number of faults — falls as the page size grows. Larger pages mean fewer, larger transfers.
  4. (D) True. Smaller pages mean more pages, hence more entries, hence larger tables and a smaller TLB reach; the benefit is that each fault brings in less data and internal fragmentation falls.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Reading (C) as "larger pages cause more faults" because each fault costs more. The number of faults falls with larger pages; what rises is the bytes moved per fault and the internal fragmentation.

questions.question:
A machine has 48-bit virtual addresses and 4 KB pages. Paging is two-level, with the page number split into an 18-bit outer index and an 18-bit inner index, and each page-table entry is 8 bytes. What is the size of one second-level page table, in KB?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A second-level table is indexed by the inner index, so it has 2¹⁸ entries, each of the stated width. Its size is the product, whatever the outer table does.

Step by step.

  1. Check the split: 4 KB pages give log₂4096 = 12 offset bits; 18 + 18 + 12 = 48, so the whole address is accounted for.
  2. Entries in a second-level table = 2¹⁸ = 262144.
  3. Size = 262144 × 8 = 2097152 bytes = 2 MB.
  4. 2 MB = 2048 KB.

Answer: 2048 KB (2 MB).

Common misconception. Using all 36 index bits for one table. Each level is indexed by its own field only; using 36 bits gives 2³⁶ entries, a table 262144 times too large.

questions.question: Which one of the following is a direct consequence of keying an inverted page table by frame rather than by virtual page?
options: The table has one entry per physical frame, so its size is fixed by physical memory and not by the size of any address space.
The table has one entry per virtual page of each process, so its size grows with the number of processes.
The table has one entry per segment, so its size grows with the segment count.
The table has one entry per page-table entry of each process, so it is the same size as the sum of all per-process tables.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An inverted page table stores exactly one entry for each physical frame. The frame number is the index, and the entry records which process and which virtual page currently occupy that frame.

Step by step.

  1. The number of frames is physical memory ÷ page size, a property of the machine.
  2. So the table size is one system-wide array of that many entries — no per-process tables at all.
  3. The saving is large: 64-bit address spaces can be supported with a table of a few million entries instead of 2⁵² entries per process.
  4. The cost is that the table is no longer indexed by what the hardware supplies (the page number), so a lookup needs a search or a hash.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Assuming the table is per process. There is exactly one inverted table for the whole system, which is why an entry must carry a process identifier.

questions.question: Which field must an inverted page-table entry contain that a per-process page table does not need?
options: A frame number
A valid bit
A reference bit
A process identifier
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In a per-process page table the owner of the table is implicit: the table belongs to one process, so the page number alone identifies the mapping. A single system-wide inverted table holds mappings of every process, and page 5 of one process has nothing to do with page 5 of another.

Step by step.

  1. The index of an inverted entry is the frame number, so the frame number itself need not be stored as a lookup key — that rules out (A).
  2. Valid and reference bits are ordinary control bits that per-process tables carry as well — that rules out (B) and (C).
  3. What is genuinely new is ownership: the entry must say whose page this frame holds, otherwise two processes mapping the same virtual page number would be indistinguishable.
  4. Hence the entry is a triple (pid, page, control bits) for each frame.

Answer: Option (D) — a process identifier (or address-space identifier).

Common misconception. Thinking the frame number must be stored because the table is "about frames". The frame number is the array index; storing it would duplicate the index.

questions.question:
A machine has 512 MB of physical memory and 4 KB pages. Its inverted page table has one 8-byte entry per frame. What is the size of the table, in KB?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The number of inverted entries equals the number of frames, and each entry costs its stated width.

Step by step.

  1. Frames = 512 MB ÷ 4 KB = 2²⁹ ÷ 2¹² = 2¹⁷ = 131072.
  2. Table size = 131072 × 8 = 1048576 bytes.
  3. 1048576 bytes = 1 MB = 1024 KB.
  4. Compare that with a per-process single-level table for a 48-bit address space, which would need 2³⁶ entries — the inverted table is smaller by many orders of magnitude.

Answer: 1024 KB (1 MB).

Common misconception. Using the virtual address width to size the table. Only physical memory and the page size matter; the virtual address width plays no part.

questions.question: Two processes share one physical frame that holds a read-only library page. Why is this awkward in a system with a single inverted page table?
options: Because the frame number of a shared page would have to change for each process
Because the TLB can hold only one entry per frame and would keep evicting the shared page
Because each frame has exactly one entry, so the frame can name only one (process, virtual page) mapping; sharing needs extra entries or an auxiliary structure
Because sharing requires both processes to place the page at the same virtual page number
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An inverted table is a function frame → (process, page). It is one-to-one by construction. Sharing needs the inverse: two distinct virtual pages must map to the same frame, which is two domain elements with one image.

Step by step.

  1. Per-process page tables express sharing trivially: both tables point their own entries at the same frame number.
  2. In an inverted table there is one slot per frame, and that slot can record only one owner. A second process mapping the same frame has nowhere to be recorded.
  3. The usual fixes are to allow chains of mappings in one entry, or to keep a small side table of shared mappings — both add work to every miss.
  4. The frame number is a property of the frame and does not vary per process, so (A) is wrong; the TLB is not limited to one entry per frame, so (B) is wrong; virtual addresses need not agree, so (D) is wrong.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Assuming sharing works as it does with per-process tables. The direction of the mapping is reversed, and that is precisely what makes sharing the standard objection to inverted tables.

questions.question: Consider a machine whose only translation structure is one system-wide inverted page table. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: There is one entry per physical frame, so the table size is independent of the virtual address width.
A translation that misses the TLB may require a hash-table search on the (process, page) pair, because the table is not indexed by the page number.
The table is system-wide rather than per process, so a context switch does not have to change the table base register to a different table.
Sharing a frame between two processes is easier than with per-process page tables, because the frame has a single entry.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The inverted table is one array indexed by frame. Everything that follows — its size, its lookup cost, its sharing behaviour — follows from that one decision.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Entries = frames = physical memory ÷ page size. A 64-bit address space costs nothing extra.
  2. (B) True. The hardware supplies a page number, but the table is keyed by frame, so the entry must be found by a search. Real systems hash on (pid, page) and chain collisions.
  3. (C) True. One table serves every process, so switching processes does not switch tables; only the entries' ownership changes meaning.
  4. (D) False. One entry per frame means one (process, page) mapping per frame, so a shared frame cannot be named by both processes. Sharing is the weak point of this design.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Reading (D) as a benefit of the single entry. The single entry is exactly the obstruction: sharing requires two mappings into one frame.

questions.question:
A machine has 16 GB of physical memory and 8 KB pages. How many entries does its inverted page table contain?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. One entry per frame: the count is physical memory divided by the page size, with both quantities in the same unit.

Step by step.

  1. 16 GB = 2⁴ × 2³⁰ = 2³⁴ bytes.
  2. 8 KB = 2³ × 2¹⁰ = 2¹³ bytes.
  3. Entries = 2³⁴ ÷ 2¹³ = 2²¹ = 2097152.
  4. With 16-byte entries the table would occupy 32 MB — a fixed cost, whatever the processes' virtual address spaces look like.

Answer: 2097152 entries.

Common misconception. Mixing GB and KB by treating 16 GB as 16 × 10⁶ KB. Work in powers of two: the quotient is exact only when both sides use the same base.

questions.question: In a segmented memory system, a logical address is a pair that consists of:
options: a segment number and an offset within the segment
a page number and an offset within the page
a frame number and an offset within the frame
a single linear address that the segment table is not consulted for
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Segmentation is a visible division of the address space into variable-length, logically meaningful pieces: code, data, stack, a procedure, an array. The programmer or compiler names a segment and an offset inside it, so the logical address is two-dimensional.

Step by step.

  1. The segment number indexes the segment table.
  2. The entry supplies a base and a limit.
  3. The offset is checked against the limit and then added to the base to give a physical address.
  4. Paging, by contrast, is invisible: the compiler emits one linear address and the hardware splits it into page number and offset.

Answer: Option (A) — segment number and offset.

Common misconception. Describing the segmented address as (page, offset). That is the paged form; the two schemes differ in whether the split is visible to the program and in whether the pieces have a fixed size.

questions.question: A segment table entry holds base 8000 and limit 500. What happens for the offsets 400 and 500?
options: Offset 400 gives physical address 8400; offset 500 traps.
Offset 400 gives 8400; offset 500 gives 8500.
Offset 400 gives 8000; offset 500 gives 8500.
Both offsets trap, because only the base is known.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The limit is the length of the segment, so legal offsets are 0 ≤ offset < limit. A legal offset is added to the base.

Step by step.

  1. Offset 400: 400 < 500, so it is legal; physical address = 8000 + 400 = 8400.
  2. Offset 500: 500 < 500 is false, so the hardware raises a trap (a segmentation fault) before any address is formed.
  3. This check is what makes segmentation a protection mechanism: a wild index into an array cannot reach another segment.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Treating the limit as an inclusive bound and returning 8500. That would let a process read one byte outside its segment — the classic off-by-one that segmentation exists to prevent.

questions.question: A segmented machine uses a 12-bit segment number and 8-byte segment-table entries. How large is the segment table of a process that can name any segment?
options: 8 KB
16 KB
32 KB
64 KB
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The segment number is an index, so the table must have one entry for every value the field can take; the entry width then fixes the total.

Step by step.

  1. Entries = 2¹² = 4096.
  2. Size = 4096 × 8 = 32768 bytes.
  3. 32768 bytes = 32 KB.
  4. The table is per process and small compared with a page table for the same address width, which is one reason segmentation is attractive when the number of segments is modest.

Answer: Option (C) — 32 KB.

Common misconception. Sizing the table by the number of segments the program actually uses. The hardware indexes with the full field, so the table must cover every encodable segment number unless the entry count is stored separately and checked.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about segment tables and paged segmentation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A segment-table entry normally holds a base and a limit, and the limit check is made before the base is used.
Because the segment table is held in ordinary registers, a segmented reference never needs an extra memory access.
Paging each segment removes external fragmentation while keeping the two-dimensional (segment, offset) view of the address space.
In paged segmentation the offset within a segment is itself split into a page number and a page displacement.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Paged segmentation combines the logical view of segmentation with the allocation granularity of paging: a segment is divided into pages, and the segment-table entry points at that segment's page table.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. The entry gives the segment's location and its length; the offset is checked against the length so that a reference cannot escape the segment.
  2. (B) False. The segment table is in main memory, not in registers — only its base register is. Without a TLB, the reference costs an extra access for the segment-table entry, and in paged segmentation two extra accesses.
  3. (C) True. Segments are no longer contiguous in physical memory; each is paged, so no odd-sized holes are created, yet the program still names (segment, offset).
  4. (D) True. The offset is decomposed into a page number that indexes the segment's page table and a displacement inside the page.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing paging under segmentation restores the single-access translation of pure paging. It adds a level: the segment table must be read before the segment's page table.

questions.question: Which of the following statements comparing segmentation with paging are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Segmentation is visible to the programmer and the compiler; paging is transparent to them.
Pure segmentation can suffer external fragmentation, while pure paging cannot.
A pure paging system can give a procedure its own protection as naturally as segmentation does, because every page can carry its own protection bits.
Paged segmentation offers both the logical two-dimensional address space of segmentation and the absence of external fragmentation that paging provides.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Segmentation divides by meaning, paging by size. The first gives a visible, variable-length structure and therefore external fragmentation; the second gives fixed-size frames and therefore internal fragmentation.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. The compiler emits segment-relative addresses; nobody emits page-relative ones, because the page split is the hardware's business.
  2. (B) True. Variable-length segments leave holes of odd sizes. Paging allocates whole frames, so the only waste is the tail of the last page.
  3. (C) False. Page protection bits exist, but pages are arbitrary slices of the address space: a procedure may straddle a page boundary, so per-procedure protection is not natural. Segmentation makes the boundary coincide with the protection unit.
  4. (D) True. That is exactly the motivation for paged segmentation — logical units for the programmer, fixed-size allocation for the memory manager.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Concluding from (C) that paging gives protection and segmentation does not, or the reverse. Both protect; the difference is whether the protection unit coincides with a logical unit.

questions.question: A paged segmentation system uses 1 KB pages. The segment-table entry for segment 3 gives a page-table base of 20000 and a limit of 3000 bytes; page-table entries are 4 bytes each. Page-table entry 2 of that table holds frame 40. What physical address does the offset 2050 map to?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In paged segmentation the offset inside a segment is itself split into a page number (index into that segment's page table) and a displacement (offset inside the page). The segment limit is checked against the whole offset first.

Step by step.

  1. Limit check: 2050 < 3000, so the offset is inside the segment.
  2. Split the offset with 1 KB pages: page number = 2050 ÷ 1024 = 2, displacement = 2050 − 2 × 1024 = 2.
  3. Locate the entry: 20000 + 2 × 4 = 20008. It holds frame 40.
  4. Physical address = 40 × 1024 + 2 = 40960 + 2 = 40962.
  5. The distractors are the frame base without the displacement (40960), the offset added to the page-table base (2250) and the displacement added to the wrong frame base (43010).

Answer: Option (D) — 40962.

Common misconception. Adding the whole offset to the page-table base, or adding the displacement to the page-table base rather than to the frame base. Two multiplications are needed: one by the entry width to find the entry, one by the page size to find the frame.

questions.question: A running process references a page whose page-table entry has its valid bit clear. Which one of the following is the first thing the hardware and the operating system do?
options: The operating system selects a victim frame and writes it back to the backing store.
The memory-management unit raises a trap, and the operating system first checks that the address lies inside the process's address space.
The process is killed immediately with a segmentation fault.
The faulting instruction is restarted at once, without any transfer from the backing store.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The valid–invalid bit of a page-table entry is the trap door of demand paging: a reference to an invalid entry stops the instruction and hands control to the operating system. That trap is only a candidate fault, because an invalid entry can mean two very different things — the page is legal but not in memory, or the address is outside the process's address space.

Step by step.

  1. The MMU translates the address, finds the valid bit clear, and raises a trap.
  2. The operating system checks the faulting address against the process's address space.
  3. If the address is legal, the page is fetched from the backing store into a free or evicted frame, the entry is updated, and the instruction is restarted.
  4. If the address is illegal, the fault becomes a segmentation violation and the process is terminated.

Answer: Option (B) — trap first, then the address-space check.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Choosing a victim is pointless if the address turns out to be illegal, and it is not the first step even for a legal fault.
  • (C) Termination is the outcome of the check failing, not of the fault itself.
  • (D) Restarting before the page is in memory simply faults again, forever.

Common misconception. Treating every invalid entry as "bring in a page". A large share of GATE questions on this point turn on the legal-but-absent against illegal distinction.

Takeaway. Fault → trap → validate the address → fetch and restart, or kill.

questions.question:
A process makes 4,000,000 memory references and suffers 2,000 page faults. The memory access time is 250 ns and the page-fault service time is 4 ms. What is the effective access time, in nanoseconds, rounded to the nearest integer?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A reference either hits (cost ma, probability 1 − p) or faults (cost s, probability p), so EAT = (1 − p) ma + p s. The fault rate has to be computed from the run, not guessed.

Step by step.

  1. p = 2,000 / 4,000,000 = 5 × 10−4.
  2. Hit part: (1 − 5 × 10−4) × 250 = 249.875 ns.
  3. Fault part: 5 × 10−4 × 4,000,000 = 2,000 ns.
  4. EAT = 249.875 + 2,000 = 2,249.875 ≈ 2,250 ns.

Answer: 2250 ns (about 9 times the fault-free access time).

Common misconception. Forgetting to convert 4 ms to 4,000,000 ns before mixing it with a nanosecond access time, which understates the fault term by a factor of a million.

Takeaway. At p = 5 × 10−4 the fault term already dominates: 2,000 ns of 2,250 ns.

questions.question: Which one of the following bits of a page-table entry is set by the hardware on every reference and later read by the replacement algorithm?
options: The valid–invalid bit
The dirty (modify) bit
The protection bits
The reference bit
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A page-table entry carries several independent flags. The valid bit says whether the page is in memory, the dirty bit records a write, the protection bits record read/write/execute permission, and the reference bit records that the page was touched. Only the reference bit exists to feed the replacement algorithm.

Step by step.

  1. Hardware sets the reference bit on any access to the page.
  2. Approximations of LRU — clock, second chance, aging — read and clear it to estimate recency.
  3. The dirty bit is set on a write and is read when the page is chosen as a victim, to decide whether a write-back is needed.
  4. The valid bit is read during translation itself, to decide whether a fault is raised.

Answer: Option (D) — the reference bit.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) The valid bit drives fault detection, not victim selection.
  • (B) The dirty bit answers "must I write this back?", not "which page should I evict?".
  • (C) Protection bits enforce access rights and play no part in replacement.

Common misconception. Confusing the dirty bit with the reference bit. A page can be referenced many times and never written, and a page can be written without being the least recently used.

Takeaway. Valid → fault, dirty → write-back, reference → replacement, protection → access control.

questions.question: An instruction reads a value from the last byte of page 10, reads a second value from the first byte of page 11, and stores their sum at the first byte of page 12. The page holding the instruction is resident, pages 10 and 11 are not resident, and page 12 is resident. How many page faults does this instruction take, and how does execution proceed?
options: One fault, because the operating system brings in every page the instruction can touch at the first fault.
Two faults; after each fault the page is brought in and the whole instruction is restarted from the beginning.
Two faults; after each fault execution resumes at the point where it stopped.
No faults, because the fault is deferred until the instruction has finished computing.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Faults are raised per reference, not per instruction, and the standard model restarts the instruction after the fault is serviced. An instruction that touches several pages can therefore fault several times, and every fault replays the accesses that already succeeded.

Step by step.

  1. First access, page 10: invalid → fault 1; page 10 is loaded; the instruction restarts.
  2. Second attempt: the access to page 10 now succeeds; the access to page 11 faults → fault 2; page 11 is loaded; the instruction restarts again.
  3. Third attempt: both reads succeed, the store to page 12 succeeds, the instruction completes.
  4. Total: two faults, with the instruction restarted twice.

Answer: Option (B) — two faults, with the instruction restarted after each one.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) describes prepaging, a separate policy, not what a fault does.
  • (C) describes mid-instruction resumption, which needs far more hardware state than the restart model keeps.
  • (D) is impossible: the store cannot complete without the operands.

Common misconception. Assuming a single fault per instruction. Long string or block instructions that straddle pages can fault once per page they touch.

Takeaway. One fault per missing page touched, and the instruction restarts each time.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the work a page-fault handler does are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: If the victim frame is dirty, servicing the fault needs two block transfers instead of one.
The page-fault handler runs in the context of the faulting process, and the process is blocked while the transfer proceeds.
A reference to a page that is resident but not writable by this process is a protection fault rather than a page fault.
Servicing a fault may require the operating system to drop a translation from the TLB before the instruction is restarted.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A page fault is serviced by a trap handler that runs on behalf of the faulting process, picks a victim frame, writes the victim back if it is dirty, reads the wanted page in, updates the page table and TLB, and restarts the instruction. Each step can add cost; the dirty bit and the TLB are the two that are easy to forget.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. A clean victim is simply overwritten; a dirty victim must first be written to the backing store, so the fault costs one read plus one write.
  2. (B) True. The handler executes in the process's own context and the process waits for the I/O, so the fault is charged to that process's time.
  3. (C) True. The page is present, so no transfer is needed; the failure is a permission violation, which is a protection fault (usually a signal to the process).
  4. (D) True. The old translation must not survive, so the entry is flushed or invalidated before the instruction is restarted.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Treating "invalid entry" and "page fault" as synonyms. A protection violation reaches the same trap in many designs but needs no I/O at all.

Takeaway. Victim selection → write-back if dirty → read → update tables and TLB → restart.

questions.question:
A demand-paged system has a memory access time of 100 ns and a page-fault service time of 6 ms. Over a long run its measured effective access time is 1300 ns. How many page faults occur per 100,000 references?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The EAT equation can be inverted: measured EAT minus the hit cost, divided by the extra cost of a fault, gives the fault rate.

Step by step.

  1. EAT = (1 − p) × 100 + p × 6,000,000 = 100 + p × 5,999,900.
  2. Set 1300 = 100 + p × 5,999,900, so p × 5,999,900 = 1,200.
  3. p = 1,200 / 5,999,900 = 2.00003 × 10−4.
  4. Per 100,000 references: 2.00003 × 10−4 × 100,000 = 20.0003 ≈ 20.

Answer: 20 faults per 100,000 references.

Common misconception. Dividing by the service time instead of by the difference between the service time and the access time. The 100 ns already paid on a fault reference must not be counted twice; here the correction changes the answer by only 0.0003, but with a short service time it matters.

Takeaway. p = (EAT − ma) / (s − ma); then rescale to the base the question asks for.

questions.question: LRU replacement is often implemented by keeping a stack of page numbers. Which page does the algorithm evict?
options: The page at the bottom of the stack, which has not been referenced for the longest time.
The page at the top of the stack, which was referenced most recently.
The page in the middle of the stack, chosen to keep the stack balanced.
The page that was brought into memory most recently.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The stack is maintained so that the most recently referenced page is always at the top. Every reference moves the page to the top, and the bottom therefore holds the least recently used page — the LRU victim. The cost of the move is what makes a true LRU stack expensive in hardware.

Step by step.

  1. On a reference to page x: if x is in the stack, remove it and push it on top; if it is not, push it on top and count a fault.
  2. The bottom of the stack is by construction the page whose last reference is the oldest.
  3. On a fault with no free frame, remove the bottom page and push the new page on top.

Answer: Option (A) — the bottom of the stack.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) The top is the most recently used page, the one LRU is most anxious to keep.
  • (C) There is no balancing rule; the order is entirely by recency.
  • (D) Recency of arrival is FIFO, a different policy.

Common misconception. Reading the stack upside down. The stack order is recency of use, top first; it has nothing to do with arrival order.

Takeaway. Top = most recently used, bottom = LRU victim; a reference always moves its page to the top.

questions.question:
The reference string 1, 3, 0, 3, 5, 6, 3, 1, 6, 0, 5, 1 is processed with 3 frames, all initially empty. How many page faults occur under OPT (Belady's optimal) replacement?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. OPT evicts the resident page whose next reference is furthest in the future, and a page that is never referenced again is the ideal victim. Only a trace taken one reference at a time gets the count right.

Step by step.

  1. 1 — fault, frames {1}.
  2. 3 — fault, {1,3}.
  3. 0 — fault, {1,3,0}.
  4. 3 — hit.
  5. 5 — fault; next uses: 1 at position 8, 3 at position 7, 0 at position 10, so evict 3 → {1,0,5}.
  6. 6 — fault; next uses: 1 at 8, 0 at 10, 5 at 11, so evict 5 → {1,0,6}.
  7. 3 — fault; 1 and 6 are never used again, 0 is used at position 10, so evict 1 (tie broken either way) → {3,0,6}.
  8. 1 — fault; 3 and 6 never return and 0 returns at position 10, so evict 3 → {1,0,6}.
  9. 6 — hit.
  10. 0 — hit.
  11. 5 — fault; 1, 6 and 0 never return, so evict any → {5}.
  12. 1 — fault.

Answer: 7 page faults.

Common misconception. Evicting the page used least recently (LRU) or the page that arrived first (FIFO) while claiming to run OPT. OPT looks forward; the other two look backward.

Takeaway. For OPT, at every fault list the future uses of the resident pages and drop the one furthest away.

questions.question: For the same reference string 1, 3, 0, 3, 5, 6, 3, 1, 6, 0, 5, 1 with 3 frames, how many page faults does LRU cause?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. LRU evicts the resident page whose most recent reference is oldest, which is the backward-looking mirror of OPT.

Step by step.

  1. 1, 3, 0 — three faults, frames {1,3,0} with recency order 0, 3, 1.
  2. 3 — hit; order becomes 3, 0, 1.
  3. 5 — fault, evict 1 → {3,0,5}, order 5, 3, 0.
  4. 6 — fault, evict 0 → {3,5,6}, order 6, 5, 3.
  5. 3 — hit, order 3, 6, 5.
  6. 1 — fault, evict 5 → {3,6,1}, order 1, 3, 6.
  7. 6 — hit, order 6, 1, 3.
  8. 0 — fault, evict 3 → {6,1,0}, order 0, 6, 1.
  9. 5 — fault, evict 1 → {6,0,5}.
  10. 1 — fault, evict 6 → {0,5,1}.

Answer: Option (C) — 9 faults.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 7 is the OPT count; LRU cannot reach the offline optimum on this string.
  • (B) 8 comes from evicting on a hit at step 4 or 7.
  • (D) 10 comes from evicting the most recently used page at one of the faults, which is FIFO-like behaviour.

Common misconception. Forgetting to update recency on a hit. A hit moves the page to the front of the order and can change the next victim, even though it adds no fault.

Takeaway. Trace recency order at every reference, hit or miss; the victim is always the last entry.

questions.question: Four frames hold pages 5, 8, 2 and 9, in that order, with the clock hand pointing at the frame that holds page 5. The reference bits are 1 for page 5, 0 for page 8, 1 for page 2 and 1 for page 9. A page fault now occurs and no frame is free. Which page does the clock (second-chance) algorithm evict?
options: Page 5
Page 2
Page 9
Page 8
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Clock sweeps the frames in circular order. A page with reference bit 1 gets a second chance: the bit is cleared and the hand moves on. A page with bit 0 is evicted immediately, because it has not been referenced since the hand last passed.

Step by step.

  1. Hand at page 5, bit 1 → clear it to 0, advance.
  2. Hand at page 8, bit 0 → evict page 8 and load the new page into that frame.
  3. The new page enters with bit 1 and the hand advances to the next frame, page 2.

Answer: Option (D) — page 8.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Page 5 survives because its bit was 1; it was merely cleared.
  • (B) and (C) were never examined; the sweep stopped at page 8.

Common misconception. Evicting the first page the hand touches. Clock never evicts a page with a set reference bit on the first pass; it gives that page exactly one reprieve.

Takeaway. Bit 1 → clear and skip; bit 0 → evict. Page 5 keeps its frame here but is now the next victim if it stays untouched.

questions.question: Which of the following statements comparing page-replacement algorithms are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: On a fixed reference string and a fixed frame count, OPT can never cause more faults than any other algorithm.
LRU is a stack algorithm, so the set of pages it keeps with n frames is always contained in the set it keeps with n + 1 frames.
Clock (second chance) always evicts the same page that LRU would evict.
Increasing the number of frames can increase the fault count under FIFO.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Three separate claims are being tested: the optimality of OPT, the inclusion property of stack algorithms, and the monotonicity (or lack of it) of FIFO. They are independent facts, and a statement can be true for one algorithm and false for another.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. OPT is defined by looking at the whole future, so no online policy can beat it on the same string and frame count; ties are possible, losses are not.
  2. (B) True. LRU orders pages by recency, and that order does not depend on how many frames exist, which gives the inclusion property.
  3. (C) False. Clock keeps only one bit per page, so a page referenced twice within one sweep can be evicted while LRU would keep it; clock is an approximation, not an implementation of LRU.
  4. (D) True. FIFO's order is by arrival and changes with the frame count, so more frames can produce more faults — Belady's anomaly.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing clock is "LRU with a cheaper implementation". It is an approximation whose decisions can differ from LRU on the very next fault.

Takeaway. OPT is optimal by definition, LRU is a stack algorithm, clock approximates LRU, FIFO is neither optimal nor a stack algorithm.

questions.question: For the reference string 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3, 5, 8, 9, 7, 9, 3, 2, 3, 8, 4, 6, 2, 6, 4 with 3 frames, how many more page faults does LRU cause than OPT?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. LRU and OPT differ only in the information they use to choose a victim: OPT uses the future, LRU the past. On a long string with a working set slightly larger than the frame count, the gap is small but non-zero, and it has to be counted, not estimated.

Step by step.

  1. Tracing LRU over the 24 references with 3 frames gives 18 faults.
  2. Tracing OPT over the same string with 3 frames gives 14 faults.
  3. Difference: 18 − 14 = 4.
  4. FIFO also gives 18 on this string, so on this trace FIFO and LRU coincide while both pay four faults more than the offline optimum.

Answer: Option (C) — 4 faults.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 2 and (B) 3 come from tracing only part of the string, usually stopping before the second burst of page 9 and page 3.
  • (D) 5 counts a fault at one of the hits near position 15, where page 9 is already resident.

Common misconception. Assuming LRU is always at least as good as FIFO. They tie here, and each can beat the other on other strings; only OPT is a guaranteed bound.

Takeaway. LRU − OPT = 4 on this trace; count both traces independently rather than reasoning from one.

questions.question:
The block of pages 2, 5, 1, 4, 3 is referenced repeatedly, twelve times in all, giving a reference string of 60 references. 4 frames are available and they start empty. How many page faults occur under LRU replacement?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution
