Concept. A cyclic string whose cycle length exceeds the frame count has no reuse distance that fits in memory: by the time a page comes round again, it has been evicted. Every reference is then a capacity miss, whatever the replacement policy.

Step by step.

  1. The cycle holds 5 distinct pages and there are only 4 frames, so one page must always be missing.
  2. First cycle: 2, 5, 1, 4 fill the frames; 3 faults and evicts the LRU page, which is 2.
  3. Second cycle starts with 2, which is absent again → fault, evicting the LRU page, which is 5.
  4. The pattern repeats: each reference in the cycle evicts the page that the next cycle will need first.
  5. Every one of the 60 references therefore faults: 12 cycles × 5 = 60.

Answer: 60 page faults.

Common misconception. Applying the "warm-up then steady state" intuition. There is no steady state without reuse: with frames fewer than the cycle length, the fault rate is 100 %, not 1/cycle.

Takeaway. If the locality (5 pages) exceeds the frames (4), every pass faults on every page. Give it 5 frames and the count drops to 5 faults in total.

questions.question: Which one of the following page-replacement algorithms is a stack algorithm?
options: LRU
FIFO
Clock (second chance)
None of these three
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A stack algorithm is one whose set of resident pages depends only on the reference string and the number of frames, in a nested way: the set held with n frames is always a subset of the set held with n + 1 frames. That inclusion property is exactly what rules out Belady's anomaly.

Step by step.

  1. LRU ranks pages by recency of use; adding a frame simply keeps one more page that was already ranked below the cut-off.
  2. OPT ranks pages by their next use; adding a frame again keeps one more of the pages already ranked.
  3. FIFO ranks by arrival time, and the arrival order that results depends on the frame count itself, so the nesting can break.
  4. Clock ranks by a single reference bit and a moving hand, which also depends on the frame count.

Answer: Option (A) — LRU.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) FIFO is the textbook counter-example to the inclusion property.
  • (C) Clock is a FIFO-like sweep over a reference bit and is not a stack algorithm either.
  • (D) LRU is one, so this is false.

Common misconception. Believing any "reasonable" policy is a stack algorithm. Both FIFO and clock are reasonable and neither is one.

Takeaway. LRU and OPT are stack algorithms; FIFO and clock are not.

questions.question: For the reference string 2, 1, 3, 4, 2, 1, 5, 2, 1, 3, 4, 5 under FIFO replacement, the page-fault counts with 3 frames and with 4 frames are respectively
options: 9 and 10
10 and 9
9 and 9
10 and 11
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Belady's anomaly is a statement about two complete FIFO traces of the same string at two frame counts. It must be demonstrated by counting both, not assumed from the string's shape.

Step by step.

  1. Three frames: 2, 1, 3 fault (frames full); 4 faults evicting 2; 2 faults evicting 1; 1 faults evicting 3; 5 faults evicting 4; 2 faults evicting 2; 1 faults evicting 1; 3 faults evicting 5; 4 faults evicting 2; 5 faults evicting 1. Total 9.
  2. Four frames: 2, 1, 3, 4 fault; 2, 1 hit; 5 faults evicting 2; 2 faults evicting 1; 1 faults evicting 3; 3 faults evicting 4; 4 faults evicting 5; 5 faults evicting 2. Total 10.
  3. One extra frame, one extra fault: the anomaly is present on this string.

Answer: Option (A) — 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the two counts, which would make the extra frame look useful.
  • (C) would mean the frame count made no difference at all.
  • (D) overstates the four-frame count; the trace above gives 10.

Common misconception. Carrying the three-frame state into the four-frame trace. The two traces start from an empty memory and must be run independently.

Takeaway. 3 frames: 9 faults; 4 frames: 10 faults — the anomaly, shown by two clean traces.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Belady's anomaly and the inclusion property are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The inclusion property guarantees that a stack algorithm's fault count never rises when frames are added.
OPT is a stack algorithm.
Clock (second chance) satisfies the inclusion property.
Belady's anomaly was first reported for FIFO replacement.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The inclusion property is the structural reason a policy is immune to the anomaly: if the n-frame resident set is always contained in the (n + 1)-frame resident set, then any reference that hits with n frames also hits with n + 1, so faults can only fall.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Containment turns every n-frame hit into an (n + 1)-frame hit, so the fault count is monotone non-increasing in the frame count.
  2. (B) True. OPT's ranking is by next use and does not depend on the frame count, so its resident sets nest.
  3. (C) False. Clock's hand position and reference bits depend on the frame count and the sweep history, so its resident sets need not nest.
  4. (D) True. The effect is named after Belady, who reported it for FIFO in 1969.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming the anomaly is a property of the reference string alone. The same string can show the anomaly under FIFO and never under LRU, because the anomaly is a property of the policy.

Takeaway. Stack algorithm → inclusion property → no anomaly; FIFO and clock are outside that guarantee.

questions.question: On the string 2, 1, 3, 4, 2, 1, 5, 2, 1, 3, 4, 5, LRU causes 10 faults with 3 frames and 8 faults with 4 frames, while FIFO causes 9 and 10. Which one of the following conclusions is correct?
options: LRU also exhibits Belady's anomaly on this string, but in the opposite direction.
The fourth frame removes exactly the fault that FIFO's fourth frame adds.
LRU does not exhibit the anomaly here, which is what the inclusion property predicts for a stack algorithm.
The counts show that four frames are worse than three frames for every algorithm on this string.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The same string can be a counter-example for one policy and an ordinary case for another. What matters is whether the policy satisfies the inclusion property, not how the string looks.

Step by step.

  1. LRU: 10 faults with 3 frames, 8 with 4 — more memory, fewer faults, the expected direction.
  2. FIFO: 9 with 3 frames, 10 with 4 — the anomaly.
  3. LRU is a stack algorithm, so its resident set with 3 frames is a subset of its set with 4 frames; a hit can be lost but never gained by removing a frame.
  4. So the two counts are consistent with the theory, and only FIFO misbehaves.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) The anomaly has a defined direction: more frames, more faults. LRU shows the opposite, which is simply normal behaviour.
  • (B) The two counts are independent traces, not two halves of one event.
  • (D) False, since LRU improves from 10 to 8.

Common misconception. Concluding from one policy's anomaly that "this string is anomalous". The anomaly belongs to the policy, and only FIFO and clock-like policies are exposed to it.

Takeaway. Same string, two policies, opposite outcomes: 10 → 8 for LRU, 9 → 10 for FIFO.

questions.question: FIFO and clock (second chance) can both show Belady's anomaly while LRU cannot. Which one of the following is the reason?
options: LRU stores more bookkeeping per page than the other two, and the extra state prevents the anomaly.
FIFO and clock evict pages that have never been referenced, whereas LRU never does.
LRU gives every page a second chance before eviction, which removes the anomaly.

LRU ranks pages by recency of use, so its resident set with n frames is always a subset of its set with n + 1 frames; FIFO ranks by arrival and clock by a single reference bit, and both of those orders change when the frame count changes.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The anomaly is a failure of the inclusion property, and the inclusion property follows from the ordering a policy induces, not from how much state it keeps.

Step by step.

  1. LRU induces a total order on pages by recency. That order is a property of the reference string alone, so adding a frame keeps one more page from the same order — nesting holds.
  2. FIFO induces an order by arrival time, but the arrival order itself is shaped by how many frames exist, because evictions change which page is "oldest".
  3. Clock induces an order by a one-bit reference flag plus the hand position; both depend on the frame count and the sweep history.
  4. Without nesting, a reference that hits with n frames can miss with n + 1, which is precisely the anomaly.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) State size is irrelevant; OPT keeps almost no state and is a stack algorithm.
  • (B) FIFO can evict a heavily referenced page; that is not the mechanism of the anomaly.
  • (C) Second chance is the clock algorithm, not LRU, and LRU gives no reprieve at all.

Common misconception. Thinking the anomaly is a bookkeeping bug. It is a consequence of the eviction order failing to nest as memory grows.

Takeaway. The order a policy induces decides immunity; LRU's order is frame-count independent, FIFO's and clock's are not.

questions.question: The working-set window Δ of a process is measured in
options: the number of most recent memory references, which is a time window.
bytes of physical memory.
frames allocated to the process.
entries in the page table.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The working set is the set of distinct pages referenced in the last Δ references. Δ is a window in time, measured in references, not a quantity of memory.

Step by step.

  1. At time t, look back over the previous Δ references.
  2. Collect the distinct pages among them: that is W(t, Δ).
  3. Its size is at most Δ and at most the number of pages the program uses.
  4. Frames are then allocated to cover that size; frames are the output, not the unit of Δ.

Answer: Option (A) — a window of recent references.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) and (C) are memory quantities; the working set is computed before any frame allocation is decided.
  • (D) The page table is a translation structure and plays no part in the definition.

Common misconception. Treating Δ as a number of frames. It is an interval of program execution; the working-set size it produces is what frames must then cover.

Takeaway. Δ counts references; |W(t, Δ)| counts distinct pages; frames must be at least that size.

questions.question: A process has referenced the pages 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3, most recent last, and the working-set window is Δ = 4. What is the working-set size at the current instant?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The window always ends at the current reference. With Δ = 4 the last four references are examined and the distinct pages among them are counted.

Step by step.

  1. The last four references are 2, 6, 5, 3.
  2. All four are different pages.
  3. So |W| = 4, and the process needs at least four frames to hold its working set.

Answer: Option (B) — 4 pages.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 2 would come from a window of two references.
  • (C) 3 would drop one of the four distinct pages, for example by sliding the window one position too far back and including 5 twice.
  • (D) 5 is the window width plus one, which the working-set size can never exceed.

Common misconception. Counting references rather than distinct pages, which gives 4 here by coincidence but is wrong in general — a repeated page counts once.

Takeaway. Window ends at the current reference; count distinct pages inside it.

questions.question: A process's page-fault rate has fallen below the lower bound of the page-fault-frequency range set by the operating system. What should page-fault-frequency control do?
options: Allocate more frames to the process.
Take frames away from the process.
Suspend the process until memory frees up.
Raise the process's scheduling priority.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. PFF control is a two-sided controller. Above the upper bound the process needs more memory; below the lower bound it is holding more memory than it needs, and those frames are better given to someone else.

Step by step.

  1. Measure the process's fault rate over an interval.
  2. Rate above the upper bound → increase its frame allocation.
  3. Rate below the lower bound → decrease its frame allocation; the freed frames go to processes that are short.
  4. Rate inside the band → leave the allocation alone.

Answer: Option (B) — take frames away.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the response to a rate above the upper bound.
  • (C) is the response to a process that cannot be given enough frames to leave the thrashing region.
  • (D) changes scheduling, not memory allocation, and cannot fix a fault rate.

Common misconception. Reading "low fault rate" as "give it more memory, it is working well". A very low rate means the allocation is over-generous.

Takeaway. Too high → add frames; too low → remove frames; in band → leave it.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about local and global replacement are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Under global replacement a process can take a frame from another process, so one process's poor locality can degrade everyone's fault rate.
Under local replacement a process chooses its victims only among its own frames, so a thrashing process mainly harms itself.
Global replacement makes it impossible for the system as a whole to thrash.
Under local replacement the number of frames a process holds does not change when another process faults.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The choice of victim pool decides who pays for a bad locality. Global replacement lets a process compete for every frame in the system; local replacement confines its victims to its own allocation.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. With a system-wide pool a process that faults often simply evicts other processes' pages, raising their fault rates too.
  2. (B) False. Local replacement confines the victims, but a process whose working set exceeds its own allocation still thrashes; the harm is limited, not eliminated.
  3. (C) False. Global replacement makes thrashing easier to spread, not impossible.
  4. (D) True. Another process's fault cannot change this process's frame count under a local policy.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing local replacement prevents thrashing. It prevents the spread of thrashing; the badly allocated process still thrashes on its own.

Takeaway. Global replacement → better utilisation, contagious faults; local replacement → stable allocations, contained damage.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about thrashing and the working-set model are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Thrashing shows up as high paging-disk utilisation together with low CPU utilisation.
Under working-set control a process is admitted only if the sum of the working-set sizes of the resident processes stays within the frames available.
The working set W(t, Δ) is the set of distinct pages referenced in the last Δ references.
Raising the degree of multiprogramming always raises CPU utilisation.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Thrashing is a positive-feedback failure: too few frames per process raises the fault rate, the processes queue on the paging device, CPU utilisation collapses, and the scheduler may respond by admitting yet more processes.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. The disk is saturated with page transfers while the CPU idles waiting for them — the diagnostic signature.
  2. (B) True. Working-set control computes D = Σ WSSi and refuses admission while D would exceed the frame count.
  3. (C) True, by definition, with the window ending at the current reference.
  4. (D) False. Utilisation rises, peaks, and then falls as memory is over-committed; beyond the knee, more processes mean less work done.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Reading high disk activity as "the disk is the bottleneck, buy a faster disk". If the paging disk is saturated while the CPU is idle, the shortage is memory, not disk bandwidth.

Takeaway. Thrashing = memory shortage; the cure is fewer resident processes or more frames, not a faster disk.

questions.question: A process faults 18 times per 1000 references with 4 frames, 9 times per 1000 with 6 frames, and 3 times per 1000 with 8 frames. PFF control sets the upper bound at 10 faults per 1000 references and the lower bound at 2 per 1000. Starting from 4 frames, how many frames will the process hold once the controller settles?
options: 4 frames
6 frames
8 frames
10 frames
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. PFF control moves the allocation until the measured rate lies inside the band. It stops at the first allocation whose rate is acceptable — it does not jump to the best allocation available.

Step by step.

  1. At 4 frames the rate is 18 per 1000, above the upper bound of 10 → add frames.
  2. At 6 frames the rate is 9 per 1000, which is inside [2, 10] → the controller stops.
  3. At 8 frames the rate would be 3 per 1000, also inside the band, but the controller has no reason to go there.
  4. So the settled allocation is 6 frames.

Answer: Option (B) — 6 frames.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) leaves the rate above the upper bound; the process would still be thrashing.
  • (C) overshoots: 3 is inside the band, but nothing drives the allocation that far.
  • (D) is past the point where the rate stops falling, and would only be reached if the lower bound were breached and frames were being reclaimed in the other direction.

Common misconception. Choosing the allocation with the lowest fault rate. PFF control is a band controller, not an optimiser: it stops as soon as the process is healthy, leaving the spare frames to other processes.

Takeaway. Walk the allocations upward until the rate enters the band: 18 → 9, so 6 frames.

questions.question:
A process makes 2 × 106 memory references per second and its page-fault rate is 1.5 × 10−5. Each page fault takes 6 ms of paging-disk time. What percentage of the disk's time is spent servicing this process's faults?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Disk utilisation is the product of the arrival rate of faults and the service time of one fault: faults per second times seconds per fault gives the fraction of each second the disk is busy.

Step by step.

  1. Faults per second = 2 × 106 × 1.5 × 10−5 = 30.
  2. Seconds of disk time per second = 30 × 6 × 10−3 = 0.18 s.
  3. As a percentage: 0.18 × 100 = 18 %.
  4. For contrast, at a fault rate of 10−4 the same process would need 2 × 106 × 10−4 × 6 ms = 1,200 % of the disk — a saturated disk and a thrashing system.

Answer: 18 % of the disk's time.

Common misconception. Multiplying the reference rate by the service time and forgetting the fault rate, or leaving the service time in milliseconds and reporting 0.018 %. The unit of the answer is a fraction of a second per second.

Takeaway. Disk load = fault rate × reference rate × service time; 30 faults/s × 6 ms = 18 %.

questions.question: A file system allocates each file as one contiguous run of disk blocks. Which one of the following must the directory entry of the file record?
options: only the address of the file's first block
the address of the file's first block together with the length of the allocation
the address of the file's index block
nothing beyond the file name, because the blocks are stored next to the directory entry
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Contiguous allocation reserves one run of consecutive blocks per file. To find block k of the file the system needs only the start address and an offset, so the extent (start, length) is the whole of the metadata.

Step by step.

  1. With only the start address, the system cannot tell where the file ends and the next file begins; the length is essential.
  2. With the start and the length, block k is at start + k, so direct access costs one seek and no traversal.
  3. An index block belongs to indexed allocation, not to contiguous allocation.
  4. Blocks of a file are contiguous with each other, not with the directory entry, which usually lives elsewhere on the disk.

Answer: Option (B) — start address plus length.

Common misconception. Reading “contiguous” as “no metadata needed”. The length is what lets the file system distinguish the end of one file from the beginning of the next.

questions.question: A file grows so large that its index block can no longer hold a pointer to every block of the file. In the classic Unix inode design, how are the remaining blocks addressed?
options: the file is split into several files, each with its own inode
the index block is moved to the last block of the file
the inode holds single-, double- and triple-indirect pointers, each pointing to a block that is itself full of pointers
the last entry of the index block points to the first data block, so the blocks are chained
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A multi-level index extends the reach of a single index block: an indirect block contains block addresses, so one pointer in the inode reaches a whole block of pointers, and two levels reach a block of blocks of pointers.

Step by step.

  1. The inode keeps a small number of direct pointers that address the first blocks of the file without any extra read.
  2. One single-indirect pointer addresses a block holding further block numbers; one double-indirect pointer addresses a block of single-indirect blocks; one triple-indirect pointer goes one level deeper.
  3. The number of addressable blocks grows as 1, n, n², n³ with the depth, so a few pointers in the inode cover files of many gigabytes.
  4. Only the blocks that the file actually uses have their indirect blocks allocated, so a small file pays nothing for the depth.

Answer: Option (C) — single-, double- and triple-indirect pointers.

Common misconception. Believing that a large file needs a larger index block. The index block keeps its fixed size; what changes is how many levels of pointer sit between the inode and the data.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about a Unix-like inode and the directory entries that name it are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A directory entry maps a file name to an inode number.
Two hard links to the same file share one inode and therefore one set of data blocks.
Deleting one of the two hard links of a file frees the file's data blocks.
A symbolic link stores the path name of its target rather than the target's inode number.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The inode holds everything about a file except its name; the name lives in a directory entry, which is only a pair (name, inode number). Several entries may carry the same inode number, and the inode keeps a link count of them.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true by construction: the directory is a table of names against inode numbers.
  2. (B) is true: a hard link is a second name for the same inode number, so both names reach the same blocks and the same metadata.
  3. (C) is false: removing one name decrements the link count from 2 to 1, and the blocks are freed only when the count reaches 0.
  4. (D) is true: a symbolic link is a small file whose contents are the target's path, so it can even point at a name that does not exist.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming that unlink deletes the file. It deletes a name; the data survives while any other name, or any open file descriptor, still refers to the inode.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the three classic file-allocation methods are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Contiguous allocation gives the fastest direct access of the three methods.
Linked allocation suffers from external fragmentation.
Indexed allocation spends an index block on every file, even a file of a single block.
FAT keeps the block pointers in one central table instead of inside the data blocks.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The three methods trade metadata overhead against access cost: contiguous needs only (start, length), linked stores a pointer in every data block, and indexed adds a dedicated index block per file.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: block k of a contiguous file is at a computed offset, so one seek reaches it.
  2. (B) is false: linked allocation places each block anywhere on the disk and chains them, so it has no external fragmentation at all, only the internal waste of the pointer field in every block.
  3. (C) is true: the index block is allocated with the file, so even a one-block file occupies two blocks.
  4. (D) is true: that is exactly what a File Allocation Table is — the chain of a linked file lifted out of the data blocks into one table indexed by block number.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Attributing external fragmentation to linked allocation. It is the opposite: chaining removes external fragmentation and pays for it with pointer space and with sequential-only access.

questions.question:
An inode holds 12 direct block pointers and one double-indirect pointer. The block size is 1 KB and a block pointer occupies 4 bytes. How many blocks of the file can be addressed in total?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A block of 1 KB holding 4-byte pointers holds 1024 / 4 = 256 pointers, and a pointer of depth d therefore reaches 256^d data blocks.

Step by step.

  1. Pointers per block: 1024 / 4 = 256.
  2. Direct pointers address 12 blocks.
  3. The double-indirect pointer addresses a block of 256 pointers, each to a block of 256 data blocks: 256 × 256 = 65536 blocks.
  4. Total = 12 + 65536 = 65548 blocks, about 64 MB at 1 KB per block.

Answer: 65548 blocks.

Common misconception. Counting the double-indirect pointer as 256 blocks instead of 256². The depth matters: one level is a block of pointers, two levels are a block of blocks of pointers.

questions.question: A file system replaces linked allocation, in which each data block stores the pointer to the next block, with a FAT, in which all the pointers live in one table indexed by block number. Which one of the following is the principal cost of the change?
options: every file now needs an index block of its own
the table covers the whole volume, so it is large, is normally cached in main memory, and every allocation writes to the same hot region
direct access becomes impossible, because the table has to be searched linearly
a file can no longer grow beyond the number of entries in its first block
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Moving the chain out of the data blocks into a table changes both the space and the locality of the metadata: the table is per volume, not per file, and it is read and written constantly.

Step by step.

  1. A volume of 2²⁰ blocks with 4-byte entries needs a 4 MB table, whatever the number or size of the files on it.
  2. Because every file's chain passes through that table, the table is cached in main memory and a write to it is a write to one small, hot region of the disk.
  3. Direct access actually improves: following the chain is a sequence of table lookups in memory instead of a sequence of disk reads.
  4. An index block belongs to indexed allocation; a FAT file needs none, which is one of its advantages.

Answer: Option (B) — one volume-wide table that must be cached and updated.

Common misconception. Thinking a FAT is “the same as an index block”. An index block belongs to one file; the FAT is shared by every file on the volume, which is why it must be resident in memory and kept consistent.

questions.question: An extent is a contiguous run of blocks described by a single (start, length) pair. Modern file systems such as ext4 keep an extent tree instead of a list of individual block pointers. Which one of the following is the reason?
options: extents remove the need for free-space management
one entry describes a long contiguous run, so the index stays small while access remains direct and the blocks of a file stay together on the disk
extents guarantee that a file never needs more than one run of blocks
extents make a file's blocks unchangeable once the file has been written
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An extent is contiguous allocation applied to pieces of a file: the index records runs rather than blocks, so a file that is mostly sequential costs almost no metadata and still supports direct access inside each run.

Step by step.

  1. A list of individual block pointers costs 4 bytes per block, so a 1 GB file needs 1 MB of index.
  2. The same file as one extent costs one (start, length) pair, and a fragmented file costs one pair per run.
  3. Inside an extent block k is found by arithmetic, so direct access is preserved.
  4. A file may of course be split into many extents; the point is that it usually is not.

Answer: Option (B) — a small index with direct access and good locality.

Common misconception. Confusing an extent with contiguous allocation of the whole file. Extents allow a file to be split into several runs, which is exactly how they avoid the external-fragmentation problem of a single contiguous run.

questions.question: Which one of the following free-space structures stores one bit per block, so that a block can be freed in constant time and the whole structure can be held in main memory for a moderately sized disk?
options: the bitmap
the linked free list
the counting method
the grouping method
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A bitmap gives every block exactly one bit, addressed by block number, so allocating or freeing a known block is a single bit operation.

Step by step.

  1. Bit i of the bitmap is 1 when block i is free and 0 when it is allocated.
  2. Freeing block i is one write to word i / 32, hence O(1).
  3. The size is n / 8 bytes for n blocks, small enough to keep in memory.
  4. A linked list or the counting and grouping methods store addresses, so each operation follows pointers and none of them can free a block without locating it.

Answer: Option (A) — the bitmap.

Common misconception. Believing a bitmap is too large to be practical. One bit per block is the smallest per-block representation there is; a 4 TB disk in 4 KB blocks needs only 128 MB.

questions.question: A 64-block disk tracks free space with a bitmap in which bit i records block i, bit 0 being the least significant bit of the first 32-bit word. The first word of the bitmap is 0xF0FF0000. Which block does a first-fit allocator that always starts its search at block 0 choose?
options: block 8
block 16
block 20
block 24
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A bitmap is read word by word, and the lowest set bit of a word is the first free block in it.

Step by step.

  1. 0xF0FF0000 has zero in its low 16 bits, so blocks 0 to 15 are all allocated.
  2. Bits 16 to 31 hold 0xF0FF, which is not zero, so a free block exists in the upper half.
  3. The lowest set bit of 0xF0FF0000 is bit 16, since the low byte of the upper half (0xFF) occupies bits 16 to 23.
  4. First fit therefore returns block 16.

Answer: Option (B) — block 16.

Common misconception. Reading the word left to right. Bit 0 is the least significant bit, so the numbering of blocks inside a word runs from the right-hand end.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about free-space management are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A bitmap uses one bit per disk block and is small enough to be held in main memory for a moderate volume.
A linked free list can be searched for a run of contiguous free blocks only by following the list.
The counting method records, for each run of contiguous free blocks, the first block and the length of the run.
The grouping method stores the addresses of every free block of the volume in a single block.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The four methods differ in what they store: bits (bitmap), addresses chained one at a time (linked list), runs (counting), and addresses packed many per block with a link to the next group (grouping).

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: n blocks need n/8 bytes, which fits in memory for volumes of ordinary size.
  2. (B) is true: the list gives no index, so finding k consecutive free blocks means walking until such a run appears.
  3. (C) is true: that pair is exactly the record the counting method keeps per run.
  4. (D) is false: grouping fills one block with as many free addresses as fit, together with the address of the block holding the next group, so a chain of blocks is needed.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Mixing up grouping and counting. Grouping stores many addresses per block and links blocks; counting stores one (block, count) pair per run of contiguous blocks.

questions.question:
In the grouping method of free-space management, a free block holds 127 free-block addresses together with one pointer to the block that holds the next group. How many free-block addresses can a chain of 3 group blocks describe in total?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Grouping packs as many free-block addresses into one block as will fit and uses one slot for the link to the next group; the chain is read group by group.

Step by step.

  1. Each group block describes 127 free blocks; the 128th slot is the link, not an address.
  2. A chain of 3 group blocks therefore describes 3 × 127 addresses.
  3. 3 × 127 = 381.

Answer: 381 free-block addresses.

Common misconception. Counting the link slot as an address, which gives 384. The pointer to the next group occupies one of the block's slots and describes no free block.

questions.question: A bitmap allocator keeps a roving pointer to the block it allocated last and starts every search from there instead of from block 0. Compared with always starting at block 0, which one of the following is the effect?
options: allocation becomes slower, because every search may have to wrap around the end of the bitmap
consecutive allocations are spread across the disk, so free space stays evenly distributed and the length of each search is amortised, at the price of longer seeks between logically adjacent blocks
the bitmap can no longer be held in main memory
runs of contiguous free blocks can no longer be found
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A roving pointer turns first fit into next fit. The pointer is an optimisation for the search and a policy for placement at the same time.

Step by step.

  1. Always starting at block 0 makes the search scan the same already-allocated prefix on every call, so the total scanning cost grows with the number of allocations.
  2. Starting where the last allocation ended means the scan resumes immediately after the busy prefix, so the amortised scan cost is small.
  3. Because successive files are placed in different regions, free space stays spread over the volume rather than being consumed from one end.
  4. The price is locality: two files written one after the other are no longer adjacent, so reading them in sequence costs more seeks, and large contiguous runs become rarer over time.

Answer: Option (B) — better search cost and distribution, worse locality.

Common misconception. Treating the roving pointer as a pure speed-up. It also changes where blocks are placed, which is why real allocators pair it with policies that prefer to keep a file's blocks together.

questions.question:
A disk has 2¹⁶ blocks and its free-space bitmap is held as an array of 32-bit words. How many words does the bitmap occupy?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A bitmap is one bit per block, packed into machine words, so the number of words is the number of blocks divided by the word size.

Step by step.

  1. Blocks: 2¹⁶ = 65536.
  2. Bits per word: 32.
  3. Words = 65536 / 32 = 2048, which is 8 KB of memory.

Answer: 2048 words.

Common misconception. Dividing by 8 (bits per byte) and calling the result words, or forgetting that the last word is used even when the block count is not a multiple of the word size.

questions.question: Which one of the following disk-scheduling policies can starve a request that lies far from the current head position, because it always serves the pending request nearest to the head?
options: FCFS
SSTF
C-LOOK
SCAN
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. SSTF is a greedy shortest-seek-first policy: it has no notion of age, only of distance, so a steady supply of near requests keeps a far request waiting indefinitely.

Step by step.

  1. FCFS serves requests in arrival order, so every request is served after finitely many others.
  2. SSTF always picks the nearest pending request; a request at cylinder 199 is postponed as long as nearer requests keep arriving.
  3. SCAN and C-LOOK sweep the disk, so every cylinder is visited within one sweep, which bounds the wait.
  4. SSTF is therefore the policy that needs aging or a sweep to become fair.

Answer: Option (B) — SSTF.

Common misconception. Thinking that a policy with the smallest total head movement is also fair. SSTF minimises movement locally and is precisely the policy that ignores waiting time.

questions.question: A 200-cylinder disk (cylinders 0 to 199) has its head at cylinder 60. The pending requests, in arrival order, are 82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16, 190, 51. In which order does SSTF serve them?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. SSTF repeatedly takes the pending request with the smallest distance from the current head, so the head always makes the shortest possible step.

Step by step.

  1. From 60 the distances are 9 to 51, 17 to 43, 22 to 82, 36 to 24, 44 to 16, 80 to 140, 110 to 170 and 130 to 190; take 51.
  2. From 51: 43 is at distance 8, the smallest; take 43.
  3. From 43: 24 is at 19, 16 at 27, 82 at 39; take 24, then 16 (distance 8).
  4. From 16 the remaining requests are 82, 140, 170 and 190, all to the right, so they are taken in increasing order: 82, 140, 170, 190.
  5. Total movement = 9 + 8 + 19 + 8 + 66 + 58 + 30 + 20 = 218 cylinders.

Answer: Option (A) — 51, 43, 24, 16, 82, 140, 170, 190.

Common misconception. Option (B) reverses the tail because the head has been moving left. SSTF has no direction: once the requests to the left are exhausted, it turns around and takes the nearest one to the right, which is 82.

questions.question:
On a 200-cylinder disk (cylinders 0 to 199) the head is at cylinder 60. The pending requests, in arrival order, are 82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16, 190, 51. Under FCFS, what is the total head movement, in cylinders?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FCFS serves the queue in arrival order, so the head simply follows the request sequence wherever it goes.

Step by step.

  1. Movement is the sum of the absolute differences between consecutive positions, starting at 60.
  2. |60−82| = 22, |82−170| = 88, |170−43| = 127, |43−140| = 97.
  3. |140−24| = 116, |24−16| = 8, |16−190| = 174, |190−51| = 139.
  4. Total = 22 + 88 + 127 + 97 + 116 + 8 + 174 + 139 = 771.

Answer: 771 cylinders.

Common misconception. Sorting the queue first. That computes SSTF or SCAN, not FCFS; FCFS is defined by arrival order and its whole cost is the zig-zag it produces.

questions.question: How does C-LOOK differ from C-SCAN?
options: C-LOOK reverses direction at the last pending request instead of at the end of the disk, so it never travels to cylinder 0 or 199 unnecessarily
C-LOOK serves requests strictly in arrival order
C-LOOK keeps one queue per cylinder and serves them round robin
C-LOOK never reverses the direction of the head
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The LOOK family stops at the last request in the current direction instead of continuing to the physical end of the disk; C-LOOK adds the circular return of C-SCAN to that economy.

Step by step.

  1. C-SCAN sweeps to the last cylinder, jumps back to cylinder 0 without servicing, and sweeps again, so wait times are uniform.
  2. C-LOOK does the same circular sweep but turns around at the highest (or lowest) pending request, so the empty travel to the disk edge is avoided.
  3. Its total head movement is therefore never larger than that of C-SCAN on the same queue.
  4. It does reverse, and it does not serve in arrival order, so the other options describe FCFS or a multi-queue policy.

Answer: Option (A) — it turns at the last request instead of the disk edge.

Common misconception. Confusing LOOK with SCAN. SCAN goes to the end of the disk because the head has no way of knowing where the last request is; LOOK uses that knowledge, which is what saves the travel.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the SCAN, C-SCAN and LOOK policies are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: LOOK reverses direction at the last pending request rather than at the end of the disk.
C-SCAN treats the cylinders as a circular list and returns to the start without servicing, so waiting times are more uniform than under SCAN.
Under SCAN, a request that lies just behind the head's direction of travel waits almost a full sweep.
SSTF always minimises the total head movement over the whole pending queue.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The sweep policies trade optimal movement for bounded waiting: SCAN bounds the wait to about two sweeps, C-SCAN makes it uniform, and LOOK removes the travel beyond the last request.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: LOOK is SCAN that stops at the outermost pending request.
  2. (B) is true: the circular return gives every cylinder roughly one service per revolution, so no region waits much longer than another.
  3. (C) is true: that region is served last on the return leg, after the whole opposite side has been covered.
  4. (D) is false: SSTF is greedy and can be beaten. On the queue 82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16, 190, 51 from head 60, SSTF moves 218 cylinders while LOOK also moves 218 but a different order can do better on other queues; optimality would require trying every order, which is the travelling-salesman problem.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Believing SSTF is optimal because each of its steps is optimal. Greedy choices minimise the next seek, not the total; the shortest total is a TSP path and is not computed by any of these heuristics.

questions.question: On a 200-cylinder disk (cylinders 0 to 199) the head is at cylinder 60 and is moving toward cylinder 0. The pending requests, in arrival order, are 82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16, 190, 51. Under SCAN, and counting the travel to cylinder 0, what is the total head movement in cylinders?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. SCAN is the elevator: the head finishes the current direction as far as the end of the disk, then reverses and serves everything on the way back.

Step by step.

  1. Moving down from 60, the requests met in order are 51, 43, 24 and 16: 9 + 8 + 19 + 8 = 44 cylinders.
  2. The head continues to cylinder 0 because SCAN does not stop at the last request: 16 more cylinders.
  3. Reversing, it serves 82, 140, 170 and 190 in that order: 82 + 58 + 30 + 20 = 190 cylinders.
  4. Total = 44 + 16 + 190 = 250 cylinders.

Answer: Option (B) — 250 cylinders.

Common misconception. Answering 218, which is LOOK: it omits the 16 cylinders from 16 down to 0. SCAN, unlike LOOK, is defined to reach the edge of the disk.

questions.question: A file has permission mode 755. Which one of the following describes it?
options: owner read, write and execute; group read and execute; others read and execute
owner read and write; group read and write; others read
owner, group and others all read, write and execute
owner read; group read and execute; others no permission
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A three-digit octal mode is three 3-bit groups: owner, group and others, each holding read (4), write (2) and execute (1).

Step by step.

  1. 7 = 4 + 2 + 1, so the owner has read, write and execute.
  2. 5 = 4 + 1, so the group has read and execute but not write.
  3. The last 5 gives others the same rights as the group.
  4. 755 is therefore the standard mode of a directory or of an executable that everyone may run but only the owner may change.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Reading 755 as “everyone can write”. The middle digit is a 5, not a 7; group and others can read and execute but not modify.

questions.question: The set-group-ID bit is set on a directory. What is its effect?
options: files created inside the directory inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group
every file in the directory becomes executable by the group
the directory can be listed only by its owner
members of the group may delete any file in the directory
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. On a directory the set-group-ID bit is an inheritance rule for the group of new files; on an executable file the set-user-ID bit is an elevation rule for the effective user ID.

Step by step.

  1. Without the bit, a new file takes the creator's primary group, which may not be the group that owns the directory.
  2. With it, a new file takes the group of the directory, so a shared project directory keeps every file in the project group.
  3. The mode bits of existing files are unchanged; only the group of newly created entries is affected.
  4. Deletion is controlled by write and execute permission on the directory and, in a sticky directory, by ownership of the file.

Answer: Option (A) — new files inherit the directory's group.

Common misconception. Confusing the set-group-ID bit on a directory with the set-user-ID bit on a program. The first changes ownership of new files; the second runs a program with the file owner's privileges.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Unix directory permissions are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Traversing a path through a directory requires execute permission on that directory.
A directory with read but no execute permission can be listed, yet a file inside it cannot be opened even when its name is known.
The sticky bit on a world-writable directory stops users from deleting files they do not own.
The group permission bits apply to every user who is not the owner.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Read permission on a directory means “may list the names in it”, write means “may create or remove entries”, and execute means “may pass through it”. The three are independent.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: each component of a path must be searchable, which is what execute permission grants.
  2. (B) is true: ls needs read, but resolving name inside the directory needs execute, so the open fails with permission denied.
  3. (C) is true: with the sticky bit set, only the file's owner, the directory's owner or root may unlink an entry.
  4. (D) is false: the group bits apply only to members of the file's group; a user who is neither the owner nor in the group falls through to the other bits.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Treating execute on a directory as “may run the directory”. On a directory, x means search, and without it every path that passes through the directory is unusable.

questions.question:
A file must be readable, writable and executable by its owner, readable and executable by its group, and inaccessible to everyone else. What is its permission mode as a three-digit octal number?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each permission triple is one octal digit formed by adding read = 4, write = 2 and execute = 1.

Step by step.

  1. Owner: read + write + execute = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7.
  2. Group: read + execute = 4 + 1 = 5.
  3. Others: nothing = 0.
  4. The mode is therefore 750, which is also the standard mode of a private directory.

Answer: 750.

Common misconception. Writing 755 out of habit. The group digit is 5, and others must be 0 here, so the answer cannot end in a non-zero digit.

questions.question: An access matrix is implemented with access-control lists, one list per object. Which one of the following questions becomes expensive to answer?
options: may subject s read object o
which objects may subject s read
who may read object o
may the owner of object o change its mode
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An access-control list is stored with the object, so it answers “who may do what to this object” quickly and the transpose question slowly.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is cheap: look up the object's list and check the entry for s.
  2. (B) is expensive: nothing records the objects per subject, so every object's list must be scanned.
  3. (C) is cheap: the list is already indexed by subject.
  4. (D) is a matter of ownership and mode, not of the matrix at all.
  5. A capability list stores the transpose and reverses the costs, which is why systems keep both views for different operations.

Answer: Option (B) — enumerating all objects a subject may read.

Common misconception. Thinking an ACL is slow for the common check. It is optimised for exactly that check; what it cannot do is answer questions asked from the subject's side.

questions.question: What does the umask of a process control?
options: the maximum size a file created by the process may reach
the permission bits that are removed from the default mode of every file the process creates
the list of users who may log in as the process owner
the group that owns the files the process creates
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The umask is a per-process mask of permission bits. A new file is created with a default mode (0666 for a file, 0777 for a directory) and the mask is subtracted from it bit by bit.

Step by step.

  1. With umask 022, a file created with default 0666 gets 0666 & ~022 = 0644.
  2. With umask 077, the same default gives 0600, a private file.
  3. The mask can only remove bits, never add them, so it can tighten permissions but cannot grant them.
  4. It has nothing to do with size limits, login lists or group ownership, which are controlled by other mechanisms.

Answer: Option (B) — the bits removed from the default mode of new files.

Common misconception. Reading the mask as the permissions granted. It is subtracted from the default; a mask of 022 leaves 644, it does not produce 022.
